Atlanta Constitution: "Alf Starr is wanted in Hampton for larceny. Early Thursday morning he stole a black cloth coat, $200 in money, and one note for $150 from a gentleman in that place. Starr is about 35 years of age, 5 feet 10 inches high, weighs 165 pounds, is a square-built yellow fellow. He gambles a great deal, and has been shot in the mouth."

Atlanta Post-Appeal: "Rapacious landlords who have been going about raising rents are beginning to discover that the boom has not struck just where they thought it had. Some tenants have been notified to pay higher rents or quit, and in some cases they have done the latter. In other cases they remain, protesting against the raise and being determined to seek other quarters. The landlord's craze will drive many to the occupancy of less pretentious quarters, or to obtaining property of their own, in which they will be advance-proof. There is a prospect that there will be places to rent at very reasonable prices just as soon as the Exposition is fairly over."

Atlanta Constitution: "Senator Hawes perfected and passed a bill on the usury question which makes some important changes. The maximum charged is still fixed by law at eight per cent, but under the new bill the lender has the right to charge whatever rate the borrow agrees upon, and can collect the same if the borrower does not appeal to the law against paying. If this is done, the lender is mulct only for the surplus of the interest above eight per cent, and not for the entire interest as under the present law. It also becomes incumbent upon the borrower to show that the lender has violated the law, and it does not devolve upon the lender to shoulder the burden of proof as under the present law."

Hawkkinsville Dispatch: "Mr. John P. Lee and his wife, May Lee, of Twiggs county, are aged respectively seventy-two years. They have reared eleven children, ten of whom are now living, and all married except the youngest son, who is twenty-seven years old, and still lives with his parents. The oldest is Mrs. Eliza Brown, aged fifty-one years. This aged couple have, in all their family, one hundred and thirteen children, fourteen of whom are great grandchildren. Mr. Lee has lived on his present place, in Twiggs county, thirty-five years, and has never purchased but sixteen bushels of corn in his life. Up to the 1st of August of this year he had three hundred bushels of old corn in the crib."

A special to the Macon Telegraph and Messenger, dated Blakely, Ga., September 29th, says: "Last night, between the hours of 12 and 1 o'clock, a party consisting of about a dozen masked men went to the residence of the jailer and demanded the jail key, which he refused to deliver, but was compelled under the muzzles of pistols to surrender to them. A guard remained with the jailer, when the balance proceeded to the jail, opened it and shot to death Zandy Wright, a negro, who was serving a sentence of imprisonment for hog stealing. His time would have expired in about ten days. He had a bad reputation, and on several occasions during his imprisonment he threatened, when released, to kill several persons, including the jailer. The affair is greatly regretted by the quiet and peaceable citizens of Blakely."

McDuffe Journal: "On Friday morning last Mr. Hillman Reeves, who lives in the vicinity of Dearing, in this county, committed suicide by jumping into a well. On the day before he attempted to cut his throat, but was prevented, and a watch kept on his movements. He was sitting at the breakfast table on Friday morning, when he suddenly arose and rushed out of the house and jumped into the well in the yard. His brother and a young man named Luckey, who were seated at the table with him, endeavored to catch him before he reached the well, but failed. The water in the well was twenty feet deep, and the unfortunate man did not come to the surface after he went under. Help was summoned, and with a pair of pot hooks attached to a rope they commenced to fish for the body. They succeeded in bringing the body to the top of the water, when a rope was tied to it and it was drawn out. Mr. Reeves was subject to spells of aberration of the mind, and it is supposed that the act was committed while under the influence of one of these spells."

Marietta Journal: "Sheriff Coryell arrested last Wednesday week Mr. Thomas Roddy, at this place, on the authority of a telegram from the Sheriff of Polk county. Mr. Roddy's attorneys, the Messrs. Winn, sued out a writ of habeas corpus, and Roddy went to trial before Judge Hammett, Ordinary of Cobb county. A. S. Clay, Esq., represented Sheriff Coryell, and the case was hotly contested. After a patient hearing, Roddy was discharged on the ground that a telegram was not sufficient to hold a prisoner. Sheriff Coryell rearrested Roddy and said he was ready for another habeas corpus; that he would continue to arrest him as he was discharged. As no further writ was sued out, Roddy was kept in custody until the arrival of the Sheriff of Polk county, who carried him back with him. A KENTUCKY FRACAS. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

LOUISVILLE, Ky., Oct. 2.—This morning about 1:30 a desperate affray occurred at a party at the house of a farmer about nine miles from this city named John Fruchtonleht, between three young farmers, his neighbors, named S. P. Waller, David Stowers, and Richard Carrio, in which Stowers was shot through the pericardium and died almost instantly. Waller was shot through the brain, the ball having entered the right front of the head and passed diagonally through the head, and by Dr. J. M. Holloway today cut out from under the skin over the left posterior lobe. He has been unconscious over since receiving the shot, and, though removed to his home, no hopes are entertained of his recovery. Carrio received desperate wounds, but their nature could not be learned, as he fled, and the officers have been thus far unable to find him, although he was traicked a long way by bloodmarks from his wounds.

SHOT TO DEATH BY A MOB.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

ATLANTA, Ga., Oct. 21—Last night a negro named Sandy Wright, in jail in Early County, was shot to death while in his cell by a party of masked men. The men went to the jailer and compelled him, under the muzzle of cocked pistols, to surrender the keys of the jail. Having done this, one of the maskers remained with the jailer at his house to guard him, while the others visited the jail, where they found Wright, and shot him to death with pistols. Wright was serving out a sentence imposed for horr-stealing. The term of sentence would have expired in about ten days. It is stated that Wright had a bad reputation, and had been heard to make threats that he would kill the jailer and several other residents of Early County when he got out. The names of none of the men are known, and there is little hope that any of the guilty parties will ever be brought before the courts of that section.

FARMERS SWINDLED.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

LEVENWORTH, Kas., Oct. 2.—The old way of swindling farmers, it has just been disclosed, has been worked very successfully in the adjacent portion of Kansas and Missouri. The swindlers represented themselves as agents of a grocery house, and obtained the signatures of their victims to orders for goods, which orders eventually turned up in the banks for collection as a genuine promissory note.

WOUNDED BY A SHOT.

Louisville, Ky., Oct. 2.—A shooting match occurred at Jeffersonville, Ind., about 9 o'clock tonight. It seems that George Cook was passing Mrs. Willis' house, and that Mrs. Willis made some remark to him, when he turned and insulted her. One of Willis' boys, hearing the remark, got a knife and demanded an apology. Cook refused to give it, whereupon Willis drew a pistol and shot twice at Cook, wounding him in the leg below the thigh.

DEATH OF A HACK-DRIVER.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., Oct. 2.—A hack-driver named Jim Adair, a notorious character, known as "Slim Jim," fatally stabbed another hack-driver named Thomas Grady, near the Union depot. The dispute arose about the joint payment of a hack bill. Adair and Grady were drunk and had been riding together. Grady was stabbed in eight places, the blade breaking off in the last cut. Adair escaped into Kansas.

THOUGHT HE WAS INSULTED.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., Oct. 2.—A colored man named Tom Androws was shot and killed by a young man named Bucher, in a livery stable at West Port, four miles from here, shortly before midnight tonight. Bucher thought the negro was insulting him, and drawing a pistol, shot him dead. Bucher is a son of ex-Marshal Bucher, who was killed by Billy Gossard about two years rgo.

KILLED IN A BARROOM.

PHILADELPHIA, Pa., Oct. 2.—A brawl in Deputy-Sheriff Smyth's barroom late last night resulted in the death of John Kistel, 23 years of age, residing at Thirteenth and Kalor streets, by blows with the list dealt by William Johnson. The cause of the quarrel was a trivial dispute about a oligar which Kistel had snatched from Johnson's pocket.

CONVICTED OF MANSLAUGH TER.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
WICHITA, Kau., Oct. 1.—In the case of the State against Orrin Traup, charged with murder, the jury returned a verdict of guilty of manslaughter in the third degree. The punishment under the laws of Kansas cannot exceed three years' imprisonment in the penitentiary. The case was warmly contested.

FOUL PLAY SUSPECTED.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
RACINE, Wis., Oct. 2.—Tonight the body of a man was discovered in the lake seven miles north of the city. He had a loaded satchel tied to his body, and it is suspected that death resulted from foul play. He was dressed in a suit of black broadcloth.

PARDONED.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
SPRINGFIELD, Ill., Oct. 2.—The Governor has pardoned Leonard Leary, who was convicted of forgery by the Knox County Circuit Court in April and sent to the penitentiary for one year. The pardon was recommended by the Judge and State's-Attorney.

IOWA MORTGAGES.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune
McGheeon, Ia., Oct. 2.—Gov. Gear some time ago requested the Recorders of the different counties in the State to find out the aggregate amount of money secured by mortgages remaining unsatisfied upon the records of their respective counties. The following is the statement for Chayton County: On real property, land, $1,754,915; on real property, town, $916,630; on personal property, $430,410. Total, $2,916,355.

REPORTED GOLD-MINE DISCOVERY.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune
LEAVENWORTH, Kas., Oct. 2.—There is much excitement about three miles from this city, in Missouri, by the report that a gold mine has been discovered on the farm of Frank Olvis, who has several hands engaged in digging down a bluff where the institutions were first discovered. Quartz rock has been discovered, and the impression is that a little further down gold of some other mineral will be reached.

Four boys were stealing a ride in a freight-car loaded with corn when the train ran off the track near Morrison, Ill., and the car they were in turned over, and all were smothered to death.

PARNELL spoke at a great open-air meeting in Dublin yesterday, and advised tenants to refuse the benefits of the Land act unless such benefits could be shared by the laborers and artisans of all classes.

Among other things promised by Turkey and not performed is the suppression of the slave trade. The Porte's long delay and inaction in this matter has called forth from the British Ambassador at Constantinople an urgent request that the treaty provisions on the subject of the traffic in human chattels be faithfully observed.

Ir required very little provocation Saturday night in Earl County, Georgia, to organize a mob of masked men, force an entrance to the jail, and shoot to death with pistols a negro prisoner named Sandy Wright. His offense was stealing hogs, and his imprisonment would have ended in ten days, but it was said he had made threats to kill the jailer and several other citizens when he got out; and hence the action of the mob.

PROF. SWING, at the Central Church, preached yesterday upon the theme, "Moral Light"; the Rev. S. E./Wishard, at the Fifth Presbyterian Church, upon "Prayer and Its Answer" considered in relation to the sickness and death of President Garfield; the Rev. E. C. Oggel, at Westminster Presbyterian Church, upon "President Arthur"; while at the dedication of St. John's Roman Catholic Church, a new and imposing edifice at the corner of Clark and Eighteenth streets, the sermon was preached by Bishop Ryan, of St. Louis. At Park Avenue Methodist Church the Rev. Thomas Harrison concluded his revival labors, preaching a characteristic sermon.

A sermon upon the death and funeral of President Garfield was preached in Cincinnati by the Rev. Isaac Errett, who delivered the funeral oration at Cleveland. The discourse mainly had reference to President Garfield's religious faith and convictions, and the speaker, who is eminently qualified to bear testimony on this point, having been the pastor of the church which the President attended, was able to say in well-chosen words that James A. Garfield was himself "a royal priest of God, by virtue of his anointing as a Christian, and needed none save the one Mediator between God and man to intercede for him with the Father." "Far better," said he, "than any death-bed testimony is the grand life of James A. Garfield."

The very absurd reflections of the senior Conkling spoils organ of this city as to what "might have been" if Mr. Potter Palmer had voted his colored waiters for the third term at the Third Ward primaries have been copied into the New York Herald. We do not object to this if the Herald has any taste for misinformation of that nature; but we do decidedly resent the crediting of the article in question to THE CHICAGO TRIBUNE. Not only is it true that THE TRIBUNE did not originally print that choice collection of blunders and absurdities, but it did expose them most thoroughly. It showed that there was not a word of truth in the article; that it had no application to the Third Ward; and that the First Ward, where some such incidents as these related did occur, was given to the third term on a mock contest at Springfield. THE TRIBUNE sympathizes deeply with Mr. Potter Palmer in this new affliction. If any

person in this wide world is at the present moment little interested in the reminiscences of the third term that person must be Mr. Palmer, who is widely known as a Tilden and Hancock Democrat, and whose hotel both in 1876 and 1880 was a headquarters for the Democratic party in Cook County.

The first case to be given to the District of Columbia grand jury today will be that of Gulteau, whose indictment for murder is of course a foregone conclusion. He will be taken secretly to the court to plead to the indictment, and if possible returned to the jail without the knowledge of the public—a precaution considered necessary in order to avoid the danger of an attack upon the worthless life of the wretch. A continuance will be asked for by Gulteau's counsel, and the trial will probably be set for some time in November, by which time the assasin hopes that the popular rage against him will have subsided. He is represented as in mortal terror of his life, but at the same time vastly pleased at the prospect of the prominence he will attain on the occasion of the trial.

Another peaceful and law-abiding Illinois community narrowly escaped a lynching horror yesterday similar to that of Saturday night at Bloomington. Otto Freese, of Aurora, while returning home with some members of a singing club from a scenading tour late Saturday evening was stabbed in the neck by Thomas Olsen, a youth of 17, and bled to death in twenty minutes. The assault was utterly unprovoked, as the party of singers had given no cause of offense to Olsen and his two companions, all of whom had been indulging in liquor. A large number of citizens repaired to the jail at 2 o'clock Sunday morning, provided with ropes, intending to lynch the murderer, but he had been secretly removed to another place of confinement half an hour before. It will some of these days be considered unsafe to commit wanton murder in Illinois.

The decision of the Supreme Court in the cases of the county officers whose terms were extended, it seems, by the amendment to the State Constitution, is final. The court decided that the new section went into force and effect as soon as the vote was canvassed and declared adopting it, and the old section thus superseded was abolished and discarded. The new section made no provision for holding an election in 1881 for a one-year term of County Treasurers and Clerks and Probate Judges, but was intended to continue the term of the existing officers for a year, and the statute passed by the last Legislature to carry this intention into effect is valid. The court consists of seven Judges; four of these—Judges Dickey, Craig, Mulkey, and Scott—united in the judgment of the court, but Judge Scott differed widely from the others as to the reasons given for the judgment. This judgment was that the officers held over until the election in 1882. Judges Walker, Sheldon, and Scholfield dissented from this judgment. The only interest on the part of the general public was in having the case decided, so that there would be no room for disputed elections this fall. In deciding that the officers may hold over until 1882 the Court set aside the two opposing theories that there would have to be an election in 1881 and that the offices would be vacant this fall and would have to be filled, the judicial offices by the Governor, and the others by the County Boards. The matter is now settled, and next year there will be a new deal at the election then.

counts footed up $335,112.

Medals in memory of President Garfield are to be struck at the Philadelphia Mint.

A gold mine has been discovered in Missouri, a few miles from Leavenworth, Kas.

Twelve buildings in Warren, Pa., were burned on Saturday morning. Loss $50,000.

An old man lost his balance by kicking at his wife, in Louisville, and was killed by the fall.

John Kistel was killed on Sunday at Philadelphia in a fight with William Johnson over a cigar.

It is proposed to erect a Garfield monument on Little Mountain, Ohio, 1,000 feet above Lake Erie.

A disease which first manifests itself in blindness has appeared among cows in portions of Bucks county.

In Dallas, Texas, a woman is gradually becoming petrified. Her feet and hands are already as hard as stone.

Caleb Fiske Harris and his wife, of Providence, R. I., were drowned on Sunday night in Moosehead Lake.

Andy Wright, a negro prisoner in the jail at Blakely, Ga., was taken out and lynched Sunday morning.

Sylvester Fretz, of Pottstown, who shot himself in the brain with two balls, nearly three weeks ago, is still living.

It is said that this State possesses more flour mills and manufactures more flour than any other State in the Union.

Thomas Stinson, who murdered his wife in Chester on the 18th ultimo and then cut his own throat, has died of his injuries.

A clergyman in Wales preached on the President's death, from the text: "I am distressed for thee, my Brother Jonathan."

A grain car at Round Grove, Illinois, was upset Tuesday morning and four boys, who had been stealing a ride, were killed.

Moses Young, of Steelton, Dauphin county, has a peach tree which now bears its second crop of ripe peaches for this summer.

Ex-Governor Franklin J. Moses, of South Carolina, was arrested in New York city on Monday for obtaining $25 by false pretepses.

Miss Sarah Downs, of Honesdale, Wayne county, while despondent because of ill-health, committed suicide last week by drowning.

A horse that had four bullets extracted from his body during the war is now doing ordinary farm work for Solomon Moist, near Gettysburg.

—Herr Krupp, of Essen, Germany, has'accepted a contract for the exportation of twenty-five thousand tons of steel rails to the United States.

—Henry Metzgar was hanged on Saturday at Titusville, Fla., for the murder of Moore. He said he had killed seven men. He died unrepentant.

—A piece of petrified bread has been found jin Iberville Parish, La. No clue to the mystery, as there is no railroad lunch counter in the neighborhood.

—Milton Rowe, of Paradise, Lancaster county, several weeks ago ran a splinter into his hand. The wound inflamed and he died of lock-jaw on Saturday last.

—Three men stole ten $1,000 bonds from a table at which their owner, Mr. S. T. Burton, was sitting in the Lafayette Bank, Cincinnati on Saturday morning.

—Charles Pierce, a young fellow of 20 in the Bloomington, Ill., jail, killed Teddy Franks, the jailor, and was taken out and hanged by a mob of 5,000 people.

—Sylvester Edsell, of Ridgbury, Bradford county, on Thursday, while cutting down a large oak got in the way of the falling tree and was crushed to a shapeless mass.

—The widow of President Lincoln is in a sad state of mind over the murder of President Garfield and fears that her son, the Secretary of War, will be assassinated.

—Miss Mary Lamphier died at Rochester, N. Y., aged 100 years, 1 month and 3 days. Up to the day of her death she could see to read, sew and knit without the aid of grasses.

—A rural dance on the farm of Henry Buchternecht, nine miles below Louisville, on Saturday night, wound up in the murder of David Slowers and mortal injury of Zula Walters.

—A weeping widower fell into his wife's grave during a funeral at Decatur, Ill., and as he climbed out his language was so shockingly profane that the clergy man felt compelled to reprove him.

—Signor La Andre, the man with the iron jaw, while performing at the State Fair, at Indianapolis on Friday night, holding a barrel of water and two men in his teeth, let go his hold and was fatally crushed.

—Patrick Kilcourse, of Chester, convived last week of murder in the second degree for killing his wife in July last, was sentenced at Media on Tuesday to twelve years solitary confinement in the penitentiary.

While being driven at full speed and in opposite disections around the race course at the Lehigh county fair at Allentown, two fast horses collided, instantly killing both. One was valued at $500, the other at $5,000.

On Monday a loafer in Erie carelessly discharged a revolver, which went through a window glass and shot a young lady in the nose. The same day a similar accident occurred in Reading, shooting a lady in the hand.

Mrs. Mary Craig, weighing 800 pounds, died at Danville, Ind., on Monday night. She was known as Barnum's "Fat Woman," and was an inmate of his museum when it was burned. Her husband is about the same size.

At Bunker Hili, Smith county, Miss., on Friday night last, H. O. Eaton, Daniel Hathorn, and Dick Yawn resumed an old feud. Hathorn shot and killed Eaton, and Yawn at once shot and killed Hathorn. Both died instantly.

The body of a young woman named Nellie Wright was found in the Erie Canal at Albion, N. Y., last Sunday. A letter in her pocket caused a young farmer of the neighborhood to be suspected of her murder and he has been arrested.

Laborers are very scarce in Ottawa, Ont. The agents of the French Phosphate Mining Company stood at the doors of the Catholic churches in Hull, opposite that city, on Sunday and offered advanced rates for 200 men to work in the mines.

The Nashville American says that President Garfield's assassination is the first national event which has called forth from the women of the South a wide and profound sympathy. This, it says, is a sign of restoration worth all the rest.

James Freeman's grandson, aged 9, of Gray's Mills, Mass., being offended at the little daughter of Allen Harris, aged 2 years, blindfolded the child on Friday last and threw her into a well one hundred feet deep, where she was found dead.

A remarkable clock has been set up in the municipal library of Rouen. It goes for fourteen months without rewinding, and shows the hour and the day of the month. It was originally constructed in 1782, but underwent some alterations in 1816.

George R. McClellan, a Syracuse, N. Y., photographer, lost $1,000 through the flight of his partner, went on a spree, and insulted Miss Burnett, a mail-carrier, on a lonely road. She beat him ovsr the head with a whip and McClellan susequently died.

The boiler in La Duc & Phinney's car factory at Carrollton, Mich., exploded on Sunday night. John and James Picard, brothers, were killed, and damage to the extent of $7000 was done. The explosion was caused by a lack of water in the boiler.

PERSONAL AND GENERAL.
made a balloon ascension with Prof. Tony White at the Guernsey County Fair, Washington. The balloon in descending caught upon a tree top and pitched Cowen out. He died within two hours from the effect of his injuries.

THE Marquis of Lorne and suite have invaded United States territory, being reported at Helena, Mont., on the 1st. They will return to Ontario via Omaha.

THE profits of the chief cotton "cornerer" in the London market, are estimated at a quarter to half million pounds.

GOVERNOR SHELDON, of New Mexico, has organized eight companies of Indian fighters, and has made a requisition upon the General Government for arms and ammunition.

SEVERAL Nebraska towns suffered severely from the recent tornado. At Madison and Stanton a large number of houses were demolished and a number of persons injured, some fatally.

ABSTRACT of public debt statement issued Oct. 1: Decrease of debt during September, $17,483,641; cash in the Treasury, $250,686,547; gold certificates, $5,248,920; silver certificates, $64,149,910; certificates of deposit outstanding, $8,315,000; refunding certificates, $639,950; legal tenders outstanding, $346,741,056; fractional currency outstanding, $7,098,506.

Disastrous floods have occurred throughout the Northwest.

T. P. O'Connor, a prominent Land Leaguer, is coming to the United States on a lecturing tour under the auspices of the League.

JASPER DELAUGHTER, under arrest for burglarizing the store of T. J. Wright in the southwestern part of the Choctaw Nation, was taken from the Deputy Marshal while being conveyed to Fort Smith and hanged by a mob of masked men.

Official notice is given that the importation into Russia of galvanic batteries, induction coils and insulated wires will be subject to the same rules of inspection as the importation of arms.

ANDY WRIGHT, a colored desperado, confined in the Blakely (Ga.) Jail for hog stealing, was taken out by a mob and shot.

The Swiss town of Nyon has been nearly destroyed by fire of an incendiary origin.

HON. GEORGE W. FOSTER, Minister to Russia, now home on a visit, has tendered his resignation. Mr. Foster is an ardent Blaine man.

JOHN MAGINNIS, a Philadelphia coal-peddler, shot and killed his wife and mother-in-law because they failed to notify him of the death of his child. The father and mother had been separated for some time.

The suspension of Preston & Mc Henry, of Chicago, has squeezed several grain firms. Half a million dollars in margins are up and $200,000 remain due to different houses with which trades were had.

While Mr. S. H. Burton was in the safety deposit of Lafayette Bank, Cincinnati, cutting coupons from four per cent bonds, three men came in. One of them occupied the President of the bank, another engaged Mr. Burton in conversation, while a third got away with ten bonds, each of a thousand dollars, making $10,000, and the three men escaped undetected.

At Gray's Mills, Miss., the nine-year-old grandson of James Freeman, offended at some action on the part of a two-year-old daughter of Allen Harris, blindfolded her and threw her down a well, where she was found dead.

HENRY METZAR was executed at Titusville, Fla., on the 1st, for the murder of an inoffensive old man named Moore. The condemned confessed the crime, and said he had killed seven men in his lifetime. He was unrepentant to the last.

JACOB WHITMORE, a young farmer residing near Bellefontaine, O., recently married a 14-year-old girl. The other day he took his wife into the woods on a nutting expedition, and while there forced her to swallow a white powder, threatening to cut her throat if she refused. Whitmore returned home alone, but was soon followed by his victim, suffering intensely from cramps, from which she was relieved by death at midnight, revealing her husband's guilt only when assured she could not live.

A RURAL dance on the farm of Henry Brichternicht, near Louisville, Ky., wound up with the murder of David Stowers and the mortal injury of Seula Walker. One of these men previously insulted Dick Carico, who on meeting them asked which was the man who had insulted him. There was a grabbing for revolvers, in which Carico did the quickest and most fatal work.

In New York City, the other day, Frederick Wagner, a saloon-keeper, quarreled with his wife, and, having turned down the gaslight in his apartments, quietly introduced a fierce and powerful blood-hound, unleashed him and set the brute on the unfortunate woman. The dog seized her by the neck and arms, lacerating and tearing the flesh badly. Her cries of distress brought a policeman, who rescued her and shot the hound. The other was fined $5.

The dead body of Nellie Wright, a beautiful girl of 20, was found floating in the canal near Albion, N. Y. The post mortem examination showed that she had not come to her death by drowning, and a number of contusions upon her head and body gave evidence that she had been foully dealt with. A man named Fred. Hopkins, with whom she had been intimate, has been arrested, charged with her murder. The parents of the girl are small farmers in the vicinity, but for some years she had not lived at home, but worked around at various places.

WHILE Ralph Durbin and wife and daughter, aged 19, and a Miss Buck, sister of Mrs. Durbin, and three small children were returning from church at Danville, Knox County, O., they attempted to cross a stream subject to high floods. Mrs. Durbin, Miss Durbin and Miss Buck were drowned. Mr. Durbin got out by his own effort, and Mr. James Shellabarger rescued the children.

The graveyard insurance business in Pennsylvania is assuming alarming proportions. At Wilkesbarre, within a month, four old people have died under suspicious circumstance, all of whom were heavily insured by outside speculators.

FATHER CONWAY, parish priest of Clonbur, Ireland, has been sentenced to two months' imprisonment, with hard labor, for assaulting a bailiff who served him with a writ at the suit of Lord Ardilaun. Notice of appeal was given.

The Treasury Department states that there are still outstanding over $21,000,000 in bonds on which interest has ceased, some of which should have been offered for redemption eleven years ago. They will be promptly paid off when presented, but it is probable that most of them have been destroyed.

An earthquake at Changeria, Anatolia, in Asiatic Turkey, killed eleven persons. The Grand Mosque and many buildings were greatly damaged.

CALEB F. HARRIS and wife, of Providence, R. I., were drowned in Moosehead Lake.

Mrs. GREEN, residing on the York-town Pike, near Muncie, Ind., was seriously shot in the breast from a toy pistol in the hands of a young son.

John and James Pickard, brothers, were killed by a boiler explosion at Carrollton, Mich.

Four boys were stealing a ride in a freight-car loaded with corn, when the train ran off the track near Morrison, Ill., the car they were in turned over, and all were smothered to death.

Orson Pratt, the oldest Apostle of the Mormon Church, is dead, aged 70.

Gov. Cullom, of Illinois, has issued a proclamation offering $500 reward for the arrest of the notorious Williams brothers, whose last murderous offense was the killing of Sheriff Lammy, of Calhoun County. They are believed to be still secreted in the vicinity.

The insurgents in Tunis are charged with fresh outrages. At Wadzergha a railway station was fired and ten employees massacred. The station-master, an ex-Lieutenant in the French army and a Chevalier of the Legion of Honor, was burned alive.

They are supposed to be three men who have been robbing travelers the past week in that section, and are thought to have been hanged by German farmers of the section referred to.

bandera-bandera-1881-12.A5:
LATEST TELEGRAMS CONDENSED.
Friday night Mrs. Martin, of Nokomis, Illinois, wife of the proprietor of the Shelbyville Union, accidentally fell down a cellarway and was fatally hurt.

Kinnie, taken to Dubuque, Iowa, recently on a charge of stealing postage stamps, was carried to Indiana Saturday, on a requisition for burglary.

A fire at Knoxville, Iowa, on the morning of the 17th inst., destroyed 12 business houses, with a loss of $$0,000. Supposed to be the work of an incendiary.

A man named Kelley, living near Tecumseh, Michigan, attempted to cut his throat Saturday, but failing in that hung himself. No cause is assigned.

Miss Lulu Barnes, of Camp township, Iowa, a sixteen-year-old girl, was found by her parents on the 17th instant, hanging by the neck, dead. No cause is known for the rash act.

J. Howard Wells, who attempted to blackmail Jay Gould has been admitted to bail on a $1,500 bond. The President of the Manhattan Gas Company became his bondsman.

Thieves entered the Mexico Woolen Mills and the Mexico City Flouring Mills at Mexico, Missouri, on Friday night last, and at each place blew open the safe. Their combined stealing was only $125.

The Trenton, New Jersey, court has granted an order placing about $100,000 worth of property belonging to Theodore and Oscar Baldwin in the hands of a receiver for the benefit of the creditors of the Merchants' National Bank.

A day or two ago, Michael Magher, recently removed from the office of Street Commissioner by the Mayor, was indicted under three different charges of misconduct, bribery and corruption. He was placed under $1,000 bond in each case.

George H. Curcon, a cousin of Dr. Tyng, of New York, and who in his day has filled his positions in the government service was discovered wandering around Santa Barbara, Cal., Friday with his throat cut though not fatally necessarily. Opium and morphine had made him insane.

Halloway, the defaulting teller of the Poughkeepsie bank, has been ordered by Judge Barnard, of Poughkeepsie, New York, to the Hudson River Hospital as an insane criminal, to be brought out for examination when the authorities say he is in proper condition.

Wm. Wixard, residing near Girard, Illinois, became suddenly deranged the other day and set fire to his residence. It was totally destroyed. Three small children were in the house, but escaped in their night clothes. He was finally captured and turned over to the Sheriff.

The bodies of three Mexicans were found hanging to a tree the other day near Bandera, this State. They are supposed to be the three parties who have been robbing travelers, and were probably lynched by the citizens, German farmers, of the neighborhood.

A man named Felds, living near Farber, Missouri, some time since had $243 stolen from him. His nephew, Woodson, living with him claimed to have lost $100 also. A young man, Franklin by name, was accused but proved not guilty. It now transpires that the nephew was the thief. He is now in jail at Mexico, Missouri.

It has been discovered by her confessions, that the wife of Henry Blankenship, who was killed a short time since near Newburg, Arkansas, was his murderer. They lived unhappily together, and she fearing he would kill her, stole into his room and killed him with an ax. Mrs. Blankenship is described as a handsome and facinating woman.

At Caldwell, Kansas, on Saturday, a party of cowboys, who were drinking, raised a row, and in an indiscriminate shooting affray between themselves and citizens, killed a gambler named Speer and a special policeman named Meagher. Meagher was an ex-mayor. The cowboys rode off pursued by citizens.

A mysterious fire occurred in Roth's kid glove store, in Cincinnati, a day or so ago. The private watchman noticed the gas out, and going to the door smelled smoke. Waking a clerk who slept next door, the door was opened and the building was discovered to be on fire. Firemen succeeded in confining the fire to the house, and the loss to stock was about $25,000. The origin of the fire remains a mystery.

A negro conjurer was fatally shot at Franklin, Virginia, on the 17th inst. He obtained a half dollar from an old darkey for a chain which he contended would lead to the discovery of a gold mine. His dupe, not finding the mine, got the town sergeant, who demanded the return of the half dollar. The conjurer refused the demand and attacked the officer, who shot him.

A horrible story comes from the Sandwich islands. A native missionary had been sent from Honolulu to one of the islands of the Gilbert group, and a number of conversions were made, whereupon the missionary levied tribute. Finally his demands became exorbitant and were refused. Thereupon he and his followers went into a wholesale butchery of the natives, outraged women and eat the dead. Returning to Honolulu the missionary was white-washed and made a bishop.

About seven months ago a negro named Bolen committed an outrage upon a white girl about seventeen years of age, Christian Hodges, they both being servants at the Central House, Indianola, Iowa. The girl kept the secret t'll her condition was revealed by nature and she then went to Des Moines and told Bolen he must take care of her. He took her to a Mrs. Moss' house on Saturday last. Mrs. Moss brutally assaulted her, causing a premature birth of her child and probably the death of the girl.

Reinsmidt, a farmer living in Washington Township, Iowa, recently sold his farm for $1,000. On the 17th inst. he saw faces around the window at night, and upon looking out received a shot, the ball fortunately striking a rib and glancing. Falling, he knocked out the light and the would-be murderers ran away, thinking the light had been purposely extinguished. Two young men of bad character in the neighborhood are suspected. Martelle, the man shot in the same county a few days since, died Saturday. Samuel Smith and his wife, of Manhasset, Long Island, have been married ten years and are parents of six children. GENERAL NEWS.
Two boys drowned at DesMoines, Iowa.

Geo. Peele was drowned at Oshkoshl, Wis.

Cincinnati had a $700,000 fire last week.

Adelphe Smith suicided at New Orleans by hanging.

Lightning killed a boy named Kraust at Milwaukee.

A negro was sunstruck at Madison, La, the first on record.

Wm. H. Stewart, suicided at Memphis, by taking Morphine.

Henry Schroeder was drowned while bathing at Evansville.

Four people were killed by a flash of lightning at Decatur, Ala.

There were eight cases of sunstroke in Cincinnati Friday, four of them fatal.

Miller and Lapham the nominees of the Albany Caucus are both Congress-
G. Field's life is insured for $25,000 in the Equitable Company of New York.

A son of Gen. Rossean, died in a Massachusetts poor house last week, a tramp.

Emory Speer the Georgia congressman denies that he has mahoned the Democratic party.

T. M. Williams killed Ira Reals at Grapeland, Texas, because they both loved the same girl.

A. J. McRae, a justice of the peace, was killed by a negro prisoner at Piuckney's Landing Ark.

A meteoric stone fell near Tusca loosa, Ala., with a loud report and buried itself in the ground.

Vice President Wilson's personal effects were sold at auction last week. A picture of Grant brought 15 cents.

Emory Speer, the Georgia Congressman, denies that he has gone over to the Republicans, but says he will vote with the Democrats.

Jas. McBride a veteran in the Soldier's Home at Dayton, O., was discharged because he ventured to express joy over the shooting of the President.

A negro church at cedar Grove Bibb county, Ala, was burned recently by white incendiaries. The next night negro incendiaries burned the white church.

A subscription fund amounting to over $300,000 has been made up and presented to Mrs. Garfield, by the New York Chamber of Commerce and some parties in London.

Jno Traynor and Olsen A. Swede two adventurers sailed from Bath, Me., July 5, in a devy fourteen feet long, twenty one inches deep, and five feet wide, the smallest craft in which passage across the Atlantic has ever been attempted. They were provisioned for 60 days.

Sheriff Nickler of Hernando county, Fla., left his three children with a negro named King, to whom he had been very kind. The ungrateful wretch murdered the children and robbed the house and attempted to waylay and murder their father but was detected lying in wait. He was arrested, and lynched after confessing his crime.

The question of who discovered the present comet has become a most momentous one. Over 500 persons have laid claim to the honor and the Warner prize of $200, and all of them are within comparatively the same time. It is desirable that no injustice be done in this matter, and to this end all parties who saw the comet during the week ending June 25th, or previously, will please forward their claims without delay to Prof. Swift, Director of the Warner Observatory, Rochester, N. Y. It is certain the discovery was made by a private individual, but who that individual is remains to be seen.

"Accute perception, readiness of repartee and affable manners," were the qualifications of a Logan county bride.

The Enterprise says that jail men are flocking to Paducah in large numbers, attracted by the proposed building of a new jail.

Wood English was seriously cut on the arm and chest by Clint Stiff near Stephenport, in Breckenridge county, Saturday.

Dr. Fayette Dunlap, of Danville had been appointed Inspector at the Inspection Station on the Mississippi river, below Memphis.

A small boy touched off a pack of fire crackers in the pulpit of a Covington church during services, and came near breaking up the meeting.

MISCELLANEOUS.

General Bob Teombs was seventy-one Wednesday.

A Georgia editor raised a car-load of watermelons.

Several hydrophobia hogs have been killed at Huntsville, Ala.

Alexander H. Stephens has employed a stenographer for the summer.

A marble mine has been discovered on the farm of Epn. Erwin, a few miles from Columbia, Tenn,

The theory that a negro cannot be sun-struck is overthrown. A plantation darkey was a victim at Madison, La.

The Houston Age, a great turf paper says: At the Ascot Derby races Lorillard's filly, Iroquois was again victorious.

Vive le Savannah News! Its correspondent is the only one in the country who has had an interview with Guiteau.

Thirteen new babies have made their appearance on the streets in Warrenton, Ga, this year. The republic still goes on.

Yale college, at its recent commencement, conferred the degree of L L. D. upon Hon. N. H. Smith, chief justice of North Carolina.

All the astronomers unite in pronouncing it "Gould's comet." Is it possible that the great railroader is trying to corner the constellation?

While the south does not say that Conkling and Arthur are guilty of the attempted assassination, it does say that the utterances of the stalwarts were the cause.

Sparta, (Ga) Times: Emory Speer may ape Mahone, when congress meets, but we don't believe it. Most any other ape would be preferable.

The negro church of Cedar Grove, Bibb county, Alabama, was burned recently by white incendiaries. The next night the white church was burned by black incendiaries.

An aerolite or meteoric stone fell with a fearful report near Mr. Jack Pearson's. near Tuscaloosa, Ala., tearing up the ground with a tremendous hole. Mr. Pearson is going to dig for it.

Atlanta Constitution: Mr. Conkling's message of sympathy was probably lost in the mails. This shows that there are still further reforms for Postmaster General James to make.

Over 2,000,000 feet of lumber was cut by the St. Simon's mills, Brunswick, during the month of May. The pine forests of Georgia would give out in the course of time with many such mills running.

A row occurred in Cuthbert, Ga., a day or two ago, in which six or eight negroes and a dog were involved. Several of the negroes were hurt by the others, and every one of them were bitten by the dog.

Mrs. Charles Carr, of Buffalo, N. Y., claims to be heir to the whole or part of the estate of $5 000 000 left by the late John Burnside, a Louisiana planter. Her name before marriage was Jean Burnside.

The Memphis Appeal thinks that, after the president's family, people most solicitous for Garfield's recovery are the telegraph operators, reporters, correspondents and compilers of the assassination news.

A little girl at Eutaw, Ala., tried to climb over a picket fence, and, when nearly on top, she slipped and fell, her chin catching between two of the pointed palings and hanging her. She was found some hours afterward dead, her neck being broken.

One of the classes in the Baptist Sunday school at Columbia, Ala., has agreed that a penalty for a failure to attend by any one of the class shall be that all the other members of the class shall go and take dinner with the one who fails to be present on the day of such failure.

A recent shipment of 150,000 feet of Dyer-county, Tenn., timber has been made direct to France. The logs were squared up in the woods, and the ends were oiled to keep the sun from cracking them. They were then rafted out of the Forked-deer to New Orleans, from which place snips took them to France.

If one of these two things is not done, and done speedily, Rugby will give a few more little kicks, become comatose and sink into oblivion.

Weekly News Summary.
The railroads have reduced the fare from New York to Chicago to $11. The scalpers are selling at $9.

The recent daily mortality at St. Louis from the heat and other causes has approximated epidemic figures.

A BALD-EAGLE was recently caught at Wilmington, Delaware, while trying to carry off a large Newfoundland dog.

The Japanese mikado is to have a new palace at Yeddo, which is to be entirely of wood, and will cost nearly $5,600,000.

General John C. Pemberton, who surrendered Vicksburg to General Grant, died at Penn Lyn, Pennsylvania, the 13th, aged sixty-seven.

A decree ordering the expulsion from France of Don Carlos, the Spanish pretender, was signed on Saturday and communicated to him on Sunday.

Insurance aggregating $1,000,000 is found to have been placed on the life of Robert Bell, an aged negro, who has just died at Westminster, Md.

Miss Ida Iveson of Chillicothe, Minnesota, a public school teacher, has fallen heir to $2,500,000 in Scotland, and has left to take possession of her property.

Mrs. Abraham Lincoln, who was supposed to be dying, is recovering in a marvelous manner. She is able to take drives, and is rapidly gaining strength.

New Orleans has realized over $1,000,000 from the sale of street railway franchises in two years.
NEW ORLEANS has realized over $1,000,000 from the sale of street railway franchises in two years, and the money is being used to extinguish the city debt.

TOM ELLWOOD, a drunken fellow at Charlotte, North Carolina, retaliated recently on a moccasin snake which had bitten him four times, by biting off its head.

WHITE incendiaries burned the negro church at Cedar Grove, Alabama, the other night, and the next night black incendiaries retaliated on the white church.

NEW YORK undertakers do not believe in wasting money on grave clothes, and now furnish false fronts of shirt, vest and coat for $10, a saving of $30 on a suit.

An army of crickets seven miles wide is marching at the rate of two miles and a half a day over Lake county, Oregon, and eating every kind of vegetation in its track.

Some fifteen hundred pilgrims from Vermont visited the church of Notre Dame de Lourdes in Montreal, Sunday. Quite a number were arrested in the evening for drunkenness.

A CANADIAN clergyman has been at Washington, North Carolina, arranging for the emigration from his parish of one hundred families, whose pastor he has been for over thirty years.

NEGOTIATIONS were closed at Peoria, Illinois, last week, for the purchase of 60,000 acres of land on the line of the Little Rock & Fort Smith railway by the Catholic colonization society.

The deaths from sun-stroke at Cincinnati were 264 in the seven days ending Saturday, and from excessive heat 150, making 414 from these causes. The number from both causes was 86 on the 14th.

LORD BEACONSFIELD was nearly insolvent when he died. It is found that his whole estate would be barely sufficient to discharge the debt upon Hughenden. The executors return the value at a little over £60,000.

JUDGE CLIFFORD of the United States supreme court has undergone amputation of a foot at Portland, Maine, for gangrene, and is as comfortable as could be expected, though the chances for his recovering are exceedingly small.

A box of ham, swarming with trichinae, was sent from Erie, Pennsylvania, to a Rochester (New York) optician recently for examination, but a thief stole it on the way, unconsciously ate the contents, and has suffered no evil effects.

A SAND-HILL crane killed at Gridley, Colorado, recently, had a wire around its neck to which was attached a silver dollar bearing this inscription: Captured at Fort du Quesne May 25, 1783. Released at Fort Dearborn November 17, 1846.

Dr. MADDOX of Clinch county, Georgia, has just sold a century plant in Cincinnati for $400. It has produced several thousand flowers. When on exhibition recently it was viewed by 18,000 people in a few hours at fifteen cents apiece.

The largest taxidermic specimen in this country is a huge elephant, shot in southern India and stuffed at Rochester, New York, for the Agassiz museum at Cambridge, Massachusetts. Mounted on a wooden platform the animal is nine feet, five inches high and his tusks are four feet long. It took over three months to stuff him.

Advices from St. Petersburg report that Russia is fast drifting into anarchy. The czar is still a close prisoner at Peterhof. Occasionally, when business of state requires his presence at the capital, he leaves the fortress to enter St. Petersburg almost by stealth, and returns quickly. A revolution such as the world has never witnessed is not far off.

The remains of the late Pope Pius IX were lately removed from St. Peter's in Rome to the church of San Lorenzo at twelve o'clock at night. Some young men disturbed the procession with cries of "Long live Italy," and the military was called in to disperse them. The fighting lasted all the way to the grave, and finally the procession became a flight.

Throwing rubber balls at a negro, who made a target of his head by thrusting it through a canvas, was one of the Fourth of July sports at New Orleans, Louisiana. Ebony proved an artful dodger, but finally succumbed to the superior markmanship of an apparently drunken fellow who paid $5 for five throws with a stone, the fourth missile fracturing his skull.

An industrial school is to be established at Poughkeepsie, New York, as a family reformatory and preventive school for young girls who are exposed to temptation. The plan is to divide the girls into groups of twenty or thirty each to be in charge of a matron, and the evils of Magdalene asylums, where young girls are brought into contact with hardened characters, will be avoided.

Mrs. ELIZA GARFIELD, mother of President Garfield, on Friday had a severe attack of cholera morbus, and is now prostrated by fever. On account of her extreme age, she being eighty-one, her condition is regarded as very critical, and fears are entertained for her recovery. Every effort will be made to keep the news from the president, as the shock might be injurious to him at present.

The numerous deaths from lockjaw caused by the reckless use of the deadly toy pistol on the Fourth at Baltimore have made considerable excitement there. Two more victims were added to the list yesterday, making thirteen who have died of lockjaw from wounds received by the explosion of toy pistols. Three other cases are reported which cannot recover. In Rochester, New York, there have been three deaths from the same cause.

It is said that, if on the longest day of the year, June 21st, the bark of a tree is entirely peeled off a new bark will immediately grow. The telegraph wires went down in the river, and only meager details can be given. It seems two currents of air swept the valley simultaneously, coming from different directions. The scene was appalling in the extreme. Stone and brick buildings were razed to their foundations, and the air was full of debris. The town and suburbs are now a mass of ruins. NEWS GLEANINGS.
An epidemic in Pulaski county, Ky., is sweeping off the dogs.

The glass factory at Moss Point, Mississippi, has commenced operations.

The wheat crop of North Carolina is about twice as large as was expected.

The Springfield coal pits, of Henrico county, Virginia, have been sold for $286,000.

Three men recently killed in ten days 300 alligators in the Miaka lakes, Florida.

Judge McGehee has ten century plants in bloom on his place, thirteen miles from Madison, Florida.

Tennessee is fast taking foremost rank as the leading wool growing State of the South.

From 3,000 to 4,000 pounds of tomatoes are being shipped daily from Chattanooga to Cincinnati.

One man in Tampa, Florida, has five varieties of the Japan persimmon, and also a Chinese prune.

Sam Clay, of Bourbon county, Ky., has sold from his farm this season 15,000 bushels of blue-grass seed.

Over $1,000,00) in the Texas state treasury to the general revenue, and the total cash balance edges closely to $1,800,000.

In Hernando county, Fla, the carnation pink, the calla lily, the verbena, honeysuckle and the woodbine bloom all the year.

Since the season in Charlotte, North Carolina, $500,000 worth of steam engines and other improved machinery has been sold.

Andrew Fitzpatrick, of St. Augustine, Fla., recently found on the coast in St. Johns county in one evening seventy dozen turtle eggs.

Every dollar of taxes paid by the colored people of Texas, and every dollar of fines assessed against criminals by the circuit courts of the State, goes into the colored school fund.

A marble mine has been discovered on the farm of Eph. Erwin, a few miles from Columbia, Tenn.

FLOGGING NEGROES.
The Novel Method of Punishing Crime Adopted in South Carolina.

GREENVILLE, S. C., March 5.—A rather novel, and certainly an economical, mode of punishing persons detected in the commission of minor crimes has recently been adopted in this vicinity. The worst of these cases is that of a colored youth named Dorritt Banks. As a number of white school-girls were returning from school to their homes, in the upper part of the county, yesterday afternoon, Banks ordered them to halt, seized the tallest and prettiest of the party and forebly kissed her upon the cheek. The number of the girls probably deterred him from assaulting others in the same way. The girl hastened home and informed her father of the indignity to which she had been subjected. The father at once visited the house of the assailant and submitted the alternative to his father of publicly thrashing the boy or submitting him to a criminal prosecution. The former was accepted and the boy was secured. A tough memory in the hands of the father of the little miss whom the negro had insulted made the woodland echoes ring. The clogging was administered in the presence of the whole household and several neighbors, who assembled to witness the unusual procedure. A similar settlement was made here a day or two ago between a merchant and a negro man who had stolen a ham of bacon. The thief admitted his guilt, and agreed to submit to have thirty-one blows delivered upon his bare back. This was promptly and thoroughly done, and the State was saved the expense of a prosecution, while all parties were perfectly satisfied.

THE "RING" DEMOCRATS HAVE THINGS ALL THEIR OWN WAY.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

BALTIMORE, Nov. 8.—This has been an exciting day in Maryland. Returns are coming in slowly from over the State, but the indications are that Thomas J. Keating, the Democratic ring candidate for Controller of the State, is elected by about 12,000 majority. The ring has also elected about seventy-five of the ninety of the members of the House of Delegates, and will also have a big majority in the State Senate. In Baltimore City the Democratic majority is 12,000. The Republican vote here was very light, and the anti-ring Democratic vote will be still lighter. The Republicans would have polled a much heavier vote had it not been for the recent split in the party. The colored vote was unusually small. At Annapolis, the Capital, there was a lively contest between the Old Line or Reform Democrats and the Regulars. When several of the polling-places were opened the anti-ring people objected to the judges and set up private polls of their own in opposition. A terrible misdeed occurred at Quenton, in Annie Arundel County, just after the polls were closed, and a crowd of anti-ring roughs made an attempt to break into the polling-room through the windows. They toro the shutters down and made a desperate effort to seize the ballot-box. They were repulsed by Deputy-Sheriff Mitchell, Dr. T. Clay Maddux, of this city, and others, which resulted in a general fight, during which Dr. Maddux was shot and instantly killed. Several other parties were slightly wounded. Dr. Maddux was a well-known physician of this city.

ed-vance-marion-1881-11-08.A12:
THE SHOT GUN.
Further Account of the Riot at Meridian, Mississippi.
The following is from the Associated Press despatches to the Northern papers, and may be true, but it would not be amiss to accept it with several grains of allowance:

MERIDIAN, MISS., Nov. 10.—In regard to the Marion troubles no new developments have been made since Tuesday night, except the arrest of one negro. After the lapse of two days and conversation with 40 or 50 different participants, the recapitulation of the whole affair in brief is as follows:—On Tuesday, while the State election was progressing at Marion, this county, Joseph Barnett, an aged white man, having just voted, was insulted by a negro at the polls. Barnett raised his arm to resent it with a blow. Some say he drew a stick on the negro. Before he could strike, another negro, named Frank Johnson, shot him with a pistol in the neck, cutting the jugular vein and killing him almost instantly. George Johnson, (colored) formerly a slave of Barrett, ran up to defend his old master, and was shot by a negro, from the effects which he died to day, and general shooting among the negroes then commenced. The whites were all unarmed. Jeff Segars (white) was killed by a negro named Sam. Gillespie.

Alexander Harvey, the Democratic candidate for County Assessor, fifty yards from the scene, was rushed upon by negroes and killed by a shot through the head. He was shot in the face by Frank Johnson after he was dead. James Hodges (white) was wounded seriously in the knee. Levy Moore (white) was wounded in the hand. Vince Segars was wounded and expected to die. The negroes doing the shooting were Gillespie, Frank Johnson, Allen and Burwell Brown, and Martin Malone. Marion was not their voting place; they were from another precinct. Will. Vance (white,) Republican, is said to have induced the negroes to begin the firing.

As soon as the news reached Meridian, six miles distant, Sheriff R. L. Henderson, with a posse of 75 men, repaired to the scene. The negroes had all left. A party of 20 men went to the house of Ed. Vance (white,) Republican, and, approaching him with warrants of arrest, demanded his surrender, and were replied to by Vance hollowing to them to go to —. They were then fired on and repulsed, one house being shot. By five o'clock in the afternoon relief came, and the Sheriff, with his men surrounded the house. The Sheriff called out to the people to surrender. A white
Will Vance and his men gathered about the yard anticipating no danger. John Vance was seen in a stooping attitude, behind the corner of the stables with a gun levelled on the horse, but before he could fire he was shot and killed. At the same time while A. G. Warrell, of the posse, was pledging protection to the females of Vance's family he was shot through the head by someone from inside the house and instantly killed. The sheriff and Harain Jones, of the posse, were slightly wounded. Ed. Vance escaped.

Several negroes were seen to fire on the posse from the house and run off. No negroes are known to be killed. Four or five are wounded. Will Vance was brought to Meridian by the sheriff at night, and ledged in jail. No harm was offered him. Young Ed. Vance, a boy of 17 was captured, but was allowed to remain without molestation. Yesterday a party of fifty men went under the direction of the Sheriff, in search of Ed. Vance and others concerned in the riot None were found except a negro named Martin Malone, who took an active part in the riot. He is now in jail.

ed-vance-marion-1881-11-08.A23:
FROM THE SOUTH.
THE RECENT MURDERS AT MARION.
Truth from Mississippi at Last—The Colored Version of the Election Riots—More Samples of Bourbonism from Two Southern States—Bad Feeling.
A letter from Marion to the editor of the Gazette, dated the 11th instant, presents the true state of the case, and we give it to our readers as an "explanation" of the disgraceful and murderous affair: "While the colored people were at the polls for the purpose of voting one Joe Barnett, white, walked up to a colored man named Sam Gillespie, and demanded of him his ticket, whereupon Gillespie refused to give it up, and then Barnett struck him with a club and knocked him down. When Gillespie arose from the ground he seized a brick and exclaimed: "Don't do that again; if you do I shall spat you in the face." Then Barnett drew his pistol and Gillespie retreated. Some one held Barnett and prevented him from shooting. Segars, a white man, drew his revolver and commenced shooting. Alexander Brown, colored, returned the shots, when a regular firing of pistols began and one of the Segars was killed and one wounded. Aleck Harvey was killed and Barnett was killed. At this juncture the colored men retreated to the old Vance house, where they assembled for safety and protection, knowing Vance to be a Republican and their friend. Vance was killed because he tried to protect and defend the colored men. The elder Vance escaped; John Vance was killed and Will Vance was wounded and is now in jail. One colored man, George Johnson, sr., was killed. That this was the direct result of the teachings of Horn, of the Meridian Mercury, who, although an amiable man personally, is a bitter and unscrupulous politician, there is no room for doubt. All through the campaign he has expressed the opinion that under all circumstances the white men shall rule, and his editorials have abounded in sentiments calculated to inculcate the idea that the "boys" should "mean business" in "stepping across the platform."—Mobile Gazette.

"IF IT COST BLOOD."

The subject to be considered and discussed is: The free negro has been put into the Constitution by folly and fanaticism; shall he be thrust out in wisdom and deliberation? * * * While the statesmen are considering our proposition—if they can be brought to consider it—the true white man of the South will be setting at naught the Fifteenth Amendment by such methods as may present themselves, and counting its abrogation cheap at the price of some blood, for nothing can be more abhorrent than negro rule or the rule of mean whites by grace of the negro. It must and will be averted if it costs blood! The free ballot and fair count of the politician as it has been announced in this State is not worth the paper it is printed on. * * * The politicians were doubtless honest in proclaiming it, but, being against nature, they could not redeem the promise. The Fifteenth Amendment in this county, if not a dead letter, is a mighty sick one. After Tuesday at Marion the man who starts out to organize the negroes to vote against the white folks had better have gone West to grow up with a new country. Lauderdale County will be unhealthy for him.—Meridian (Miss.) Mercury, November 10.

"THE GUITEAU PRESIDENT."

Now that the Readjusters and their "faithful allies" have secured the State government and the Legislature, we shall see what use they propose to make of their victory. They will have supreme power, and can settle the State debt upon their own terms, the only barrier in their way being the Supreme Court of the United States. How would it do for the Guiteau President to pack that, as it is proposed to pack our Court of Appeals? Grant did it, and there is no reason why Arthur should not "follow in the footsteps of his illustrious predecessor."—Lynchburg Virginian, November 11.

WARNED TO KEEP AWAY.

A Mississippi dispatch puts Lowry's majority at 25,000, and closes with the assurance that "all is well." Of course, Ben King's supporters had been warned by the Bourbons to keep away from the polls, and to give their private affairs their exclusive attention on election day, if they did not want to get into trouble.—Memphis Avalanche, 15th instant.

"It is WICKED."

If there had been no stirring-up of the negro population to get their votes this thing never would or could have occurred. That was wicked in itself, and the consequences are justly upon their heads.—Mercury, Meridian, Miss., November 13.

THANKSGIVING.

The honest people of Virginia will be in a good mood to observe Mr. Arthur's recommendation of a day for thanksgiving. There is certainly one thing they should be thankful for, and that is that they have no regard for Mr. Arthur's methods.—Virginian, Lynchburg, Va., November 11.

THE TWO ARMIES.

The Southern army endured four years of war and its hardships, not from compulsion, but from a patriotic sentiment to defend their rights. * * The Northern army fought for hire, pelf, or booty.—Mercury, Meridian, Miss.
ed-vance-marion-1881-11-08.A26:
A Shot Gun Story Spoiled.
of the history of the shot gun affair at Meridian, Mississippi, on election day, in which the negroes were accused of raising a riot and of shooting down in cold blood a number of innocent white men. A correspondent of the New York Times evidently a resident of the place where the affair occurred, has been investigating the affair, and after waiting to see the untruthful published report contradicted through some other source, volunteers to do the work himself. The first published version coming through biased shot gun sources, it will be recollected said, that a number of negroes went to the polls armed, insulted a peaceable old white man named Barnett, and then killed him with a pistol shot, the white men around all being unarmed. In the general shooting that followed, two other white men, one of them the Democratic candidate for Assessor, were killed. A white family named Vance, Republicans, were accused as being responsible for the shooting, and the Sheriff with a posse 75 strong, started for Vance's house, six miles distant, to arrest the Vance's and a body of armed negroes, 100 in number, who had barricaded themselves in Vance's house. In the attempt to arrest the Vance family—father and three sons—the Sheriff was wounded, one of the so called "posse" killed, one of the Vance boys was killed, the father escaped, two sons were arrested, one of whom was afterwards released. This is one side, now for the other and no doubt the true one.

Edward Vance and his sons were all at the polls on election day and the usual crowd of negroes and white men were around. Joe Barnett, an elderly white man, was drunk and went around abusing and cursing all negroes who were Republicans. Edward Vance, the father of the Vance boys, because he was a white Republican, was selected for his most bitter curses. Vance, by request of his sons and by Harvey, paid no attention to Barnett, but said he would resent an attempt to assault him. Barnett then went to a crowd of negroes and cursed them and finally went so far as to strike one of them on the head, when another negro said if he would do that again he would hit him with a brick. Upon this, Harvey and a number of white friends with their hands significantly in their pockets, approached the negroes, who knowing what was coming, started and ran.

The white men who lying shot guns reports says were so terribly outraged, pursued the flying negroes fifty or sixty yards shooting at them as they ran. The negroes believing they were all going to be killed, turned and fired with deadly effect upon their pursuers, killing the old man Barnett, Harvey the Democratic candidate, Jeff Segars, also mortally wounded Vincent Segars. The Vances with one white man, a Democrat, and one colored man, believing their lives were in danger, drove home by a roundabout way. About an hour afterwards the house was fired upon, and two of the Vance boys ran out to take a hand in it, but the guns would not go off, the loads having become rusty, and then they escaped back into the house although more than twenty shots were fired at them. The mob then left, but having drummed up more recruits returned with the Sheriff a short time afterwards. Everywhere they went they reported that they had warrants for the arrest of the Vance family, and when they went to the house to serve them they were fired upon by 200 negroes, when in fact the only men in the house were the four Vances, the Democratic friend alluded to and the old negro.

The Sheriff and his crowd gathered at a gin house in the neighborhood, when Mrs. Vance and the Democratic friend went out to see what they wanted, and came back with the word that they had warrants for all in the house The Vances then sent word that if the crowd would disperse and none come to the house but the Sheriff they would surrender. The Sheriff promised protection and started to the house, but the crowd followed. The Vances still kept telling the Sheriff to keep off the crowd but they pressed on, some of them inside the gate. About this time the inmates made an attempt to escape by the back way, but were met by a crowd of armed men and fired upon, one of the Vances being wounded. John Vance exasperated rode upon the crowd and was shot to pieces. The old negro was also killed and one of the crowd was killed. After the firing had ceased the Sheriff came into the house expecting to find all the inmates dead, but all except the negro and John Vance were ready to defend themselves to the last. They still told the Sheriff that if he would drive off the crowd they would submit to arrest. This the Sheriff succeeded in doing when the two boys surrendered and were taken to jail, but the father made his escape as he knew it

THE BOTTOM FACTS OF THE MISSISSIPPI MASSACRE. How Colored Men Were Shot Down at the Polls and the Facts Distorted and Sent by Wire to the Country—The Work of Bourbon Devils.
MERIDIAN, Miss., Dec. 10.—After its usually comprehensive style, THE REPUBLICAN has frequently cautioned its readers against receiving as true the reports coming through Democratic sources of the late election riot at Marion Station, Lauderdale County, Mississippi, where a number of white Democrats were killed by colored men and Republicans. Marion is only five miles from Meridian, the county seat, where the writer of this resided nearly four years, and, being well acquainted with most of the persons named in the dispatch in connection with the so-called massacre, I have taken great pains to learn the bottom facts in regard to it, and here present them as they come to me through the most reliable and trustworthy sources. My informants, some of them eye-witnesses, embrace every shade of politics; all live near the scene of the riot, and agree as to the main facts.

LAUDERDALE IS HOPELESSLY DEMOCRATIC, but the precinct of Marion Station, when a free vote and a fair count can be had, is largely Republican, and it is the only Republican precinct in the county; hence at every election since the organization of the party in the State there has been "trouble" at Marion. It appears from good Democratic authority that "trouble" was anticipated on the day of the late election. This will be seen from the following: "We encountered a squad of young men of the city last night who are intent upon going to Marion to the election to-day. We think they mean business; and every one of them has a white skin, and, we believe, a white heart. They will keep the peace there themselves to-day, and see to it that everybody else does. They are true, and some on elections."—Mercury (Meridian, Miss.), November 8.

ONE OF THESE "YOUNG MEN"

who went to Marion on that day, being "some on elections," was Moore, the foreman of the Mercury office. Moore has acted as a bully and general fighting man for the Mercury for the past eight or nine years, the editor himself having no capacity whatever for that branch of the profession, though in Mississippi it is the most essential qualification of an editor. It is a melancholy feature in reviewing this matter to learn that Moore escaped with a slight wound. The two Seagers brothers spoken of in the dispatches, one of whom was killed at the polls that day and the other mortally wounded, were young drunken desperadoes, one of them but a few weeks before he was killed having murdered a colored man in cold blood, but escaping the gallows on the ground of "temporary insanity, superinduced by the use of intoxicating liquor." Harvey, candidate for assessor, who also lived at Meridian, was the only one killed at the polls that day whose loss the community will mourn. Joe Barnett, spoken of in the dispatches as an "innocent old man," and the first victim of the slaughter,

WAS THE ONLY DEMOCRAT KILLED

who belonged in Marion or had any legitimate business there other than that foreshadowed by the Mercury. This "innocent old man" (about forty years of age) was the prime mover of the difficulty, as he was first to pay the penalty. When the polls opened, at nine o'clock in the morning, says an eye-witness, there were about forty whites and seventy-five colored men on the ground. Barnett carried a cudgel about two inches in diameter and three feet long, which he used in the most approved Bourbon style. As the situation became more alarming the colored men huddled together some thirty yards distant from the polls, Barnett and Harvey and these young devils from Meridian following them up with sticks and pistols in their hands.
ABOUT THIS TIME BARNETT STEPPED UP to a colored man named Gillespie and demanded his ticket. Upon his refusal to comply with this demand Barnett struck Gillespie with his club, knocking him down. When Gillespie rose from the ground he seized a brickbat. Then Barnett drew his pistol and Gillespie retreated. Some one held Barnett and prevented him from shooting. When Gillespie returned some four or five of his colored friends and relatives gathered round him, apart from the body of colored men assembled. While thus awaiting developments they were confronted by about an equal number of whites, headed by Barnett and the two Seagers, when the fight began in earnest, Seagers firing the first shot

ONE COLORED MAN—ALEX. BROWN—did nearly or quite all the shooting for the colored side. When the smoke of battle had cleared the polls were deserted, and not a colored man was to be found on the ground, but the bloody corpses of the Mercury's "young men" lying here and there told too well the result of the contest. Ed. Vance, an honest, plodding, hard-working Irishman, who lived some three miles from his voting-place at Marion, at once took refuge with his two young boys in his own house. A few negroes living on Vance's place, becoming alarmed, went into the house with Vance for safety, those who did the shooting at Marion having ridden off in another direction. Vance, it may be well to mention in this connection, was a loyal man during the war, and has been a Republican ever since, in consequence of which his persecutions have been enough to drive any man to desperation.

IT WAS DOUBTLESS THOUGHT by the Democrats that a good opportunity now offered for setting the Vances out of the way, as they were becoming quite an important factor in the politics of the county. Accordingly they rallied in large numbers, surrounded Vance's house, and demanded the surrender of all within. The demand was not complied with, Vance being master of the situation, until the sheriff arrived with reinforcements from Meridian, at which time a parley ensued, Mrs. Vance coming out with a white flag and acting as spokeswoman. Warren, of the sheriff's posse, approached Mrs. Vance in an angry and threatening manner, with pistol in hand. Just at this time the eldest of Vance's sons, who had not been engaged in the melee at all, riding up from the outside, was shot dead by the sheriff's posse. Seeing his brother shot down and his mother's life being threatened, one of the young brothers from inside the house shot and killed Warren. Vance, it is supposed, then fled from the rear of the house, followed by the colored men who were barricaded with him, but in doing so a number of the latter were shot and killed.

VANCE IS STILL SECRETED IN THE WOODS, and one of his sons, with some eight or ten negroes, are in the Meridian jail. What their fate will be is hard to tell at this time, but it is generally conceded now that Vance had nothing whatever to do with the trouble at Marion Station. It is important to state in connection with this affair that the Republicans had no ticket in the field in Lauderdale County, and gave only a negative support to what is known there as the "Anti-Monopolists." Consequently there could have been no unusual inducement for Republicans to have precipitated a riot on the day of the election. It is no more than justice to say that Henderson, the sheriff has acted fairly and manfully throughout in this matter, and it is doubtless owing to his influence that scores of lives have been saved since that fatal day.

ADDITIONAL INFORMATION.

Since the above was written I have been furnished with additional information bearing upon this subject. The following is a copy of an anonymous letter received in the post-office at Meridian but a few days ago:

J. M. W.
