MISSISSIPPI MASSACRE. The Farce of Trying Republicans for Alleged Murder Commenced.
MERIDIAN, Miss., Dec. 22.—The trial of Will Vance for the murder of the Segars brothers and others at the recent election in Marion was commenced here to-day. The first witness, C. H. Hopgood, a Bourbon, testified that a short time before the riot he heard Will Vance remark to his father, Ed Vance: "I'll attend to him." Will appeared to be offended at something. Ed replied: "Hold on! This thing is going to be started up in the nicest manner you ever saw directly." Soon, Sam Gillespie and the Brown negroes came around to the polls. A short time after witness saw a fuss a short distance off between Barnett and a negro. The negro drew a pistol and ran up the street with it in his hand and joined a negro named Bill Clark. A big crowd of negroes rushed on Barnett and the other white men with pistols drawn, threatening to shoot Barnett's head off. A negro fired a shot, when a general shooting began. Witness saw a negro put a pistol to Barnett's breast and shoot him. Barnett fell back and died in a few seconds. Witness saw no pistol about Barnett, nor any among the whites; saw about seventy-five or one hundred pistols in the hands of the negroes.

D. W. S. Sims, a Bourbon, testified to about the same effect as the preceding witness, except that he saw the Segars boys with pistols. Witness was beside Vint Segars when the latter was shot. He and the two Segars boys were attacked by t. e negroes. He saw Jeff Segars clinched with a negro. Jeff had his pistol at the negro's breast and fired, and the negro shot at Jeff. Jeff's shot did not take effect.

Julius Jackson (colored) testified that a short time before the riot occurred he saw Ed, Will, and John Vance, the Browns (colored), and Samuel Gillespie (colored) in conversation; heard Will Vance say to Allen Brown, "Are you fixed?" Brown replied, "By God! I came fixed." Defendant said: "If you ain't fixed I'll fix you, and if anything commences here to-day I want you to leave it to me." Brown replied: "I'm bound to see you through." These negroes then rushed to the spot where the difficulty commenced, and defendant waved his hand and cried out: "Go ahead, boys!" The difficulty began by Barnett asking Sam Gillespie to let him see his ticket. Sam handed it to him. Barnett laughingly tore it into three pieces. Sam then kicked Barnett. The latter turned and struck him over the head with a stick. Allen Brown took Sam's part, and threatened to knock Barnett's head off if he came closer. The negro drew a pistol and Burwell Segars said: "Come, let's arrest that negro and take his pistol away." Witness saw Alexander Harvey with a pistol. The remainder of the testimony was not materially different from that of these witnesses.
ed-vance-marion-1881-11-08.A34:
THE VANCE TRIAL.
The Story of the Mississippi Elec tion Riot.
Meridian, Miss., December 24—In the Vance case to-day Charles Hopgood corroborated the evidence of Julius Jackson, colored, to the effect that Brown and Vance, negroes, were in close consultation behind a house a short time before the riot. The witness did not hear what was said. He saw fifteen pistols among the negroes during the riot.

John Daniel, colored, testified that he saw the defendant, with Bill Brown, Bill Stark and other negroes, near where the riot occurred. Soon afterwards the riot commenced. He saw Burwell Brown, colored, and Alex. Harvey close together, shooting at one another. Harvey's shots seemed to have no effect on Brown, who ran off. Witness saw Elias Brown afterwards stoop and fire at somebody. The smoke was dense. Elias cried out, as he turned and ran off, "I got him."

Isaac Brown, white, testified that he saw Joseph Barnett embroiled with a negro, and went with the Segars boys to prevent his shooting him. The negro had a pistol drawn. Barnett had been drinking a little and witness wanted to get him away. Barnett was jocose rather than insulting during the morning. When drinking he was always in good humor, and never belligerent. Witness kept with Barnett, and the negro turned on Segars, who had his pistol drawn, and shot at him, when they clinched and shot at each other four or five times. Segars had his pistol against the negro's side, but the shot had no effect. Witness thought it strange that the negro was not killed. When Segars and the negro commenced firing a negro named Frank Johnson stepped up to Barnett, and putting a pistol to his breast shot him dead. Witness looked around, and seeing that all the whites had been killed, thought he would get out of the way himself. When leaving the negro shot twice, and the bullets flew by him, but he did not know whether they were fired at him or not. Witness had a pistol at the time.

Charles Page, white, saw defendant come to Marion that morning with about twenty negroes. Just before the riot he saw a large crowd of negroes in the streets. Forty or fifty of them had pistols drawn. He saw no pistols among the whites. Witness could not see the shooting. A house ob-
large crowd of negroes in the streets. Forty or fifty of them had pistols drawn. He saw no pistols among the whites. Witness could not see the shooting. A house obstructed his view.
Willey Brooks, a clerk in the employ of Jas. Baums, of Meridian, was sworn, and testified that on October 22 he sold the defendant a Smith & Wesson revolver and charged the same to his father, E.J. Vance. A few days later he sold one to John Vance.
Pending a motion to allow the prisoner bail on account of ill health the court was adjourned.

edmund-davis-union-1881-10-20.A1:
The present number is gotten out under great difficulties.
The United States Senate took a recess on Monday until Friday, to attend the Yorktown celebration.

Col W H Crow's card in another column will have interest for Life Insurance folk.

Senators Vance, Ransom, Lamar, Wade Hampton, and Joseph E Brown, board at the Metropolitan Hotel in Washington.

At the fair, Mr. Charles Kerr took premiums to the amount of seventy five dollars. Robert Scott took several premiums on farm products.

Guiteau has been brought into court, and plead "not guilty." His actions and demeanor plainly indicated that he was demented.

Capt Ashe writes from Washington that the troubles of Messrs. Winstead & Tuck, distillers of Person, will be compromized. They are keeping non est, until the matter be arranged.

T. e Wilmington & Weldon R. R. has finally been ordered to pay $5,000 for the killing of Hon. Edward Conningland. The Goldsboro Messenger says that after the first trial the company offered to pay $7,500.

Our young friend, Samuel T Niehelson, of Whitakers, sent to Atlanta Exposition heads of oats raised by him, measuring 23 and 24 inches, three times the usual length. See advertisement elsewhere. It must be a rare article.

A gold headed cane was yesterday presented to Mr Wm J Best, by the ladies of Goldsboro who enjoyed his hospitality during the recent excursion to Beaufort, says the Messenger. The Newbern News reports three miles of track graded to the west of Goldsboro.

Julius Setzer, of Charlotte, went to sleep with his door open, and was robbed of $475. Heavy penalty for carelessness. The Observer of that town says Charlotte has more burglaries than any town of its size in the world.

There are Public, or "Free," school buildings at the North which cost more than the Capitol of North Carolina. There are Free School teachers who get from $4,000 to $5,000 a year salary. The Free school tax in Boston is $5 per capita. In North Carolina it is 25 cents; which two cents a month the year round!

A young lady residing in the central portion of the state would like to hear of a situation as Housekeeper, nursery maid, ladie's companion, or almost any similar position in which an honorable, christian woman can make herself useful, and exchange her services for a reasonable support. A country home preferred, but it is not material. The young lady is said (by a lady, who informs us) to be amiable and intelligent, with a knack of looking after domestic or household duties. Families needing such an assistant can get the name by writing to this office.

At the meeting of Directors of the Cape Fear and Yadkin Valley R. R., on Thursday, no definite action was taken as to the sale of the Road. But we understand it is now as good as settled that the road will pass into the hands of a wealthy syndicate, who will finish it at a rapid rate. It is now stated that the explanation of the sale of the English iron to a Florida Railroad after its arrival at Wilmington, was due to some dissatisfaction on the part of the English parties who had agreed to furnish the iron, and accept the bonds of the company in lieu of cash. They declined to take the Bonds, and the trade fell through.

A call from Col. Wharton Green and B. A. Capeheart, Esq., of Kittrells, led to some interesting "fish talk." Both of these gentlemen take interest in the finny tribe. Col. Green's Carp pond was stocked about four months ago. During that time his German Carp have grown from 2-inch minnows to handsome table fish, 15 inches long, and 5 in breadth. This is rapid growth. But we believe Col. Roger O. Greggory reports some of his carp as doing quite as well, or better.

Mr. Capeheart has not yet stocked his pond; but he is an old "fisherman," having formerly owned "Avoca," on the Chowan, the home of Dr. Wm. R. Capeheart, and reputed as one of the loveliest, if not the most so, of homesteads in Eastern Carolina. It seems incredible to hear these gentlemen speak of catching 6,000 shad at one haul, and nearly half a million herring in one day. But Mr. Capeheart says it is not uncommon with the larger fisheries which are operated by steam, to take 300,000 fish at one haul!

—A terrible affair in Union county. Edmund Davis, an ex-convict, not long out of the Penitentiary, went to the house of Messrs. Goodfray, a respectable widow lady, ten miles South of Monroe, and ravished her daughter. The mother heard the struggle going on in her daughter's room; but was too old and feeble to bring assistance in time. The negro escaped, but was captured ere night. The officers hid him in the woods, and crowd of revengers hunted all night for them. About sunrise on Monday they were found, and the negro made to confess. Then he was hanged. Many negroes took part, and wanted to burn him, but were not permitted. We get these particulars from the Charlotte Observer.

The prevalence of rape renders it necessary to warn parents to be on their guard at all times.

edmund-davis-union-1881-10-20.A2:
IN MEMORIAM.
Death of Rev. A. A. Boshamer—Meeting of the Official Board of Tryon Street Church, Charlotte.

The recent death of Rev. A. A. Boshamer, late of Edenton Street Church, Raleigh, former pastor of Tryon Street Charlotte, has affected the hearts of his former charge with deepest sorrow, and is felt in the whole community. During his pastoral charge of Tryon Street Church, through a period of four years, his ministry was marked by gentleness, faithfulness and ability—the most perfect esteem, affection, and confidence of his flock was maintained, while not a single discord occurred to mar the harmony of the relation between pastor and people.

The impress that he left upon this community was only for good. The fervency of his piety, the purity of, and transparency of his character, the simplicity and geniality of his social life, and the attractiveness of his preaching made him a general favorite in his own Church and won the admiration and esteem of the community.

Richly endowed with these qualities, he was prepared to be a "workman that need not be ashamed"—a faithful shepherd to those "over whom the Holy Ghost made him overseer"—a "wise master-builder" in the temple of the Lord—attractive and loving in the social circle, patient toward the erring, kind and tender in the sick room and house of mourning.

Deeply impressed with his character, we are deeply affected by his early death. We feel that we and the whole Church have suffered a great loss. We feel that the grief of his family is our grief, and the grief of the Church.

Hence, as we are bowed with a common sorrow, we mingle our tears with theirs. While wife, and father, and mother, and child, sit solitary in the shadow of this great grief, our hearts not only feel a kindred pang, but respond in sympathy and condolence to the appeal that comes from bleeding hearts.

Again we are impressed with the inscrutable mystery of Providence in removing a life so full of promise to the Church, just as it was approximating its prime, while there are so many waste places uncultivated and harvests ungathered. The workmen fall, still work goes on. The soldier dies at his post, still the battle does not cease; nor are the banners furled. "God buries His workmen, but carries on His work." So is it ever. We reverence this wisdom. We bow to this power. We adore this goodness. We are subdued under a sense of infinity!

While we stand with uncovered head in the presence of the Disposer of events, and bow our hearts in profoundest grief, we recognize in it the special providence of God, who is "too wise to err and too good to be unkind." Thus endeavoring to submit to the supreme decision of the Head of the Church, and to acquiesce in all the developments of His providence, we, the officers of Tryon Street Church, representing in this case the sentiments of the whole Church, while expressing our own sorrow at the death of our former pastor and friend, desire most heartily and sincerely to express to the bereaved family of the deceased our deepest sympathy; and we do most devoutly pray that God, in whose service he lived, labored, and died, may communicate to them His richest consolations in this trying hour, and so sanctify this afflictive dispensation of His providence as that it shall prove to them a blessing, both for time and eternity.

It was ordered that this communication be sent to the Charlotte papers and Raleigh Christian Advocate for publication—also that a copy be sent to Mrs. A. A. Boshamer as a testimony of our sympathy and affectionate regard.

OFFICIAL BOARD.
Charlotte, N. C., Oct. 13, 1881.

Local Items.

There have been fine rains in this section this week, greatly encouraging farmers in their small-grain work. While there have been killing frosts in the central part of the State two weeks ago, vegetation about here has scarcely been nipped or colored by frost.

A workman, W. A. Sing, in Mr. Josiah Asbury's planing mill, had his hand nearly severed from the wrist by a buzz saw. The saw caught his wrist band which drew the arm also. He will be detained from work some time.

The Almanac sellers or drummers on the streets are about as big a nuisance as the boot-blacks in New York.

Considering the very dry and hot Summer and Fall, the health of Charlotte has been remarkably good, equal to any Mountain city or town.

Sheriff Mays, of Alexander county, considering it unsafe to keep the murderer of Miss Thompson, E. H. Dockery, in the Alexander jail, or even in the jail of any adjoining county, brought the prisoner to this city to be committed to jail here. It was through Dockery's confession that Church, one of the murderers, was lynched, and it is thought his testimony in Court will seriously implicate two others. One, Adams, is under bond to appear at Court now. Evidently it was the friends of these that lynched Church.

The notorious female Minstrels are advertised to appear in Wilmington at an early day. There is an Ordinance in this city against permitting such vulgar performances in the Opera House or elsewhere in Charlotte.

The Hornet's Nest Riflemen of this city, about 30 in number, went to the Yorktown Centennial celebration, under command of E. F. Young.

Mr. Julius Setzer, grocery dealer on Trade street, says he went to sleep in the back room of his store on Sunday night, leaving the back door open, and when he awoke he found his trunk broken open and about $500 in money stolen. No rogue is fool enough to miss such an opportunity as that to steal.

Another Circus (Forepaugh's) will be here on the 4th of November.

The woman who cruelly beat and maimed a poor little bound white child should be punished more severely than by a fine of $6.

In Jackson Township, Union county, resided an aged widow lady, Mrs. Godfrey, with her daughter and a small negro boy as servant. On Sunday morning last Mrs. Godfrey was awakened by cries from her daughter, who slept in an adjoining room; being old and feeble she could not herself render any assistance, but sent the boy to the house of a colored man near by. On the arrival of the man the scoundrel ran out and escaped in the darkness. He found that Miss Godfrey had been outraged and choked to stifle her cries. There were found a stick and wagon hammer. The former was identified by a colored man as one he had seen in the possession of Edmund Davis, negro and ex-convict. A party of men in the neighborhood followed and captured the negro eight miles from Mrs. Godfrey's house. He was brought back to Union and taken before Miss Godfrey—but she could not identify him as the room was dark. He was placed in jail where he soon confessed the crime. When it became known a party of three hundred men, one hundred of whom were blacks, took him and hung him to a tree near the scene of the crime. After the crowd was satisfied he was dead they dispersed, leaving the fiend hanging. The party was composed of the best citizens of Union county, and many of the black people insisted he should be burned. Miss Godfrey is 35 years of age, of unblemished character and her condition is quite critical, as she was seriously hurt. The negro was indifferent and said he was willing to be hung. We are glad his request was carried out.

The North Carolina Industrial Association (colored) will be held at Raleigh October 31st to November 4th. Thanks for a pass.

A Pennsylvanian has leased 10,000 acres of land near Woodbury, Cannon county, Tenn, and will bore for oil.

The area of Tennessee is 26,800,000 acres, of which 10,771,396 acres are still covered with the original forest.

In Salisbury, on the 12th inst., by Rev. F. J. Murphy, Dr. John Clingman and Miss Cora Hackett.

HANGED BY A MOB.
An Ex-Convict Lynched in Asheville North Carolina.
ASHEVILLE, N. C., October 21.—Edmund Davis, an ex convict, captured in Union County on Wednesday, confessed to having made an outrageous assault on Miss Godfrey. A mob took him from the officers yesterday, and a large crowd, among them some of the best citizens of the place, assembled, and Davis was hanged to the limb of a tree. After hanging forty minutes he was pronounced dead.
edmund-davis-union-1881-10-20.A4:
General News Summary.
— L. R. Hill, Esq., son of Mr. Albert Hill, of Spartanburg County, is now Judge of the County Court of Summit County, Colorado.

— Mr. C. E. Satterthwaite, of Aiken County, made clear of all expenses as the proceeds of his splendid orchard $1,100 during the past season.

— The Varnville (Hampton County) Messenger is satisfied that three-fourths of the cotton crop is in the market, and the other fourth in the caterpillar.

— On Tuesday night of last week Thomas Hatcher killed Sam McNeil, both colored, on Mr. Thomas Barnes's place, about twelve miles east of Camden.

— The citizens of Abbeville County are greatly behind in paying taxes, and a large number of taxpayers will necessarily have the penalty added. Not more than a hundred a day are paying.

— The gin-house of Mr. J. M. Ivy in Lancaster County was destroyed by fire on Thursday morning last. About seven bales of cotton and other property were consumed. Accidental. No insurance.

— A bloody encounter took place on last Friday evening at Cane Savannah, in Sumter County, between two negroes, brothers-in-law, Oliver Robinson and Archy Andrews. Oliver was stabbed five times, but not fatally.

— Mr. Wesley Walker of Aiken County, had his dwelling house, kitchen, furniture, clothing, &c., destroyed by fire last week. Mr. C. E. Satterthwaite's three and a half story ginhouse, in Aiken County, was also burned down last week at a loss of $5,562.

— There are thirty prisoners now confined in the Greenville County jail. Of these twelve are United States prisoners, ten under sentence and two awaiting trial at the next August court. The remaining eighteen are State prisoners, seven under sentence and eleven awaiting trial at the next court.

— Of a list of between nine and ten thousand taxpayers in Greenville County only about three thousand had paid their taxes up to last Saturday night. The smaller taxpayers have paid more promptly than the large owners of property.

— At Edgefield Courthouse on Monday the anti-stock law men held a convention and passed resolutions against the passage of the stock law by the South Carolina Legislature next winter. The majority of the county favor the fencing of stock instead of crops, however, and the change will almost certainly be made.

— At Cleveland, Saturday morning, President Garfield's body was removed from the public vault in Lake View Cemetery, as it is required for other purposes, to the finest private vault in the grounds, there to remain until the completion of the crypt, where it will permanently repose.

— Work was commenced last Thursday on the long-talked of telegraph line between Newberry and Laurens. It will be completed, it is said, in about one month.

— At Newton, N. J., Friday, 21st inst., in the Sussex Independent libel cases, in which the editors on Wednesday pleaded guilty, W. H. Gibbs, the oldest editor, was sentenced to ten months with hard labor in the State prison and to pay $200 fine; J. J. Stanton, the other editor, to six months and the same fine. The sentences are considered very severe.

— Two negroes, Yearby Centry and Prince Hodge, were found dead upon the track of the Wilmington, Columbia and Augusta Railroad, near Spann's crossing, about six miles from Sumter, last Saturday morning. Saturday afternoon an inquest was held and a verdict returned that death was caused by being run over by the cars.

— The Marlboro' Friend says: "The coroner was called on Saturday last to view the dead body of Henry Williams, who was shot and killed near Hunt's Bluff on the night before. It appears that he was trying to force an entrance into Mr. Reynold's store at that place and fortunately was found out in time not escape."

— On last Wednesday night soon after dark, while Mr. Wim. V. Black, constable for Trial Justice Gibson, was going home from Greenville, he was fired upon at the five mile post on the Chick Spring road. The would-be murderer was in ambush on the roadside, and fired the shot, apparently from a pistol, a few feet from Mr. Black's head. It is supposed that robbery was the motive of the assault.

— They do some things in a queer way in Missouri. We find in a dispatch of the 22d inst., from Warrensburg an account of the arrest and punishment there of an old man who had married a blind widow, spent all her money, and then deserted her. The dispatch says that under the law in such cases, he was put up for sale to the highest bidder for his six months' servitude, and was finally knocked off or sold for $10. That looks like our penitentiary lease system in a retail way.

— The New York Herald thinks it "mighty onartin" which party in that State will elect its State ticket; its opinion is that the contest will be exceedingly close, the majority of the winning party probably not exceeding two or three thousand votes. It rather inclines to the belief that the Republicans will retain a majority in the Legislature, though it says that the Democrats are sanguine. One great trouble about making a reliable estimate is the difficulty of striking a balance between the Kelly defection on the one side and the stalwart disaffection on the other.

— A negro, ex-convict, named Davis, living in Union county, N. C., near Heath's store, outraged Miss Godfewis, a white woman, 55 years old, entering her room and effecting his purpose by choking her into silence, on Sunday morning at 1 o'clock. A party of men in the neighborhood followed the negro into Lancaster county, S. C., and arrested him. He was given a preliminary examination Sunday night before Justice McIlwain. On Monday a party of men of both colors, numbering three hundred and twenty-six took the negro and hung him to a tree near Health's store. He confessed, the victim being unable to identify him, and said he ought to be hanged.

Another Ravisher Lynched.
Another Ravisher Lynched.

The Charlotte Observer of the 18th inst. publishes the following story of the lynching of a negro for an outrageous assault upon a white lady in Union County, N. C.:

About twelve and one-half miles from Monroe, one mile from the South Carolina line, in Union County, N. C., lived an aged widow, Mrs. Godfrey, with her daughter and a small negro boy as a servant. About two o'clock Sunday morning Mrs. Godfrey was awakened by the smothered cries of her daughter who slept in an adjoining room. She waked the boy and sent him for assistance to the house of a negro man who lived about one hundred yards away. She was old and helpless, and her agonizing efforts and realization of her helplessness during the fifteen minutes which elapsed before the boy returned with the man can only be imagined.

The man proceeded at once to strike a light, but before this could be done some one ran across the floor and escaped in the darkness.

A light was made and Miss Godfrey was found in a desperate state. She had been outraged and the prints of hands upon her throat showed that she had been choked into silence. She was seriously hurt.

Upon the floor were found a stick and a wagon hammer.

The stick was identified by a negro man in the neighborhood as one he had observed in the possession of a negro who had supped at his house Saturday night and had left in the direction of Mrs. Godfrey's, declaring that he was going to attend church in Lancaster County, S. C. His name was Edmund Davis, an ex convict, out of the Penitentiary only six months.

A party of men from the neighborhood pursued in the direction of the church which Davis had said he would attend. This party overtook and captured him about 11 o'clock Sunday morning in a negro cabin in Lancaster County, eight miles from the scene of the rape.

He was taken to Union and presented before a magistrate, who ordered him before Miss Godfrey, but she failed to identify him, as the room where the crime was committed was entirely dark. The identification of the stick, however was sufficient to warrant the magistrate in sending him to prison. The hammer found on the floor had been taken from a wagon near the house of the Godfrey's.

The prisoner was committed to the charge of a constable and a guard deputized to escort him to Monroe jail. Whilst on the way to prison the negro confessed to crime and it soon became known to the people. A lynching party of one hundred men was organized, and the guard, despairing of taking the prisoner in safety to Monroe, hid him from the infuriated populace.

During the whole of Sunday night the mob made for the concealed ravisher, who was found about daylight, when it was at once announced that he would be lynched, and by 8.30 o'clock yesterday morning a crowd of 326 men, about 100 of whom were blacks, assembled to witness the execution. Among the crowd were some of the best citizens of that portion of Union and others from Lancaster County.

Edmund Davis is described as a very black and brutal looking negro. He seemed entirely indifferent to his fate, confessed the crime without reserve, and said he was willing to be hanged.

Some of the blacks in the crowd insisted that he should be burned, but at 9 o'clock he was hanged within one and a half miles of the scene of the crime. He hung for forty minutes, when the crowd, satisfied that he was quite dead, dispersed, leaving him still hanging.

Miss Godfrey, the victim of the outrage, is about 35 years of age, and a woman of unblemished character.

LYNCHED BY POPULAR VOTE.
Vicksnuo, Miss., Oct. 9.—Information was received here today of a flendish deed perpetrated on the person of a white woman by a negro unmed Ellas Robertson, near Morgan's Fork, in Franklin County, Miss. It seems that Mrs. Ellen Johnson, a white lady 65 years of age, a widow and resident of Morgan's Fork, while visiting a lady in the neighborhood, was overtaken by Robertson in a lonely part of the road and outraged. He inflicted several wounds on her with a stick, knocking her down, then choked her until the marks of his fingers were left on her throat, and then told her if she did not submit to him and make no more fuss he would cut her throat. The news in a short time spread far and near, and large crowds of men made diligent search for the perpetrator of this outrageous act. The search was indefatigable until Robertson was captured near the Jefferson County line by colored man, who at once conveyed him to Morgan's Fork, within half a mile of the place where the deed was committed. The news of the capture spread rapidly, and in less than two hours after the capture of the flend not less than 300 or 400 people, both black and white, had assembled at Morgan's Fork, where the prisoner was held. The question as to what disposition was to be made of him was agitated, and it was finally proposed to take the vote of the large crowd assembled, which was done, showing the crowd to be unanimously in favor of hanging the brutish scoundrel, which was at once done. The affair is described as one of the most quiet and orderly hangings. Good order prevailed throughout, and it was done in open daylight on the public highway, witnessed by as many as 400 people, both white and black. This ended the career of this young demon, who was only 10 years of age.

In Knoxville Lizzie Moran, a beautiful young girl, has been sleeping eight days, awakening only a few moments for food. This ease puzzles the doctors.

The ship Bolton Abbey, from New Castle, N. S. W., for San Francisco, has been totally wrecked on the Pratas reef, China Sea. Seven person were drowned.

In Plain City, Ohio, William Wilcox, “a dissipated member of a prominent and wealthy family,” fatally beat his wife, and then, going into a wood near by, hanged himself.

A fire at Olean, N. Y., yesterday destroyed Clement’s bakery, Franklin’s grocery, Whitney’s tenement house and Osborne’s dwelling. The loss aggregates about $4,000 and is fully insured.

Mrs. Margaret Noughton, the oldest citizen of the state of Illinois, has died in Danville, aged nearly one hundred and sixteen. She was born in county Mayo, Ireland, 1765.

Owing to the long continued drought and the low water, the Passiac river at Paterson, N. J., below the iron bridges, is covered with dead fish, which drift against the bank, get strained and lie decomposing in the sun, emitting a terrible stench.

It is reported that a new conspiracy against the life of the emperor of Russia has been discovered, Nihilists in the telegraphic service having on various occasions betrayed to the conspirators news concerning the emperor’s intended journeys.

In Bloomville, Ohio, Clarence Opt and W. Swassick had a desperate duel in the street. Opt, who is a young desperado and ex-convict, attacked Swassick, a quarry laborer. Both drew pistols. Each fired three times, Swassick shooting Opt through the breast and arm. Opt missed each time. Opt was carried home and died.

In Franklin county, Miss., a mob captured Elias Robertson, colored, who attacked Mrs. Ellen Johnson, an old white lady. There were nearly four hundred in the crowd. A vote was taken and it was decided that Elias should swing. He was without loss of time hung to an oak limb. The lynching was in broad daylight.

FRANKLIN J. MOSES, formerly Governor of South Carolina, has been up in the police headquarters at New York for swindling William L. Hall out of $25.

THERE have recently arrived by steamship at New Orleans 800 German and 300 English immigrants, for settlement in Texas, and 250 Italian laborers for work upon the New York, Texas & Mexican Railway.

An oil train of fifty cars on the Eric Railway, took fire near Port Jervis, N. Y. Fifteen cars were cut loose from the rear of the train, where the fire occurred, and the remainder of the train was pulled off to a safe distance. As the burning cars exploded volumes of flames shot hundreds of feet into the air, and the burning oil and fragments of tanks were thrown 1,000 yards. So intense was the heat that the telegraph wires were melted.

ARIZONA BILL, an old Government scout, whose real name was James A. Lewis, was shot and killed by the Marshal of Crested Butte, Colo., the other day. Bill got drunk and tried to "run the town."

Two men were killed and three others badly injured by the falling of some masonry near Livermore, Pa.

WILLIAM KROEGER, aged 60, and his wife, aged 50, residing near Vincennes, Ind., were brutally beaten by two negroes, who broke into their bedroom at two o'clock in the morning for the purpose of robbery. Kroeger rose up in bed and was immediately knocked back by a blow on the head. His wife then raised up, with a similar result. After striking the woman two blows and Kroeger five, rendering them senseless, the villains searched until they found what money was in the house, $15, and then escaped. As soon as they were out of the room, Kroeger, whose reason had returned, sprang out of bed, grabbed his gun and fired both barrels after them, but his eyes were full of blood and his aim was poor. They got away, but were subsequently arrested. There is great excitement, with some talk of lynching.

PULASKI, N. Y., burned on the 6th to the extent of $200,000.

At Shenandoah, Page County, Iowa, Robert Bell was shot and killed by his wife in a fit of insanity. She declares that she was commanded by an angel to commit the deed.

A FIRE at Pine Bluff, Ark., on the morning of the 7th, destroyed about $100,000 worth of property, including the office of the Press, E. L. Taylor & Co.'s dry-goods store and J. H. Dellman's hardware store. Partially insured.

THE Rose City Flouring-mills of Little Rock, one of the largest manufacturing establishments of the Southwest, were totally destroyed by fire on the 6th. Loss between $30,000 and $40,000, partially insured.

SEVERE frosts have occurred in the Carolinas and Virginia, injuring tobacco and, it is feared, killing the late growth of cotton.

THE Protestant ministers of Washington called on the President on the 7th.

MISS SADIE SIMS, of Raleigh, N. C., was fatally poisoned by the administration of arsenic by mistake for quinine. Her sister, who committed the fatal error, was crazed with grief.

Wm. Cox, Jesse Monroe and Wm. Delancy, the three young men who robbed the Iron Mountain Express Company and the passengers on train No. 4. near Hope, Ark., September 22, pleaded guilty to fourteen indictments for robbery, and were each sentenced to seventy years in the Penitentiary.

HAM WHITE, a Texas highwayman, has been sentenced to the Penitentiary for ninety-nine years.

Two robbers, known as Clark alias Butch, and Frenchy, both formerly of the notorious Stockton gang, were lynched at Socorro, N. M. William Nicholson was lynched at Saunders Station, N. M., for murder. Church, the murderer of Miss Thompson, Newton, N. C., was taken from tail and hanged.

A Colored Murderer Lynched.
LOUISVILLE, July 27.—A special to the Commercial from Tiptonville, Tenn., says Felix Wyley, colored, was taken from jail by one hundred and fifty masked men and lynched. He was committed on a charge of outraging and murdering a young lady named Hall on the 13th. When found her body was mashed to a jelly and the flesh nearly eaten off the bones by hogs. MURDER NEAR TIPFONVILLE — In formation has reached here to the effect that the body of a white woman—a hired girl of good character—was found dead in the river, near Tiptonville, Tenn., last Friday or Saturday, and that the body showed marks of violence and rape. This much is known to be a fact by our informant; but since, the report has obtained that the citizens had become satisfied that a certain negro man was guilty of the horrid crime, and had actually hung him and burnt his body. In regard to the hanging and burning, our information is not authentic, but it appears to be a fact that the terrible crime was committed, and we know the good people on the river below us have had so much of dastardly crime lately, that they are not in a frame of mind to show much mercy to such fiends; and neither should they. Hence we are prepared to believe the rumors.

Hanging of the Negro Felix Wyley by the Citizens of Tiptonville East Wednesday Evening. Details of the Fiendish Crime for Which the Black Scoundrel Was Strangled.
TIPTONVILLE, TENN., July 28.—One Felix Wyley, a large, black, desperate negro, was taken out of jail at this place between 8 and 9 o'clock Monday night and hanged. He had been in this community a year or more, and came here from Union City, where he killed a man and put him on the railroad. He was also an escaped convict from Nashville, prior to coming to Union City. He boasted to some of his most intimate acquaintances of these facts, and that he had committed a rape on a woman, and would not stand back to kill anybody, black or white. He committed a rape upon the body of a young white lady and then murdered her, on the evening of July 13th. The young lady had been to town and was returning home when seized upon by the black fiend, and after accomplishing his aim destroyed her life to hide his deed. After the young lady was discovered missing search was made for her, but with no success, until more than a week afterward, when a portion of her body was found near the road. The hogs and dogs had devoured it, leaving only a part of the bones, her fan, parasol, and hat to mark the spot where the hellish act was perpetrated. This negro gave good reasons for suspicion, and after finding her remains he was arrested and placed in jail. A number of men appeared at the jail Sunday night and demanded Sheriff Pittman to surrender his prisoner, and it was only through the most earnest appeals by the Sheriff that saved the prisoner's life then. Mr. Pittman asked them to wait until next day and let the negro have his preliminary trial before taking his life. They finally concluded to do so, but assuring him that they intended to have the prisoner to-morrow (Monday) night if they had to burn the jail. The negro had his trial the following day, and the chain of circumstantial evidence was so strong and conclusive against him that they more firmly resolved to put him to death that night. A large number of people were in town during the trial, and much interest was made manifest over the occasion. Everything being made ready, a band of about fifty men, white and black, suddenly made their appearance before the Sheriff and Jailer, and ordered of him the keys. He had summoned a number of our citizens as guards that night, but only a few of them had arrived before the mob dashed in, and that is why the mob was successful in reaching the jail and surrounding the sheriff and his posses. sheriff and his posse, for Lay at first thought it was a party of their own men coming in. The mob placed cocked pistols and guns to She sheriff's face and breast and requested him at once to give up the keys. They would not listen to any reasoning, but told him to surrender the keys or his life and no hesitation. The Sheriff promptly unlocked the jail doors, and the crowd rushed around him so closely, and there being no light in the house, that one Sam Hudson, who was in jail on the charge of murder, and awaiting our approaching Circuit Court, was let out before the Sheriff had any knowledge of it. It is supposed he crawled out between the negro's legs, which, no doubt, was a part of the mobs programme. This part of the proceedings is especially regretted by our people, and diligent search is being made for Hudson. Mr. Pittman, the Sheriff, was much grieved over the results, but it was beyond his power to prevent them, under such unpleasant circumstances. He felt his great responsibility, but could not do otherwise than to surrender to the demands of the raving mob. Mr. Pittman has the sympathies of the law-abiding people over the misfortune, and also their thanks and a still warmer support for so nobly endeavoring to do his whole duty in protecting his prisoners. He offers a reward for the capture of Hudson.

The Nashville American of yesterday has the following special telegram from Hickman: "Reliable information from Tiptonville, Tennessee, thirty miles below here on the Mississippi river, gives the particulars of a horrible crime and its punishment by mob law. A few days ago the body of an orphan girl, — Hall, who had been missing for ten days, was found in a fence corner near the public road, bearing evidences that she had been ravished and murdered in the most shocking manner. The hogs had farther added to the horrors of the body's condition. Monday last a negro named Felix Wyley was arrested, and from evidence elicited on the trial was supposed to be the criminal. Testimony showed that Wyley had been seen near the place where the outrage occurred, and that he carried a heavy club with him; that a negro woman who did his washing found his clothes spattered with blood about the time of the murder. Suspicion centered on Felix Wyley, and a warrant being issued he was accordingly arrested that night (Thursday) and placed in jail. By Saturday the matter became widely known and the excitement grew warm. Sunday night a number of citizens visited the jail and demanded Mr. Pittman, the sheriff and jailer, to give them the prisoner. It was only through the most earnest appeals that Mr. Pittman succeeded in getting them to let the negro remain undisturbed until he could have a preliminary trial. On Monday he had a preliminary hearing before R. S. Bradford, Jas Hogan and Thes. Keete, Esqs., and the chain of circumstantial evidence was so close and convincing that the visiting delegation more firmly resolved to give the negro a hearing before their tribunal. The court-house was filled with an eager and interested crowd, and some thought the negro would not be able to reach jail again. He did, however, but only for a short season, for between 8 and 9 o'clock that night a number of citizens, white and black, suddenly appeared at the jail and demanded of Mr. Pittman the keys. He and what few of the guards that had arrived endeavored to reason with the party, but with cocked pistols placed at his face he was ordered to hand over the keys at once. Under such unpleasant circumstances Mr. Pittman could not do otherwise than to surrender to their wish, so he promptly unlocked the doors. There was no light about the building and they crowded so closely around Mr. Pittman at the cage door that Hudson escaped before Mr. Pittman had any knowledge of it. The visiting statesmen lost no time in getting hold on the negro and starting off with him. They went as far as Dan Tipton's old gin shed, where they spent some time trying to get all the information they could from the negro, but he had nothing of especial interest to impart to them. They then proceeded up the cross lane about two hundred yards and about twenty-five yards beyond Jo. Tipton's barn, where they struck camp under a sycamore tree in the middle of the road. They again requested the negro to tell all he knew about the matter, whether there were others implicated. Every time they drew him up and let him down he told a different story. They could get no satisfaction out of his statements, and finally pulled him up for good and left him swinging until morning, after firing several shots into his body. The next morning Esquire Bradford, with his coroner's jury, held an inquest and rendered the necessary verdict, then had him interred.

Galveston, December 30. Mr. T. M. Healy, Irish member of Parliament, who is to address the citizens of Galvestan at the Tremont Opera-house Monday evening upon the subject of "Ireland and Her Cause," telegraphs from New Orleans that he will arrive in the morning. The Journal this afternoon, reviewing the crime for which the negress Nancy Holmes was pardoned a few days since by Governor Roberts and who was sentenced to life imprisonment in the penitentiary, presents it in all its fiendishness and concludes: "The exercise of the pardoning power in this case in an insult to the decent, law-abiding residents of this city."

The details of the crime are as follows: On the morning of November 16th, 1872, at Frogtown, near the freight yards of the Galveston, Houston & Henderson Railroad, was discovered the dead body of a white woman, clad in a single thin garment. The inquest developed the fact that the deceased, Mrs. Mary Madden, a woman of intemperate habits and well-known in the city, went into the negro settlement in Frogtown, on the 14th of November, 1872, while drunk, where she was set upon by several women, taken to a vacant house, terribly beaten with sticks and clubs by two negresses, Nancy Holmes and Pleas. Sydnor, and a nameless outrage perpetrated on her. The body was disinterred and a second inquest was held and the post-mortem examination resulted in a verdict of "death from violence, at the hands of parties unknown." November 27 an indictment was presented, charging Nancy Holmes and Pleas. Sydnor with murder. Thursday, December 5, 1872, Nancy Holmes was put on trial in the Criminal District Court. The details of the trial were of a repulsive character. The prisoner evinced no concern whatever during the trial, and when the jury rendered a verdict of murder in the first degree, punishment assessed at imprisonment in the penitentiary for life, she moved not a muscle of her countenance.

The Galveston News at the time said: The case in all its features was the most outrageous disclosed by the records of Texas, one for which no punishment is within the scope of human power.

BOSTON, December 30.—The Common Council of the city of Somerville, Massachusetts, passed an order to-night expelling Councilman Hiram A. Pratt for appropriating to his own use some $1500 water tax, collected by him. He had previously made good the amount.

PHILADELPHIA, December 30.—The grand jury, at the December term, in their final presentment to the court, call attention that the number of houses of ill-fame are rapidly multiplying, and are now numbered by thousands. New York, December 30.—Louis Henri, a saloon keeper on West Twenty-sixth street, was shot and instantly killed in his house this morning by burglars.

Lindsay, the noted Missouri land swindler, who was convicted there on the 20th instant, was brought into court this evening and sentenced by Judge Patrick to nine years in the penitentiary. PHILADELPHIA, December 30.—George Wood, alias Miller, who personated Frederick Schutz on a recent election jury, pleaded guilty to the charges of perjury and embracery, and was sentenced to five years and ten months on the perjury charge, and one year for embracery, the latter concurrent with the former owing to pleading guilty.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., December 30.—Police Officer Martin Hynes was shot and killed by Clay Crenshaw, proprietor of the White House saloon. LITTLE ROCK, December 30.—Details of a horrible tragedy at Bentonville, Ark., reached the city to-day. It appears that last Saturday morning Coroner Hazard was notified that a man had been murdered at Rogers the night previous. On his arrival at that place it was found that a jury had been impanneled by Mayor Sickles and the inquest was in progress.

The murdered man, named Eson Bollin, a carpenter by trade, lately moved into the State from Stone county, Mo., and found work at Rogers. He was living in a small house, with an old man, named Martin, boarding with him. It seems that both Bollin and Martin took their supper as usual and retired to bed at an early hour. Sometime before midnight Martin was aroused by the report of a pistol in the house and saw Bollin's wife advancing towards his bed, when she exclaimed that some one had shot him (meaning her husband). He says she did not seem to be affected any more than to shed a few tears. He at once went out and made the fact known.

Both Martin and the woman were arrested, but it was soon discovered that Martin was in no way connected with the crime.

During the examination of Mrs. Bollin she confessed to the killing of him herself. The pistol was then found where she had hastily concealed it, everything confirmed her statement. The ball passed through his head, killing him instantly. She justified the crime by saying that her husband had killed two men, was a horse thief, and had made stealing his business in every place in which they had been, and that he had threatened her life at various times. On two occasions he had drawn a knife on her, and that her life was most mite able with him. It is said that her statements were made in a cool, unaffected manner, while the dead body of her husband was so near that she could have touched it. The verdict of the jury was rendered in accordance with the statements made by her. She, together with her four little children, were brought to Bentonville, where she was lodged in jail. Three of the children were sent to the poor house, and she was permitted to take the youngest, an infant son three months old, into the jail with her. She was placed in the cell with Mrs. Arney, who is indicted for murder, and which is situated in the northeast corner of the third story of the court house, entirely separated from the cage in which all the prisoners are confined. When being placed in jail she made inquiry as to whether it was a bailable case, stating that she had two brothers in good circumstances who would arrange bail for her. On being informed that she would not be permitted to give bail she, for the first time, seemed to realize her situation and wept bitterly. Since that time Mrs. Arney says she has slept but little if any. She conceived the fear that she would be mobbed, and said frequently that such would be the case, that she had been told so by some party while being brought from Rogers.

Judge Elliott visited the jail Monday morning to learn the whereabouts of her relatives so he could inform them of her situation. She informed him that she was the daughter of a widow lady named E A. Gibson, who resides near Savannah, Mo. She also stated that she had a brother named James Johnson residing in Savannah, Mo., and a half brother named Sam'l Gibson at Gainsboro, Tenn.

The jailor, Captain Patton, took the prisoners their dinner at 2 o'clock P. M. and returned from the jail for a short time and then returned to show some parties through the prison. After the spectators had spent some time in prison he let them pass down, and when he returned to get some vessels in which he carried their dinner, Mrs. Bollin asked him to let her have his knife, as she wished to cut up a dress to make her baby some clothing. As he had frequently loaned Mrs. Arney his knife he mistrusted no evil' design, and handed it to her. During the time Mrs. Arney was engaged in sweeping the room, he stepped outside for some little time, then opened the door and asked if she was through with the knife, and replied, "Not quite." At this time Mrs. Arney had swept out and was shoveling it into a kettle. Mr. Patton again opened the door, when a most ghastly sight met his eyes. St. Louis, May 21.—Information from Poplar Bluff, Mo., is to the effect that Hamilton, Meyers and Brown, the outlawaws who shot Sheriff Davis and Collector Hatten yesterday, near Greenville, were overhauled near Mill Springs by a searching party under Capt. W. T. Leeper, early this morning, and Hamilton killed, Meyers mortally wounded and Brown captured. Meyers and Brown are now at Mill Springs under guard, and threats of lynching have been made. It appears that Sheriff Davis was not killed, as first reported, but perhaps mortally wounded, and it is feared Hatten's injury will prove fatal.

LAKE CITY, COL., May 21.—The Sheriff of Rio Grande county last night captured three of a gang of highwaymen near this place, among them the notorious criminal Billy Leroy, who escaped some time ago from a deputy United States Marshal on a Kansas Pacific train while being taken to the Detroit penitentiary. Leroy resisted capture and was badly wounded in the leg by the Sheriff's revolver. This gang robbed a mail coach on the 18th, instantly killing a passenger named Frank Bartlett. The citizens threaten to lynch the robbers.

CINCINNATI'S MAYOR.

Ha Has Become Very Unpopular with the Democrats—They Propose to Hold a Public Meeting and Denounce His Conduct Since His Elevation to Office.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

CINCINNATI, O., May 23.—A hall has been hired and a meeting called by a number of Democrats of this city for the purpose of denouncing the policy of the Reform Mayor, Mr. William Means. The meeting will be held on Saturday night next, and is called by some of the most prominent Democrats who are accustomed to mix in local politics. The complaint against Mayor Means is, that he is untrue to the party who elected him, and it is proposed to formally announce his disloyalty at a public meeting called for that purpose, and to give him back to the easy-going and wealthy clique from whom he came. The Mayor was elected six weeks ago by a combination of the Democratic party and a considerable class of Republicans who were anxious to see certain reforms carried out touching liquor-selling and the observance of the Sabbath. Means, it was thought by the Democrats, could be easily handled, and half a dozen of the old party leaders each flattered himself that he would be the new Mayor's confidential adviser and the power behind the throne. When elected, however, Mr. Means announced that he wanted no advice from anybody, and, though supported by the whole Democratic party, would give none of its leaders a hearing as to how the patronage should be distributed. A few Democratic politemen received appointments, but it was entirely through their own efforts. Those who depended upon the leaders of the party for recommendation and assistance had no attention paid to their applications. "The same was true of applicants for other offices, and the rank and file of the party, as well as its leaders, have naturally became very sore, and the step which they have now resolved to take has been talked of for some time. The Reform Republicans have been better satisfied with the Mayor's course, for the reason that there has been some effort at reform, although the results are hardly appreciable. The Mayor is a life-long Democrat, but knows nothing about politics, and, being of an obstinate disposition, he got his party by the ears at the very outset. The effect, of course, has been to greatly strengthen the Republicans. The Democratic victory at the spring election, unexpectedly to everybody, is proving to be one of the best things for the Republican party that could have happened.

Sheriff Davis was carried back to Greenville, where he died Sunday morning. Mr. Hatton was crazed by the wound received in his head, but is reported to be in fair way of recovering.

The people of Wayne county were thoroughly aroused, as Davis and Hatton are both among the most popular citizens of the county, and five hundred men commenced searching the woods, and a reward of $2,000, in addition to the $2,000 offered by New Madrid county, was offered for the capture of the murderers.

Capt. W. T. Leeper, an old and substantial citizen of Wayne county, was called on late Friday night to engage in the search for the desperadoes. He consulted with three other gentlemen, Messrs. Ambrose Beatty, Cal. Thomas and Taylor Fulton. Mr. Leeper said he was almost certain that the men would try to cross Black river, about two miles below Mill Springs, at a place known as "Campbell's Switch." He and a party therefore spent Friday night at the above place, where there is a ferry across the river. Saturday morning, just as day-light approached and the faithful guards were permitted to distinguish an object at some distance, the hunted game, Myers and Hamilton, made their approach walking up the railroad. At first Leeper and party mistook them for a party of their own men who had been watching at a station down the river two miles below their stand. As the party approached and when within five feet of Leeper and posse he recognized them as the famous New Madrid desperadoes and immediately prepared to give them a warm reception. Cocking his gun, Leeper hailed them with, "Hold on there," when they at once wheeled and presented their shot-guns. Simultaneously Leeper and party fired upon them. Both men fell in their tracks, James Hamilton being killed outright, receiving not less than ten buckshot in the back of his head, while Jesse Myers, his companion, was only temporarily stunned by an ugly shot in the forehead. The pursuing party had gotten the drop on them so completely that they were unable to get a shot, though both men fell with double-barrel shot-guns cocked in their hands.

The posse then obtained a hand-car and transported the dead and wounded prisoners to Mill Springs. The third and last of the gang, Frank Brown, was still at large, but Saturday morning word was brought to Mill Springs that he was seen swimming the river a few miles east of town, and a number of pursuers started in pursuit. Taking up the trail they tracked Brown a distance of ten or twelve miles, and about dusk in the evening crossed over into Reynolds county. J. N. Morrison, Prosecuting Attorney of Wayne county, in company with the others, spied a man in the timber ahead, and pushing on until within speaking distance drew a bead on one who proved to be none other than Brown and ordered hands up. Though heavily armed Brown saw he was caught and surrendered without resistance. He was ironed and taken to Mill Springs where he was kept until the morning passenger train passed, when he was taken to Poplar Bluff.

Brown's statements are conflicting, and he evidently thinks that the greater stories he will tell the better his chances. His wounds are not dangerous. Sunday morning he was sitting up conversing freely.

At six o'clock Sunday morning Myers and Brown were heavily ironed, and, under guard of the New Madrid party and W. T. Leeper and J. N. Morrison, were taken from Poplar Bluff on the east-bound freight for Sikeston, from where they were taken to New Madrid by wagon.

LATER.—The prisoners were taken to New Madrid and lodged in jail; but the Sheriff secretly took them out to the river and crossed in a skiff to Hickman, Ky., where they took a steamboat for St. Louis. Monday night the Sheriff landed his prisoners safely in the St. Louis jail. If they had remained in New Madrid they would have been lynched ere this. Three hundred citizens were on the alert for the job which was to have been done Sunday night.

"The following circular was published by order of the County Court of New Madrid county, Mo.
"Two thousand dollars ($2,000) reward is offered for the capture of the outlaws, Jesse Myers, James O. Hamilton and F. Brown, who fired into the Sheriff's posse, killing one and wounding two others in New Madrid county, Mo., on Wednesday. May 11th, 1881, or if either of them is captured, the reward will be paid in the following proportion: One thousand dollars ($1,000) for Meyers, and five hundred dollars ($500) for each of the others.
The crime for which a Sheriff's posse was pursuing the outlaws at the time of the above tragedy, was their attack on William Knox's house in New Madrid county on Monday night, May 9. A gang of four consisting of Jesse Meyers, James O. Hamilton, Robert Rhoades and F. O. Brown went to Knox's house, with the avowed intention of killing him. Being informed of the purpose of their visit, Knox fled by a backdoor and thus saved his life. As the party approached the house they saw George Williams enter the house from the yard, and supposing it was Knox, they immediately opened fire upon him, shooting some twelve or fifteen volleys of buckshot at the house. Williams was wounded in the leg, and a little girl who was living with Knox received two wounds. The women fled from the house to the barn, followed by several volleys of buckshot, but without effect. The villains followed them to the barn, but as the women had climbed up into the loft and hid themselves, they escaped detection, and after a short search the murderers returned to the house, and after shooting a few more shots into it, they entered in search of Knox. In the meantime Williams had left the house and dragged himself to the back of the field, where he passed a sleepless night of agony. Having made diligent search for Knox, they then dressed the wounds of the little girl and left the house, but watched around for Knox until daylight. The girl died from wounds. Being attracted by the cries of Williams, they went to him, and carrying him to a pond near by, they gave him some water, washed and dressed his wounds for him, and assured him they did not wish to hurt him—it was Knox they were after. The origin seems to have been an old grudge.

Knox at once procured a mule from a near neighbor and started to town for help. A warrant was promptly issued, and the sheriff summoned a posse and started in pursuit. Keeping a sharp look out on one of the murderer's houses with a telescope, the sheriff's posse saw one of the women take a basket to the barn, and correctly supposed that it contained dinner for the objects of their search, and that they were in the barn, but in this they were mistaken.

Accordingly they mounted their horses and rode to the spot, but as they approached the place they discovered the four men just emerging from a dense thicket of hazel brush that stood distant but a few hundred yards. The parties discovered each others' presence about the same time, and the fugitives immediately retreated to the thicket, and as the pursuers passed the house they were tauntingly told by one of the women that some of their party would be hauled back from the chase.

The fugitives soon regained the cover of the bushes, and as the place was small, the sheriff's posse immediately surrounded it on all sides, but little did they know of the condition of that fatal thicket, or of the character of the enemy they were confronting. This was their secret hiding place. In the midst of it they had a breastwork of oak logs three feet high, which entirely surrounded them on three sides, and armed with a double-barrelled shotgun and four navy six-shooters to each man, enabling them to fire 101 shots before having to reload. they could fight four times their number with ease. In addition to all this, it now appears that they were shielded both back and front with steel plates made with their own hands from cross cut saws. Unconscious of all these things, and unable to see this pitfall on account of the denseness of the thicket, the sheriff's party formed and started through the thicket, unconsciously dividing and passing on both sides of it. The first note of warning was the crack of a pistol from the murderers, less than ten paces distant from the left wing of the party. The shot struck a pistol in the belt of Mr. John Schafer, shattering the handle and driving the splinters into his body. Scarcely had the sound been heard, when it was followed by a deafening report of firearms from the same spot, and Robert Laforge, a most worthy and exemplary young man, fell dead upon the ground. Next to him stood Albert Hunter, who was shot through the neck with a large ball; the blood streamed forth from the wound in profusion, but his wounds are not considered dangerous. Another man who was near by was wounded in the leg. They next turned their attention to the right wing of the party, and the first move was to order Dr. L. A. Waters to give up his gun, to which the doctor responded by giving them the contents thereof. Mr. J. Ellis also fired two loads of buckshot at them, and then the firing ceased, and as they could not see the parties they were forced to retire.

As soon as the Sheriff could collect his men he sent for a physician and more help. In the meantime, Dr. Bogan went into the thicket and recovered Mr. Laforge's body, by the consent of his murderers, but it was robbed of his gold watch, pistols, and about $19 in currency. His body was horribly mutilated, and made his death the more painful to his relatives and friends. A very short notice was sufficient to fill the country full of armed men, and it does not seem possible that any of the scoundrels can escape.

Robert Rhoads was captured on Wednesday evening, May 11, at the residence of Mr. J. D. Stepp. He received five wounds in the battle of the thicket, and was forced to seek shelter. He died Thursday morning.

A later account gives intelligence of the killing on Thursday, May 19th, of John T. Davis, sheriff, and the wounding of James F. Hatton, collector of Wayne county, by the three desperadoes. The men fled. The people of Wayne county are intensely excited, and 500 are said to be scouring the woods in all directions for the murderers. A reward of $2,000 was

STARBING AFFRAY. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. KANSAS CITY, Mo., Aug. 16. — Peter Hughes, one of the men stabbed into last night by William Bailey, alias "Dago Bill," died at the Sisters' Hospital at 9 o'clock this afternoon. Bailey was met by Hughes and a young man named Baughman in the Marble Hall saloon, and the two began "skylarking" with him. At last the fun was carried too far, and when Hughes threw his arms about Bailey's neck, and Baughman had his hand in his pocket, he struck at them with a knife, cutting both. Baughman only received a slight cut in the chest, but his companion received a terrible stab in the abdomen, from which he never rallied. SAFE ACROSS THE BORDER.
JEFFERSON CITY, Mo., Aug. 10.—Mr. Willis, the Warden of the Missouri Penitentiary, received a telegram to-day from his son, who went as State Agent to Halifax to bring back the notorious swindler and bogus priest Gallen Derohan, with a score of alluses, who escaped from the Missouri Penitentiary some months ago, stating that the authorities there refused to give him up on the ground that forgery, the crime of which he was convicted. is not an offense for which a prisoner is subject to extradition. It is stated in this connection by Mr. Willis that the document to which President Garfield attached his signature a few days ago was the extradition paper in this case.

GALVESTON, Tex., Aug. 10.—A San Antonio special says an unsuccessful attempt was made yesterday to wreck an excursion-train having on board 550 men, women, and children, by laying ties across the track. The train was going at the rate of thirty miles an hour when the engine struck the ties, which were thrown from the track, badly bruising five men riding on the cow-catcher.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
GRAND HAVEN, Mich., Aug. 10.—The Coroner's jury rendered a verdict this morning that John Alguiro killed both his mother and the colored man Green,—the negro by shooting him in the head with the shotgun, and his mother by a blow on the back of the head with the stock of the gun, which was broken.

ASSASINATED. Memphis, Tenn., Aug. 10.—Henry Foster, a colored farmer, five miles north of Covington, Tenn., was called out of his house last night and shot to death. The assasin escaped.

HYMENEAL.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune,
BLOOMINGTON, Ill., Aug. 16.—Mr. Edward B. Gridley and Miss Ora Wulton, two leading members of Bloomington society, were united in marriage at noon to-day at the home of the bride on East Locust street in the presence of a few intimate friends and relatives. As Mr. Gridley is perhaps the wealthiest young man in McLean County, and both groom and bride are greatly respected, the event was one of far more than ordinary importance. The Rev. Dr. Read, pastor of the First Baptist Church, spoke the mystic words, and after handshaking and farewells the happy pair took the Chicago & Alton train for Chicago and the East. They will be absent about three weeks, visiting Coney Island, Isle of Shoals, and other watering-places, and on their return will take up permanently their residence here, for the time occupying part of the magnificent Gridley homestead. Mr. Gridley is the younger son of Gen. Ashbel Gridley, whose recent death was chronicled by Dirk Turrone, and who was one of the ablest financiers and lawyers and most public spirited men who have ever lived in Central Illinois. His bride is the eldest daughter of John T. Walton, plow manufacturer, an old an honored citizen and prominent business man. She is a graceful and stately brunette and has been much admired and honored by Bloomington society, of which she has always been a leading mem-

ber. She was dressed in a travelling costume of surah satin of hunter's green, trimmed in green and gold, with bonnet to match, face at throat fastened with a costly and beautiful brooch of diamonds presented by the groom. The groom wore a plain and simple business suit. The wedding was entirely devoid of show and ostentation.

CASUALTIES.

ACCIDENT AT A COAL-SHAFT.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
CENTRALIA, Ill., Aug. 16.—Last night William Craig, out of curiosity, went behind the wires stretched to guard the coal-shaft, and craned his neck over the hole just in time to catch the cage. It started ten feet above and came down with a rush, jamming Craig's head between it and the curbing, and crushing that member to an unrecognizable mass. Marks of the teeth were left in the hard wood of the curbing. Craig was a well-known and respected man and leaves many relatives here. He was not married.

HINTON.
TOO MUCH CHRISTMAS—A ROW—ONE POLICE-MAN SHOT AND BADLY BEATEN—ANOTHER BARELY ESCAPES—GREAT EXCITEMENT—THE WEATHER.

[Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.]

DECEMBER 30, 1881.

On Sunday morning last three drunken rowdies going down Third street passed a negro, whom one of them (Farris) commenced to beat most unmercifully and without the least provocation. The negro ran into the Central Hotel, where he is employed as porter. The case was reported by the proprietor to Mayor Benedict, who sent policeman John Palmer to arrest Farris. Farris resisted, but was brought by Palmer to the Mayor's office. Some of Farris's friends followed him for the purpose of taking him from the officers, but did not succeed. Considerable excitement prevailed during the trial, and pistols were freely drawn, but no shots fired. Finally things were quieted down, and Farris, after being allowed, was allowed to take his departure.

Palmer is a stranger in town, and has only recently been put on the force. He is considerably disliked by Farris and friends, and they made frequent threats to mob him, and nearly succeeded. On Monday night between 8 and 9 o'clock, as Palmer and his assistant, Policeman McCreery, were walking up Summers street near the Mayor's office, they were attacked by a mob of fifteen or twenty and fired upon. They ran and returned the fire. Palmer succeeded in getting inside the Mayor's office. As he got in the door one of the balls fired at him barely missed him, burying itself in the edge of the door. Policeman McCreery was not so fortunate, but was shot through the knee. Three of the mob then took away his revolver and beat him terribly. He is lying in a critical condition at his home, on Fourth street. The sheriff had to be called out to quiet the row. The three principal perpetrators of the above cowardly act have disappeared, and up to this time have not been caught. The town is quiet now. Another paper, Republican in politics, will be started here the first of the year. Rains very general through this country, and the New river high. Weather warm. CHARLIE.

Western Lunatic Asylum.
In the Whig of the 31st December 1881 the appeared an article signed "A Stalwart Readjuster" purporting to give an account by an escaped lunatic from the Western Lunatic Asylum, of his cruel treatment whilst confined there. Ocourse no credence was given to it by say one in this community, and we are pleased to find that it is utterly scoured by such an intelligent and competent writer as Alexander Hunter of Alexandria, who writes to the Whig as follows

RICHMOND, VA., Dec. 31st, 1881.
To the Editor of the Whig;

I see by darkly mysterious, blood-curdling communication in the "Whig" of to-day, signed "A Stalwart Readjuster," that readful doings are hinted at as regards the Staunton Lunatic Asylum. The writer has all the imagination of Chs. Reed. A high spirited young man. Four escapes! A homeless fugitive and cruel attendants! It only needs a beautiful maiden, who falls in love with the h. f., to complete the tale.

Now Mr. Editor, I have been through the Western Lunatic Asylum many times, both in my official capacity as member of the Legislative Committee on Asylums and Prisons and as a professional journalist on the qui vive to find out all kind of romances and horrors and retail them to the press. I have examined the asylum from top to bottom; I have eaten of the meals furnished the imates; I have interviewed the patients, both confined as incurable and discharged as cured, and I have never heard me charge of either inhumanity or ill-treatment against either attendant or orsegeous.

I write this in a spirit only of fair-mindedness; do not know personally, a single offer of the asylum, and I dislike to see my wild, scatter-brained, go off-at-half-cock scribbler make false charges, based on an escaped lunatic's tale, against in institution that is a pride to Virgis.

It is wrong and many people who have some unfortunate inmate of their family—some itch and kin immured in its walls—reading such communications are rendered miserable and unhappy.

In kindness tenderness to the ones afflicted by Go, in cleanliness, in diet, in treatment, there is no institution that has done or is doing more or stands higher than the Western Lunatic Asylum.

CHASSEUR.

A SERIOUS AFFAIR at HINTON, W. VA.—We learn from the Hinton Herald that quite a serious affray occurred in that place on Monday night after Christmas when a party of men assaulted the sergeant of the place, and Fred McCreery who was appointed to act as special policeman. The Herald says:—

"Everything passed quietly until about 7 o'clock on Monday night, when the Sergeant and McCreery were coming up Summers night, near the residence of Capt. Sharp they met a party of ten or twelve men coming from an opposite direction. The two officers stepped aside to let them pass, when some of the party assaulted Fred McCreery with a club, and felled him to the ground; he attempted to draw his pistol, but it was taken from him, and several shots fired at him one of which took effect in his leg near the knee. The gang of raiders then turned their attention to the Sergeant, and run him into the store of Mayor Benedict. They fired several shots at him, and he returned the fire as he ran. McCreery, after being badly beat with sticks and stones, was left abug, and started for home. He had not gone far before he was again set upon by some of the party, severely pummeled and misused, in a most cowardly manner, seeing he was alone and wounded. * * * * *

Deputy Sheriff Lilly was informed of the trouble, and summoned a posse to arrest the men, but they fled, and under cover of the darkness made good their escape. Warrants are out for Beardon, Michaels and Faris, the ring leaders in the trouble. They have left the State, and it is not likely they will have the temerity to return again soon."
