WESTERN MURDERS. DENVER, Colo., April 18.—Saturday night Jim Dovine, alias Jones, an escaped convict from California, where a reward of $1,40 was offered for him, was lynched near Las Vegas for the attempted murder of a sootlon hand. Campbell, proprietor of the Bonton Restaurant at Doming, N. M., shot and killed a Chinnman Sunday night. Saturday night Mormon Jones, at Crano's Station, on the Atlantic & Pacific Railroad, was shot and killed by a man named Halloran in self-defense. KILLED WITH A SCALE-WEIGHT. CINCINNATI, April 18.—In the village of Rural, on the Ohio River, in Clermont County, last week, at a singing-school taught by a young Kentuckian named Carr, Alfred Reed and Harvey Hicks, both roughs, created a disturbance and were reprimanded by Carr. On the way home Reed met and whipped Carr. Afterward Reed went into a drug-store where Carr was, and the latter struck Reed with a scale-weight, killed him, and escaped. FRAUDULENT DRAFTS.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribute.

FORT WAYNE, Ind., April 18.—United States Marshal Harper has arrested Francis E. Depew and Lyman Depow at Jackson Depot, charged with fraudulently using United States malls by drawing drafts on Eastern firms, intending to twindle them. A preliminary examination takes place to-morrow.

A FIENDISH CRIME.

Pittsburgh, April 18.—On Saturday night, while a little 6-year-old girl was being undressed for bed, it was discovered that she was badly hurt. The child said Francis Heaver, 60 years old, enticed her into his workshop, and, smothering her screams, succeeded in accomplishing his hellish work. He was lodged in jail.

THE MICE AT PLAY.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

DUNDEE, Ill., April 18.—A fourful and disgusting light occurred in an East Side saloon, called by "Mouso-Trap," this afternoon, in which about fifteen men were engaged. It resulted in several men being severely pounded and one man dangerously hurt.

A RAILROAD CROSSING.

GALVESTON, April 18.—Whilo circus men were loading cars at the railroad crossing at Tunis, where men leaving town insisted on crossing at that particular place. A light ensued, in which amphell, one of the showmen, was seriously light twice through the body. Two other citizens were seriously cut.

AN OLD DARKY KILLED.

CINCINNATI, April 18.—At Hopkinsville, Christian County, Ky., Kish Baker, an old colored man, was shot and killed by an unknown person at Friday night. He said he met three men on horseback, one of whom shot him. Others say he was shot while robbing a hen-roost.

A MISSOURI FRATRACIDE. Br. Louis, April 17.—The Post-Dispatch special on Kansas City says: News has just been relied here that William Mutiox shot and killed

his brother, Heziah Muttox, four miles from Liberty, Clay County, at noon to-day. No particulars.

A FORGER ARRESTED.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
GRAND HAVEN, Mich., April 18.—Sheriff Van Pell arrived home from Canada this morning, bringing J. P. Dougherty, the forger, who chanted Dephorder, of Holland, out of $1,000 and escaped to Canada.

BURQLARY.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
DAVENPORT, Ia., April 18.—Crucksmen early this morning blew open the safe in the office of the Rock Island & Mercer County Railroad at Reynolds, getting there from $175 and a lot of tickets.

MURDERED HER CHILDREN.
CAMDEN, Ark., April 18.—Mrs. Nutt, living near this city, while in a fit of insanity Saturday last, killed five of her children by throwing them into a well. The older was 12 years, and the youngest 11 months.

GUILTY OF MURDER.

GUILTY OF MURDER.
NEW HAVEN, Conn., April 18.—The trial of the case of the State, against "Chip" Smith for the murder of Chief-of-Police Daniel J. Hayes, of Birmingham, in this county, in December last, resulted in a verdict of guilty.

LYNCHED.

JACKSONVILLE, Fla., April 18.—A negro charged with the assassination of a leading citizen of Gadesden County, some time since, was taken from jail in Quincy Sunday by disgusted men and hanged.

DISCHARGED.
READING, Pa., April 18.—Gottschalk, Butterwick, and Eyler, arrested Saturday, charged with a murder fifteen years ago, have been discharged.

LABOR AND CAPITAL.

CLEVELAND,
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

CLEVELAND, O., April 18.—Considerable talk is indulged in among street-railway employers over the movement in other cities for better wages and less hours, and there is a disposition to follow the example of the strikers. A meeting will be held on Wednesday night after working hours, at which the men will decide on some definit action. They will probably send a written petition to their employers, asking for a raise, the drivers wanting $2 a day and the other employes a proportionate amount. The drivers say they will also ask for shorter hours. They are now paid $10 a week.

CLEVELAND, O., April 18.—The molders are out in all but three or four foundries of this city, leaving between fifteen and twenty works like. The employers have also combined, and obedient to their order the proprietors of the Globe works, who yielded to the demand of 15 per cent advance, to-day notified their men that they could no longer pay the advance and the men went out. Both sides are determined and both organized. All classes of workingmen seem to be preparing to strike if not paid what they may decide to demand. Nearly all kinds of tradesmen here, even hod-carriers, have been called to meet and organize unions, and a call has been issued to all street railway employees to meet at midnight, after work is done, to arrange a demand for more pay. Apparently some central power is at the bottom of the organization of so many labor unions throughout the country. Doubtless strikes are contemplated everywhere like 1877.

HORSEHOERS' NATIONAL UNION.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

Pittsburgh, Pa., April 18.—A convention of the National Association of Journeymen Horse-shoers is in session at the Globe Hotel, on Penn avenue. The Association includes ten cities, viz.: Chicago, Baltimore, St. Louis, Philadelphia, Toledo, New York, Boston, Cincinnati, Brooklyn, and Pittsburgh. The officers of the National Association are Joseph Snyder, of Baltimore, President; William Frazer, of Toledo, Vice President; Ed F. Butter, of St. Louis, Treasurer; Dennis Mitchell, of Chicago, Secretary. The Convention is composed of only ten delegates, when all are present. Up to last night only five had arrived, they being the following: From Union No. 2, Baltimore, E. V. Foster; No. 3, St. Louis, Ed Graham; No. 4 Chicago, Edward Carroll; No. 6, Philadelphia, William Brown; No. 10, Toledo, William Frazer. The Pittsburg Union is counted among the ten Unions, although it is an independent organization and does not belong to the National Association. It is connected in some way with the Knights of Labor, and the members don't know hardly what to do. A meeting of the Union was held last night to decide whether or not they should go into the Association. The Association is a beneficial organization. It allows $5 a week benefits for sickness or disability from injuries. One of its objects is to prevent strikes rather than encourage them, only asking "a fair day's wages for a four day's work." The Convention will be in session four days. The Association was organized eight years ago, and this is the seventh annual meeting.

Murder in North Carolina.
RALEIGH, N. C., November 25.—Thomas M. Lynch, an old citizen, and widely known, who resided outside of Oxford, North Carolina, disappeared on Tuesday night. A hunt was made for him by his two sons, who found his body in the road. Beside him lay a fence rail, in which was a heavy nail. His head was crushed and the nail had penetrated into the brain. His sons found two young negro men under a bridge dividing money taken from their father's body. One had Mr. Lynch's watch and the keys of his store. The men were arrested and are now in jail.

RALEIGH, N. C., November 26.—A special from Oxford says there is strong talk of lynching the workman who murdered the jeweler, Lynch, at that place. A guard has been placed around the jail to protect the prisoner.

The Report of the Secretary of the Navy.

WASHINGTON, December 1st.—The annual report of the Secretary of the Navy was made public to-day. Secretary Hunt at the outset calls the attention of Congress to the neglected condition of the navy, and says that unless some action be had in its behalf it must soon dwindle to insignificance. He devotes considerable space to the consideration of the reports of the bureau officers of the navy, and generally indoles the recommendations submitted by his subordinates.

The Life-Saving Service.

WASHINGTON, December 1st.—The Superintendent of the Life-saving Service, in his annual report, says that at the close of the fiscal year the service included 183 stations—143 on the Atlantic, 34 on the lakes and six on the Pacific; number of casualties on the Atlantic coast within the scope of the service, 151; on the lakes, 94; on the Pacific, 53; number of persons lost, 26; number brought ashore by life-saving appliances, 408, and succor was afforded to 407 at the various stations. One hundred and seventy-eight vessels were helped by the life-saving crews to get off when stranded, and piloted to places of safety.

Two Men Lynched.

RALEIGH (N. C.), December 1st.—Early this morning masked men took from the Oxford Jail John Brodie and Shadrack Hester (colored), charged with the murder of T. M. Lynch, and hanged them in a small grove near the spot where the murder was committed. The jailer was taken from his home and forced to open the jail, and the guard were disarmed and shut up in the guard-house. Hundreds of people visited the grove. The victims are reported to have made a full confession. Everything was conducted with the utmost secrecy. The bodies were not found till 8 o'clock this morning.

IRONTON (O.), December 1st.—Dr. Joseph A. Beggs, bookkeeper and chemist at the Alice furnace, was cruelly murdered last night about 8 o'clock, a short distance above this city. The murderer used a shotgun loaded with buckshot and slugs. John Waggoner and Bill Zeck have been arrested. Waggoner confesses firing two shots at Beggs, but says it was in self-defense. People believe it was for robbery. Beggs bore a high character, but the accused have bad reputations.

YAZOO CITY (Miss.), December 1st.—Two negroes—Jordan and Craig—were caught and confessed to the assassination of Robert Cattlin, near Hunt's Landing, on the 17th of last month. Murder at Oxford.
A citizen murdered in cold blood by two negroes.

Tuesday night was indescribably dark and inclement, and will be memorable, since on it was perpetrated a crime not committed here before within man's memory. Mr. Thomas Lynch, a citizen of high repute and respectability, the beloved husband, the honored father of a large family, a deacon in the Presbyterian church, a man without a known enemy in the world, and universally beloved and respected, is wantonly, deliberately and cruelly murdered on the streets of Oxford, in the dark hours of the night, for the sake of a paltry amount of miserable money. For a number of years past Mr. Lynch has been the only jeweler of Oxford. His home was about three-fourths of a mile from the Court House. Tuesday night he left his store for home. Not arriving there by midnight, his wife, becoming uneasy about the absence of her husband on such a night, sent one of her sons to see what had become of his father. Walking in the direction of town he stumbled over the body, the feet lying across the path. He immediately gave the alarm, and soon a number of the neighbors were on the spot. The body was stretched on the back, and from all appearances Mr. Lynch died instantly, and without a struggle. The skull was terribly fractured in a number of places, the result of one or two blows, given with all the force of a powerful man. A piece of fence paling, $1\frac{1}{4}$ inches in dimensions, was found not far from the body, and the next morning it was discovered that one piece of paling was missing from the fence. His pocket book was carried away, and a number of letters left scattered near by, but, for some cause, the murderer and robber failed to take his watch. About $20 was in his pocket book. A thorough post mortem examination was made.

Wednesday morning suspicion began to be attached to Shadrack Hester, a negro, who when questioned told many different stories. Late in the afternoon he confessed his complicity in the murder, and charged John Brodie, colored, with having committed the deed. Brodie has not long been discharged from the Penitentiary, to which he was sentenced from Fayetteville for larceny. In consequence of this statement Brodie was immediately arrested and both the negroes were locked up in jail. Hester, when in jail, denied all knowledge of the matter, and said he had lied the day before. Brodie also protested his innocence, and complained that Hester had told lies on him.

Wednesday and Thursday the inquest was held, when the guilt of the two negroes was fixed beyond question. Both were placed in jail. The excitement both white and colored citizens exceeds anything ever known here. The entire community is wrought up to the highest pitch.—Oxford Free Lance.

Shadrack Hester, when examined before the Coroner's jury, substantially repeated the statement he had previously made, implicating himself and John Brodie, in the murder. Based upon this confession and other strong evidence, the Coroner's jury returned a true bill.

Negroes Lynched.
CXFORD, N. C., Dec. 2—The bodies of the two negroes, John Brodie and Shadrack Hester, who have been incarcerated since the day after the Lynch murder, were yesterday morning found hanging from the limbs of a large oak tree near the western outskirts of the town. There was a settled conviction that they were guilty of the most atrocious crime ever committed in that section. All is quiet and no apprehension is felt of any trouble about the lynching matter.
john-brodie-oxford-1881-12-01.A16: The two negroes, Hester and Brodie, murderers of Mr. Thomas Lynch, were taken from the jail at Oxford, Thursday morning before day, and hung near the spot where Mr. L. was killed. It is said that they confessed their guilt. All persons who engage in robbing and murdering, may expect to be hung or it might be better, when sure of the guilt of the prisoners, to roast them alive.
john-brodie-oxford-1881-12-01.A20:
Retribution!
Within a week after Mr. Thomas M. Lynch, of Oxford, was murdered, for the pitiful sum of $20, vengeance overtook the assassins as is detailed in the Free Lance:—

About 3 o'clock on Wednesday night the jailor, Mr. Wm. R. Turner, was awakened at his home, just on the edge of town, by a body of disguised and armed men, numbering between fifty and one hundred, who told him that he must accompany them to the jail and deliver up the two negroes. He positively refused at first, but seeing that resistance was useless, he obeyed, and getting the keys, proceeded to the jail. Arriving there, the guard of two men, Capt. A. F. Spencer and W. H. Crews, a colored constable, were forced to go in the guard house and the door closed upon them. They were made to keep silence at the muzzle of pistols and under threats of instant death. The lamps about the jail were then knocked out, and the doors having been opened by the jailor, the lynchers proceeded to the cells.

The cell containing Hester was first opened, and one of the party told him he must now tell about the murder. While stammering and hesitating, he was hustled out in the passage and taken in charge by others. Brodie's cell was next visited, and the jailor told him that some wanted to see him. He came to the door and, seeing the crowd, was about to make an alarm when pistols were pointed at his head and he was ordered to keep quiet or he would killed then and there. Permission was given him to put on his clothes, when he was marched out of the jail. Having secured the prisoners, the jailor was ordered to lock up the doors, and while he was so doing, the whole party disappeared down the street.

No alarm was made, and there appeared to be no excitement or confusion among the men engaged in this awful event. They proceeded to their work with remarkable deliberation and seemed to have provided against every emergency.

Nothing was known of the affair until early next morning, and for some hours it was uncertain what disposition had been made of the prisoners. About 8 o'clock information came that the bodies had been discovered hanging dead in a small grove in Taylor's field. This information proved correct, and in a short time the spot had been visited by hundreds of people, who quietly looked at the hanging bodies and walked away.

The grove in which the bodies were found is about one hundred and fifty yards from the spot where the murder was committed, and in reaching it the prisoners and their executioners had to pass almost exactly by the place where Mr. Lynch received his death wound.

The bodies were hanging on separate trees, about twenty feet apart, and were suspended by a small rope, which was placed around the jail, and which had been carried off when the men were removed from the jail.

N. 5. — From an Oxford friend, "G. R. Mr. V. C. Lentz, of Dry's Mill, this county, last week gathered a second crop of apples from a tree in his orchard. The apples were large, ripe and fully equal to those of the first crop.—Concord Sun.

SPEEDY JUSTICE.—The two negroes who waylaid and killed and robbed Mr. Thos. Lynch of Oxford last week, were taken from the Jail and hanged by citizens of Granville county. The villains confessed their guilt. The Raleigh Observer says: "In their confession the doomed men stated that they had planned to kill one of three men, or, if possible, all of the three. These three were Mr. Lynch, Mr. Brogden and Mr. Clements, the latter being the Register of Deeds of Granville county. All these gentlemen live in the suburbs of the town. Mr. Lynch, whom they murdered, was the only one of the three they were able to come up with.

A pair of mules being driven by a young man named George Johnston, in Rowan county, last Monday, ran away and threw the young man against a tree. He walked to his house, lay down on a bed and soon expired.—Salisbury Watchman.

The Asheville Citizen states that the superintendent of convicts on the Western North Carolina Railroad is having stockades put up on the Ducktown line, west of Pigeon River. It will not be long before the convicts will be transferred from the Paint Rock line.

A brutal murder was committed in Battleboro last Saturday morning. A white woman, Mary Eliza Hawkins, was killed by a negro man, who placed the body upon the Railroad track, where it was terribly mangled. The murderer was arrested and placed in the Nashville jail. —Oxford Free Lance.

SUDDEN DEATH.—On Monday Mrs. Caroline Black was taken with a stroke of paralysis and rendered speechless. She lingered until 11 o'clock of the same evening, when death relieved her. —Mr. Rutus Stallings, of Perquimans county, was severely cut in an affray at Sandy Cross, from which he instantly died. —Captain Josiah Simmons, an old and respected citizen dropped dead at the residence of his son in this city, on Saturday night, at about eight o'clock. His complaint was heart disease. —Elizabeth City Falcon.

THE RIVER FREE.—The Fayetteville Examiner says that the Cape Fear Navigation Company received, a few days ago, from the U. S. Government, a check for $10,000, the sum named in the act of the U. S. Congress to be paid the company for the surrender of their rights in the Cape Fear River. The deed of surrender has been signed, sealed and delivered, and the river is now free to all navigators and all craft. The next thing is to increase the depth of water, which practical men say can be done. It is not probable that anything will be done in that direction until the season of low water, which may be expected during next summer.

A DWELLING BURNED.—There was great excitement last Friday night, when the alarm of fire was raised. Everybody rushed from their houses to see whose building was burning, and the flames bursting from the roof of Mr. James Moore's residence soon attracted a crowd to the scene. The alarm was given too late, for although every effort was made to save the building, the flames could not be stayed, but the furniture was all hurriedly carried out and saved, though much of it badly damaged. The origin of the fire is unknown. The building was quite a comfortable dwelling, and its destruction is a serious loss to its owner, as there was no insurance.—Chatham Record.

A PARAGON AMONG GIRLS.—There is a young lady in this city, yet a school girl, whose life is at this time a really remarkable one. She resides with her brother, who is a widower with several children. In the morning she tidies the house and cooks the breakfast for the family. She passes the day at school, and on her return in the afternoon attends to sewing for the household and cooks the supper and after supper she teaches a small night school of her own. During the past three years she has not missed a lesson, nor has she had a mark against her for being late at school during that entire time. If this young lady doesn't make a splended wife for some lucky fellow some of these days then a sore lack of appreciation will be evident somewhere. — Wilmington Star.

Asheville Citizen: The new buildings going up in all parts of the city are absolutely astonishing to our inhabitants, and our contractors all say they are crowded with orders. Many more are already contracted for, to be erected early in the spring. —Died, last Saturday, Julian, little son of Hon. James H. Merrimon. He had been afflicted all his life with heart disease, and died suddenly. —One of the most creditable expenditures made by our county authorities is for the erection of the iron bridge across the French Broad River at this place. This bridge has to accommodate traffic for many counties. —Capt. C. C. McPhail, in charge of the Richmond and Danville Railroad department at the Atlanta exposition, says he knows of over one hundred and sixty people who have left Atlanta to come to western North Carolina, attracted by the display of minerals, timbers, &c. We know of several parties now in our western counties examining some mines with a view of purchasing. The western half of North Carolina is the richest spot of equal extent in the Union.

Lynchting Cases.

On the night of Nov. 20, Charles Lynch, a jeweler at Oxford, N. C., while returning from his store at night to his home in the suburbs of the town, was waylaid and brutally murdered by Louis Burke and John Booker, two negroes with half a dozen aliases. The affair occasioned intense excitement and the friends of the victim at once instituted search for the perpetrators. About a week ago Burke and Booker were arrested, charged with the assassination and were lodged in jail. Last Friday night an armed body of fifty or sixty men visited the jail, and forced the jailor to deliver the two murderers up. They made a full confession of the crime, after which they were carried to the outskirts of the village and hanged to a tree. The negroes begged pitiously for mercy, but their executioners only reminded them of how little they had exhibited toward the man whose life they had so recently taken. After disposing of the negroes the mob quietly dispersed to their homes.

On the same night two negroes, named Jordan and Craig, having been caught at Yazoo, Miss., and confessed to the murder of Robert Catlin, near Huntsfield Landing, Miss., on the 17th ult., were carried by an infuriated mob to Shephardstown and hanged.

ARIZONA.
Homicide—Narrow Escape from Lynching
PHENIX, August 15-b —At Tempe vester-
Homicide—Narrow Escape from Lynching
Phoenix, August 15th.—At Tempe yesterday afternoon Juan Merales shot and killed Joaquin Negreles, while drunk. A gang of lynchers was immediately organized, and pursued the prisoner, who, in charge of Constable Gallardo, was riding for his life. The Constable succeeded in lodging his prisoner in the jail in Phoenix a few minutes before the pursuers came up. The murdered man was a Lieutenant in the band of Marquez. The prisoner is safe.
juan-morales-phoenix-1881-08-14.A5: A shooting affray took place in the upper town of Tempe yesterday, resulting in the death of Juan Nagrels at the hands of Santos Morales—both parties being Mexicans. The particulars of the affair, as gleaned by a Gazette reporter from an interview with Manuel Gallardo, the officer who made the arrest, are as follows: Some six weeks ago Nagrels, who it is said was formerly a Lieutenant of Marquez Mexican handits, came to Tempe and shortly thereafter made the acquaintance of Morales and family. His attentions to Mrs. Morales soon became so marked as to arouse the distrust and jealousy of her husband, who forbade Nagrels visiting the house. But remonstrances and threats proved alike of no avail—Nagrels appeared more amused than otherwise, and persisted in his visits. Morales complained to Constable Gallardo of the matter, but no steps could be taken to prevent these intrusions as Tempe was without a Justice of the Peace at the time. On Sunday morning Morales returned home to find his wife and Nagrels in social converse, and his rage knew no bounds. He informed the destroyer of his domestic peace and happiness that he would take the law in his own hands. The latter only laughed, while the self-supposed outraged husband went about to prepare for his bloody work. Liberal potations of forty-rod whisky served to produce the necessary courage, and a six-shooter furnished the instrument of death. At four o'clock Morales was in good condition to assume the leading role in most any tragedy, and it was at this hour that he met Nagrels, in Gallardo's saloon. Morales addressed Nagrels with the remark, "Now I am going to kill you." It is evident that the latter recognized that the remark was made in earnest, for he started to run just as Morales drew his revolver. The first shot missed Nagrels, but the second ball struck him just above the left shoulder blade, coming out on the opposite side above the collar bone. In two minutes he lay dead upon the floor—another victim to jealousy and strong drink. —Gazette.

A Negro Wants Lynching.
News and Courier
Wants Lynchin
News and Courier.
UHG, March 14, Ofr Eri

ORANGFBURG, March 14. On Friday, while the daughter of a white man named Cunningham was going to visit a neighbor a mile distant, with her little sister, she was violently assaulted by a negro who had followed her. She resisted with much force, and, finding her too strong for him, the negro seized a tightwood knot and knocked her senseless.

The little sister ran for help and the negro dragged the senseless girl for one hundred and fifty yards to a swamp. She partially rallied and made an attempt to scream when he renewed his attack upon her. Hearing persons coming he made his escape into the swamp, and ever since has been hotly pursued. If he is found he may have a short shift.

The girl is lying dangerously ill. One eye almost beaten out, and she is badly cut in the head. The outrage occurred for four miles from this place.
manhunt-orangeburg-1881-03-11.A3: A desperate attempt was made Thursday, on the highway, at Orangeburg, to outrage the person of Miss Conningham by a negro, who sprang out from the bushes, in a lonely part of the road, and assaulted the girl, who is about 22 years of age. Miss Conningham made such a forcible resistance that her assailant picked up a billet of light wood and felled her to the ground. A little sister who accompanied the victim ran to a neighbors house to summon assistance. During her absence the fiend dragged Miss Conningham to a swamp, where he renewed his attempt to outrage her. The noise made by persons approaching frustrated this design, and the man ran off, escaping by hiding in a swamp. Miss Conningham is dangerously ill, one eye having literally been beaten out of its socket. Her recovery is regarded as extremely doubtful.
manhunt-orangeburg-1881-03-11.A5:
Arrest of the Supposed Perpetrator of an Outrage.
A negro was arrested in this County yesterday (Monday) who is supposed to be the wretch that committed an outrage on a young white girl, named Jane Cunningham, in Orangeburg County the 10th instant. He has been for several days in the neighborhood of Mr. Sims Brown; when arrested he was making his way towards Maybinton. A reporter of the Herald visited him in jail, and had a talk with him. He says his name is George Bouner, that he is from Charleston; that he formerly worked for Mr. L. J. Jones in Newberry; that he afterwards returned to Charleston, and a week or two ago he came back to Newberry, walking all the way. Being asked if he came through Orangeburg County, he said, no; that he came "the other way"; said he did not know anybody in Orangeburg; but being afterwards asked whom he worked for in Orangeburg he said Dr. Jones, that Dr. Jones lives near St. Mathews, five miles from the Court House, having previously said, however, that he did not know Dr. Jones, but had heard of him. Being asked how far Mr. Cunningham lived from Orangeburg he said about a day's drive; being asked the name of Mr. C.'s children, he said one was named Sallie, another Mary and another he couldn't remember. The reporter asked him if it was Jane, and he answered yes. The reporter then asked him if he had heard of a negro trying to kill Jane Cunningham. He said he had. What did he try to kill her for? was the next question. His answer was that the negro made an improper proposal to her, and she ran from him; he ran after her and caught her; put his hand over her mouth to prevent her screaming, and knocked her in the head with a piece of lightwood; that three men came along (giving the name of one of them) and the negro ran off. Being asked what he had done with his black hat (he now wears a white one) and his shoes (he is barefoot) he said he had worn them out and thrown them away since he left Orangeburg.

There seems to be little doubt that this is the negro wanted. He is not a mulatto, nor is he exactly black; he is rather under the medium size, and is about 21 years old. He is a negro of very little intelligence; almost an idiot from his appearance and conversation.

The Sheriff of Orangeburg was telegraphed to last night to send some one up to identify him, and it will very probably be known to-day whether this is the right man.

This is the same negro that was arrested in Laurens County about six months ago on the charge of knocking a little child in the head with a rock on Mr. Fed Dominick's plantation. When arrested he acknowledged that he did it, but it was afterwards ascertained, beyond all doubt, that when the thing happened he was not in this County.

Maj. Jones says he is very peculiar, at times he appears as sane as anybody, and again he seems to lose his mind almost entirely.
manhunt-orangeburg-1881-03-11.A6:
The Supposed Orangeburg Negro.
The sheriff of Orangeburg came up last week to get the negro who was arrested in this county the 28th inst., on the supposition that he was the person who committed an outrage in that county. After seeing him the sheriff was very doubtful as to his being the proper party, and therefore declined to take him, requesting, however, that he be held over till further evidence could be obtained as to his identity. He sent up Saturday the following description of the negro who committed the outrage: almost a mulatto; heavy build, weighing not less than 150 pounds; knock-kneed; bad teeth; thick lips. The negro in jail is almost black; is of light build, weighing not more than 125 or 130; is not knock-kneed, on the contrary is bow-legged; has a perfect set of teeth; and for a negro has thin lips.

The only evidence against this negro is his own confession, which, considering his utter imbecility, is not worth a copper. Besides this, if reports be true, there is another reason that would render the confession worthless even tho' the negro were of sound mind; it is said that the confession was forced from the negro by threats and demonstrations of the pistol and the rope. If this be true it was a grave offense and an outrage of law and order. Suppose the negro had been lynched upon a confession thus obtained, as he would very probably have been had he been taken to Orangeburg.

It seems to be quite evident now that this is the wrong negro.

The negro was examined yesterday by Drs. Folk and Gilder, and pronounced a lunatic. The Sheriff sends him down to the Asylum to-day.

South Carolina Notes. colored troops of the State are
The colored troops of the State are to be organized into a brigade.

The cold winter killed many small pines in the woods throughout Fairfield county.

A meeting of the Executive Committee of the Water Company was held Monday evening, at Columbia, without action, but adjourned until to-day, having decided to wait until consultation can be had with Capt. W. N. Brown, of Boston, who is expected daily.

William Meredith lost his leg and Thomas Leonard had his back badly injured by a wharf post giving way under the strain of a hawser of the steamship Delaware as she was swinging into dock in Charleston Tuesday.

The English bark Isabel Craig, Captain Ninnes, arrived at Charleston on Sunday night from Liverpool, having been on the passage since the 29th of January. The vessel experienced heavy gales during a portion of the voyage, and one of the compartments containing water ballast was injured, shifting the ballast forward and rendering the vessel almost unmanageable. The Captain, however, fortunately succeeded in bringing her into port without serious injury.

The habeas corpus case argued in the Supreme Court on Monday, ex-parte Henry Duckett and Griffin Duckett, was a test case to determine the legality of hiring out convicts sentenced under the usual formula to hard labor in the penitentiary. Col. R. C. Watts, of Laurens, appeared for the petitioners and Attorney General Youmans for the State Colonel Watts argued that "until the passage of an act authorizing the transfer of prisoners, notwithstanding the sentence, such transfer was unwarranted." The court reserved its decision, but is expected to render it in a few days. This being the first legal protest made against the custom of leasing out convicts, the result will be eagerly looked for.

The State Superintendent of Education has succeeded in securing the services of Prof. Louis Soldan to conduct the exercises of the next Normal Institute. This announcement will doubtless be sufficient of itself to attract a large attendance. The session of the institute will be held during the month of August. The place of meeting has not yet been selected, but will be announced immediately after the meeting of the State Board of Examiners, which will be held during the first week in May.

Returns for the past month to the State Agricultural Department from two-thirds of the counties show that preparation and planting are from twelve to fifteen days later than last year; the acreage in cotton is considerably increased, and a much larger quantity of fertilizers will be used. The small grain crop has been very much injured by the severe winter, but the stands are generally good, and with a favorable season henceforth will result in a fair yield. Fruit prospects are very bad; peaches have been entirely destroyed; a good crop of apples, however, may be made. The farmers are generally buying more supplies than last year. Every report shows a scarcity of labor, higher wages being generally offered, but without much effect, and the labor when secured is very unsatisfactory.

Isaac Cossach, formerly pastor of the Calvary Baptist Church, Ten-Mile Hill, and two of his lay brothers and three church sisters were before Justice Gleason, in Charleston, Monday, to answer the charge of the burning of the church. It appears that Cossach and some of his church people had had a falling out, which led to his being supplanted as minister by J. Pugh. This occurred about a month ago. Cossach's friends, as a matter of course, seceded with him, and established a meeting place elsewhere for themselves. On Saturday, the 9th, grand preparations were made at the church for Palm Sunday service. When Palm Sunday came the Ten-Mile Church was burned to ashes. The Rev. Pugh, thinking that the secessionists had committed the act, took out a warrant for them and their minister; but when the investigation was had no proof whatever was produced, and the Justice dismissed the case.

On Sunday morning between 10 and 11 o'clock the body of a colored man named Henry McCants was found lying in a ditch on Mr. Latham's place, near Red Top Church, in St. Andrew's Parish. The deceased, who had been engaged as a carpenter at Mr. Latham's phosphate works, was last seen, before his death, in Lindstedt's store, near Red Top Church, between 7 and 8 o'clock on the same morning. He was at this time sober, and the short time that elapsed before he was found dead led to the suspicion of foul play. Coroner DeVeaux went up to the place Monday to investigate the case, and found that the body of the deceased had been forced through a cane thicket into the ditch. Dr. M. S. Whaley held a post mortem examination and discovered that the neck of the deceased had been dislocated. No marks of other violence were found on the body. Executive Chamber,
COLUMBIA, N. C., April 22, 1881.
WHEREAS information has been received at this Department, that in the County of Orangeburg of this State, on the 10th day of March 1881, Miss Jane Cunningham was atrociously assaulted by a colored person whose name is unknown and that the said person has fled from justice:

Now, therefore, I JOHNSON HAGOOD, Governor of the State of South Carolina, in order that justice may be done, and the majesty of the law vindicated, do hereby offer a reward of Fifty Dollars for the aprehension and delivery to the Sheriff of Orangeburg County of the said colored person.

The said person is described as being about 5 feet 6 inches in height, brown complexion, stout built and about 18 years old. He was dressed in black pants, a light colored brown coat and a blue check shirt with a large brass button on the bosom, and congress shoes. He was scratched in the face during the struggle. He worked for a Mr. Benj. Crum near Bowesville, S. C., the day before the assault was committed and gave his name as Govan Brown, and said he was from Sumter, S. C. After, in his flight, he gave his name as William Johnson.

In testimony whereof I have hereunto set my hand and caused the Great Seal of the State to be affixed this 21st day of April 1881, and in the 105th year of the Independence of the United States of America.

[L.S.]

JOHNSON HAGOOD, Governor.

R. M. SIMS,
Secretary of State.

mcallen-wilson-1881-08.A1:
VIRGINIA NEWS.
The foundation for the Yorktown monument has been dug.

Foxes are reported to be unusually abundant in many counties of the State.

Dr. C. Quarles, of Louisa county, died last Saturday, aged 68 years.

One hundred and twenty five locomotives are now in operation on the Chesapeake and Ohio Railroad.

They survey of the Keysville and Clarksville railroad in Mecklenburg county has been completed.

A democratic meeting at Warrenton on Monday night was addressed by Gen. Payne, Hon. James V. Brooke, Maj. Taylor Scott, and Hon. Eppa Hunton.

Elder, the Richmond artist, is engaged in studies for the figures of a large painting representing a wharf scene on James river in ante bellum times.

A colored woman residing in Campbell county, died a horrible death one day last week from the effects of a poisonous drug administered to her by several of her own race.

Major John W. Daniel's resignation as Senator for the district including Campbell and Lynchburg, was forwarded to Gov. Holliday yesterday. His successor, who will be elected in November, will be a democrat, as the district is strongly democratic.

Captain James Barron Hope, editor of the Norfolk Landmark, has been selected to represent Virginia on the press committee at the Yorktown Contennial celebration. This committee consists of one representative from each of the thirteen original States.

The owner of the Libby Prison, Richmond has put up a notice stating that all persons depruding upon the building will be dealt with according to law. Relio hunters and curiosity seekers have been clipping off pieces from the bricks extensively, and hence the necessity for the notice.

In Grayson county, last week, a colored man named Mack Allen attempted to commit an outrage on a little white girl ten years of age. He was followed and overtaken by Jerome Pasley and other men of the neighborhood, and when they found him he refused to be taken, and drew a pistol and fired upon the party. The shot took effect in the wrist of Mr. Pasley, who at once raised his gun and sent a load of buckshot crashing through the negro's body. He died instantly.

Two freight trains collided on the Richmond, Fredericksburg and Potomac Railroad at North Anna Bridge, about twenty eight miles north of Richmond, last night, wrecking both engines and a number of cars. Engineer Carroll, of one of the trains, and a colored fireman are reported seriously injured. The mail train from Washington, due in Richmond, at 10 p.m., could not pass the obstruction, and the mail and passengers were transferred to a freight train on the Chesapeake and Ohio Railroad at Hanover Junotie.

Yesterday morning the hands employed on the Chesapeake and Ohio Railroad, at Newport News, struck for higher wages, less hours, and more frequent payments. It appears that the company has deferred paying the men for five or six weeks, and two hundred of them yesterday determined to strike, and with banners flying and armed with clubs, pistols, etc., the marched up the entire reccion, compelling all they met to join them. They then seized the engine, and declared it should not proceed on its usual trips. All work has been suspended from Newport News to Williamsburgh, and great excitement prevails. The commissary has been closed, and the scrip issued by the company debarred from circulation. It is stated the Governor has been telegraphed, and that the Peninsula and Libby Guards are to be sent down to quail the disturbance if it continues today.
mcallen-wilson-1881-08.A2:
For the SENTINEL News From the Old Dominion State.
A friend writing from mouth of Wilson, Va., says:

"Pandemonium has suddenly broken loose hereabouts. Jerome Pasely, a young man who has been with me for some time, shot and killed a negro while endeavoring to arrest him for an attempted outrage on the person of a little girl nine years of age. The particulars are as follows: The negro came to Mr. Masten Halsey's where Pasely was at work, fired his pistol as he came into the yard, peremptorily ordered Mrs. Halsey to get his breakfast, and then went up stairs. Pasely summoned assistance, went up stairs and ordered him to surrender. His answer was a pistol shot fired point blank at Pasely's breast. The officer caught the ball in the fleshy part of the forearm, promptly knocked the negro down, while his assistants grappled with him, caught up a shot gun and fired the contents into his abdomen, making a ghastly wound from which his bowels and liver protruded. He was a spunky negro, fought desperately to the last, and met death with steal, voiceless indifference. The location of the tragedy is near here, on the Carolina line; the negro's name was McAllen, and he claimed to have come from Yadkin county.

A negro husband and wife who live in Ashe county, "Old North State," some seven miles away, had "a little tuff tother day." The woman (to use her own elegant diction) "just mopped cuten the lazy cuss with a piece of fence rail," and stabbed him in several places with a "case" knife. He fainted from loss of blood. No arrests.

Four prisoners broke jail at Independence, Va. a few days since. Among them was a negro sentenced to be hung in October for killing a couple of his brothers-in-law. Another man in the prison for deliberate murder refused to be liberated. The leader in the gang is a sharper, locks and bolts were little in his way. He stole a horse and crossed the mountain twenty miles away before day on the same night they escaped.

A little negro dwarf was hung in Helton township Asho county, not long since, for stabbing a white girl. A man by the name of Lynch performed this Tristran hanging work.

Three loads of Davie and Alexander county men passed through this village a few days since, making a mountain tour.

Crops are good; fine crops of tobacco that will find a market in Winston this winter. D. I.

Col. L. L. Polk, Secretary of the State Agricultural Society, makes the following announcement in the Raleigh News: I will establish on the fair grounds at Raleigh an office, in charge of a competent gentlemen, who will keep during the week of the fair, a register of all ex-soldiers in the city, together with such notes or information as they desire to be exchanged with each other. Each command will have its own register, and the members on arrival could report to the office, register their names and old commands, their present residence, etc. These registers will be open at all times for the information of the public. It would be a general intelligence office for all the ex-soldiers and their friends, where cards could be exchanged, messages deposited and delivered, appointments for meetings made, etc. Programmes for each day will be published and distributed gratuitously each morning, and in these the announcements of meetings would be published.

Commissioner Raum has decided that "Rock and Rye" is not a medicine, but a beverage, and taxable as such. That settles it. If Rock and Rye is not a medicine editors will no longer drink it. If any of them have formed an appetite for the stuff, which they find it difficult to overcome, they should try cod liver oil which is a medicine but not a beverage.

FREEDING THEM OUT OF THEIR OWN Spoon.—The prohibitionists hereabouts are getting all they asked for, if they did have their hind sights knocked off in the late election. They can't get whiskey except on a doctor's prescription! We have heard of two who applied at bars in this place since the election, who couldn't get it without a paper in due form. And "they say" it is the law as to them, and like the laws of the Medes and Persians, which change not. What will they do when a fellow gets snake bit and there is no doctor around?—Salesbury Watchman.

Gold mining was begun in North Carolina in the early part of this century, and up to 1827 she was the only gold producing State.

pat-rhodes-skidmore-1881-05-12.A6:
Outrage, Desperadism, and Lynching.
ATTEMPTED ASSASSINATION BY A BAND OF
DESPERADOES—TERRIBLE ENCOUNTER WITH
A SHERIFF'S POSSE—ONE OF THE ASSASSINS
SURRENDERS AND IS LYNCHED.

CINCINNATI, O., May 13.—The Republican's Charleston, Mo., special says: "Four men—Frank Brown, Jesse Meyers, Joseph Hamilton, and Pat. Rhodes—visited the house of William Knox, five miles south of New Madrid, last Monday night with the intention of killing him and his half-sister on account of an old grudge. A man named Coleman was carrying a child and walking the floor in the house, and, mistaking Coleman for Knox, the party fired on him and wounded both him and the child. A warrant was issued Tuesday for the arrest of the assassins, and Sheriff Walters, with a posse, started in pursuit and soon overtook them. The men fled to the woods and secreted themselves behind a fallen tree. When the posse came up they received a volley from the concealed party, and Robert Larfage was killed. The sheriff's party returned the fire, but receiving a second volley they retired. The desperadoes then robbed the dead body of Larfage of his watch, money, and shirt-studs, and fled. In the evening Pat. Rhodes, one of the gang who had been wounded by the sheriff's posse, came in and gave himself up. This morning a party of vigilants took him out and hanged him. Hundreds of men are scouring the country in every direction for the remainder of the party. If caught they will be lynched."
pat-rhodes-skidmore-1881-05-12.A7:
THE MURDER.
bloody affair which occurred near New Madrid on the twelfth instant, and to which reference was made in a letter published in yesterday's BULLETIN:

"Four men, named Rhoades, Meyers, Hamilton and Brown, had formed a secret organization for purposes unknown to anyone save themselves, but now generally supposed to have been robbery and outlawry, and by accident let their plans become known to William Knox, who, not being in sympathy with them, gave them away, whereupon they concluded to kill him, and on last Monday night visited his house for that purpose. Knox succeeded in evading them by disappearing through a back door. The other inmates of the house becoming alarmed at the threats of the four men, also attempted to make their escape, but were fired upon, one shot taking effect in the legs of a man who had an infant in his arms. Three shots also struck the infant in the legs and body. The scoundrels also fired at one of the women as she ran through the orchard, but without effect. They then remained around Knox's house until daylight, when they left, taking the direction the man had run whom they had shot. They had gone but a short distance when they found the wounded child lying on the ground. They took it back to the house and dressed its wounds. They then proceeded in search of the wounded man. They soon found and also assisted him back to the house and called a neighbor, whom they instructed to attend to the wounds. Early Tuesday morning Knox swore out a warrant for the arrest of the four men and had it placed in the hands of the constable, who proceeded to perform that duty. Finding the quartet, the constable was promptly and coolly informed that they would not be arrested by him, but after some conversation they consented to go, telling him to lead the way and they would follow. After proceeding some distance they changed their minds, and turning in to the woods ran off and were not seen any more until yesterday morning. The sheriff of New Madrid county, being notified, went with a posse of ten or twelve men to the scene of action, which was near Bayne's store, ten miles below Sikeston. The sheriff and his party stopped at Bayne's store, and while there saw the four men coming down the main road to them, and discovering who they were mounted their horses and gave chase. The quartet seeing the officers advancing took to the woods and concealed themselves in the brush. In about an hour the sheriff and his men came upon them concealed behind a log, the first intimation they had of their proximity being a volley of buckshot fired into the party, instantly killing one of the deputies, Rob't LaForge, and wounding another, Albert Hunter. The sheriff's party returned the fire, and for several minutes a regular battle ensued, but the ambush gave the outlaws such an advantage as to force the officers back, leaving the murdered man, LaForge, on the ground. The desperadoes quickly relieved him of his money, jewels and pistols, and then retreated. The sheriff's party soon rallied, and with an increased force of forty men continued the pursuit. Early in the afternoon they found one of the desperadoes, Rhoades, who had been so badly wounded as to be unable to travel, and took him prisoner. Rhoades' statement is that his comrades, finding him shot, through the leg and in the face, concluded that they would be unable to escape with him. Leaving him one pistol, they sent him to the house of a widow woman and told him to do the best he could for himself, and then deserted him. He was kept under guard until he escaped, but was soon afterwards found in a stable hanging by the neck to the rafters. The sheriff and party are still hunting the other three, but had not discovered their whereabouts at a late hour. The desperadoes are armed with double-barreled shot-guns and four shooters each, and are determined not to be taken alive. The whole community is in a terrible state of excitement, young LaForge having a large and influential circle of relatives and friends. The citizens of New Madrid have offered a reward of $600 for the three desperadoes. These are the facts as near as they can be obtained at present, there being so many conflicting reports under the excitement."
pat-rhodes-skidmore-1881-05-12.A8:
ROUGH WORK.
Lawlessness in the Country About New Madrid.
By the arrival of steamers from up the river to-day news is brought that New Madrid, Mo., seventy-five miles below Cairo, has had a tough time with a lot of roughs. Four, named Frank Brown, Jesse Myers, James Hamilton and Pat Rhodes, went to kill Mr. Knox and his half sister, five miles south of New Madrid, last Sunday night. A man named Coleman, walking the floor with his sick child, was mistaken for Knox and both were wounded by shots fired from the gang. Warrants were issued, and Sheriff Walters with a posse went on their trail, overtaking them near Bayhes store, five miles from Sykeston. They took the woods, fired a volley from ambush, and killed Robert LaFarge. The desperadoes robbed LaFarge's body of money, watch and shirtstuds, then fled, the sheriff's party doing the same first. Pat Rhodes, of the gang, being wounded, afterwards went from his hiding place and surrendered. Last Thursday morning a crowd of vigilants hung him and they are trying to find the others with the same object.
pat-rhodes-skidmore-1881-05-12.A12:
Terrible Affair in New Madrid County.
[Correspondence to Charleston Enterprise.]

SIKESTON, Mo., May 12.—This community and the whole of New Madrid county has been intensely excited for the present week over the outrages perpetrated near New Madrid by four of the most remorseless banditti that ever infested this county. For bloodthirsty ferocity, the jungles of Africa do not furnish a parallel.

The four in question have been living in New Madrid county for about four years. One of them named Rhodes married a widow by the name of Knox, who had previously been married to two brothers named Knox—her maiden name being Edmonson, sister to John and Ruck Edmonson who live near Sikeston. She possessed some property, all of which her husband, Rhodes, squandered, except a small farm. Rhodes made several efforts to get that in his possession, but was prevented by his wife's brother-in-law, a Mr. Knox. Thereupon Rhodes and three others—one named James Hamilton, one Myers, and a Brown—organized, with a determination to kill Knox and his whole family.

They had provided themselves with breastplates, helmets, etc., so report says, and had secured three pistols and a shot-gun each—making twenty rounds to each man, or eighty in all. On Monday night they visited Knox's house to kill him, and after commencing the firing, Knox escaped from the house, but they had wounded one of his laborers, also one woman and Mr. Knox's little child. They then went to the house, dressed the wounds of the child, expressed regrets at having wounded the laborer, and then left.

Knox hurried to New Madrid and got Sheriff Watters and a posse to go in pursuit. The Sheriff started with a dozen men, and came upon the gang half a mile of Bayne's store, between New Madrid and Sikeston, 10 miles from New Manrid.

The desperadoes ran on the approach of the Sheriff's party, to a thicket near by. The officer and men followed them. After having summoned fifteen men from around the neighborhood, they unexpectedly came upon them in the edge of the thicket. The four men, when the officer's party was within fifteen feet of them, rose up from behind logs and commenced firing.

Robert LaForge, a young man of New Madrid, was killed instantly, being riddled through and through with bullets and buck-shot. Upon the death of LaForge, and the wounding of Albert Hunter and two others, the Sheriff's posse retreated to Bayne's store. Sheriff Waters then got the wives of two of the desperadoes to go and get the body of LaForge—this was five or six hours after he was killed—and the ladies and a doctor packed the body and dragged it from where it lay nearly to Bayne's store. The desperadoes had, before the women arrived for the body, come up to the dying man, shot him again, robbed him of about eighteen dollars, a collar-button, a gold watch, shirt studs, a finger-ring and his pistols. After they left him, the hogs had come and had mutilated the body some by eating off the ear, nose and part of the lip. While this was going on, a dozen men went out from Sikeston to assist in the pursuit, and others were congregating from every direction. While all had scattered themselves around the thicket again to watch them, Rhodes went to a woman's house near by, and gave himself up. He was wounded severely and suffering much. He was sent for and taken to Bayne's store and guarded till to-day (Thursday), at 11 o'clock, when he was found in the stable near by, suspended between heaven and earth—his spirit having passed up before that tribunal from which there is no appeal.

There are, at this writing, one hundred and fifty men in pursuit and watching for the other three around Bayne's store. One of the three appeared to-day at a farmhouse near the store, and begged something to eat. He was wounded in several places and bleeding profusely.

All that could be learned from the ruffian Rhodes was that they had organized to murder Knox and family, and then go West.

ANNIE MYRTLE, a girl thirteen years of age died at Racine, Wis., from the effects of "jumping the rope" 102 times.

A storm at Worthington, Ia., lifted the barn of John Pittman, containing six horses, and carried it a distance of half a mile without injury to the horses; also two barns belonging to R. Baker were blown a distance of two miles.

Four desperadoes in Missouri wounded an old man and a child, and killed one of a sheriff's posse in pursuit of them. One of the desperadoes gave himself up and was lynched.

While Brice Stough, his wife and two children and his sister, Mrs. Barbara Losch, were rowing in a small skiff at Newark, Ohio, the boat capsized. Before assistance could reach them all were drowned except Mrs. Stough.

A singular phenomenon is reported from Bedford, Ind., a cloud as low as the tree-tops having rushed over the trees with the roar of a hurricane. Only thirty-five seconds intervened from the time it was seen approaching until its disappearance. The sky was clear at the time and the sun shining.

Lieutenant Cherry, of the Fifth cavalry, United States army, was killed by one of his own men while in pursuit of a party of deserters who had robbed a ranch and murdered two men. Lieutenant Cherry was a young officer of great promise.

LEADING citizens of Denver, Col., are taking steps to have a national mining and industrial exposition.

HARRIMAN came out ahead in a six-day "heel-and-toe" walking match in Chicago, covering 530 miles and winning $1,000. Tracey, the second man, made 523 miles and won $750, and Krohne came third with a score of 520 miles and a prize of $500.

CAMERON's silk house in Windsor, Ont., opposite Detroit, was burglarized of $2,000 worth of goods. The robbers took their plunder to the American side in a small boat and secreted it in a field at Grosse Point. It was discovered by a farmer, who notified the police, and the property was recovered.

In a battle with four thieves, near Sikeston, Mo., Deputy Sheriff Laforge and Albert Hunter were killed. One of the desperadoes was captured and hung. His companions are in Little River swamp, with the people of the whole region in pursuit, and a lynching will be in order at an early date.

The saloons at Springfield, Ill., by order of the mayor, are closed on Sundays, and thousands of thirsty ones go out to the shadow of the shadow of Lincoln's monument to guzzle. A general fight occurred there in which one man was shot. The mob tore the boards from the fences, and the sheriff and police force were called to the scene.

'LISH COATES, of Dublin, Ga.. is an incorrigible scoundrel. Only a few weeks ago he was released from the penitentiary, where he had been confined for four years for whipping a colored woman to death. He was arrested for resorting to his old practice and so badly whipping a woman that she can hardly live. The scoundrel ought not to escape hemp this time.

Sheriff Davis was carried back to Greenville, where he died Sunday morning. Mr. Hatton was crazed by the wound received in his head, but is reported to be in fair way of recovering.

The people of Wayne county were thoroughly aroused, as Davis and Hatton are both among the most popular citizens of the county, and five hundred men commenced searching the woods, and a reward of $2,000, in addition to the $2,000 offered by New Madrid county, was offered for the capture of the murderers.

Capt. W. T. Leeper, an old and substantial citizen of Wayne county, was called on late Friday night to engage in the search for the desperadoes. He consulted with three other gentlemen, Messrs. Ambrose Beatty, Cal. Thomas and Taylor Fulton. Mr. Leeper said he was almost certain that the men would try to cross Black river, about two miles below Mill Springs, at a place known as "Campbell's Switch." He and a party therefore spent Friday night at the above place, where there is a ferry across the river. Saturday morning, just as day-light approached and the faithful guards were permitted to distinguish an object at some distance, the hunted game, Myers and Hamilton, made their approach walking up the railroad. At first Leeper and party mistook them for a party of their own men who had been watching at a station down the river two miles below their stand. As the party approached and when within five feet of Leeper and posse he recognized them as the famous New Madrid desperadoes and immediately prepared to give them a warm reception. Cocking his gun, Leeper hailed them with, "Hold on there," when they at once wheeled and presented their shot-guns. Simultaneously Leeper and party fired upon them. Both men fell in their tracks, James Hamilton being killed outright, receiving not less than ten buckshot in the back of his head, while Jesse Myers, his companion, was only temporarily stunned by an ugly shot in the forehead. The pursuing party had gotten the drop on them so completely that they were unable to get a shot, though both men fell with double-barrel shot-guns cocked in their hands.

The posse then obtained a hand-car and transported the dead and wounded prisoners to Mill Springs. The third and last of the gang, Frank Brown, was still at large, but Saturday morning word was brought to Mill Springs that he was seen swimming the river a few miles east of town, and a number of pursuers started in pursuit. Taking up the trail they tracked Brown a distance of ten or twelve miles, and about dusk in the evening crossed over into Reynolds county. J. N. Morrison, Prosecuting Attorney of Wayne county, in company with the others, spied a man in the timber ahead, and pushing on until within speaking distance drew a bead on one who proved to be none other than Brown and ordered hands up. Though heavily armed Brown saw he was caught and surrendered without resistance. He was ironed and taken to Mill Springs where he was kept until the morning passenger train passed, when he was taken to Poplar Bluff.

Brown's statements are conflicting, and he evidently thinks that the greater stories he will tell the better his chances. His wounds are not dangerous. Sunday morning he was sitting up conversing freely.

At six o'clock Sunday morning Myers and Brown were heavily ironed, and, under guard of the New Madrid party and W. T. Leeper and J. N. Morrison, were taken from Poplar Bluff on the east-bound freight for Sikeston, from where they were taken to New Madrid by wagon.

LATER.—The prisoners were taken to New Madrid and lodged in jail; but the Sheriff secretly took them out to the river and crossed in a skiff to Hickman, Ky., where they took a steamboat for St. Louis. Monday night the Sheriff landed his prisoners safely in the St. Louis jail. If they had remained in New Madrid they would have been lynched ere this. Three hundred citizens were on the alert for the job which was to have been done Sunday night.

IS IT OUR JESSE
Who Has Become a Bold, Bad Missouri "Cutter?"
"The following circular was published by order of the County Court of New Madrid county, Mo.
"Two thousand dollars ($2,000) reward is offered for the capture of the outlaws, Jesse Myers, James O. Hamilton and F. Brown, who fired into the Sheriff's posse, killing one and wounding two others in New Madrid county, Mo., on Wednesday. May 11th, 1881, or if either of them is captured, the reward will be paid in the following proportion: One thousand dollars ($1,000) for Meyers, and five hundred dollars ($500) for each of the others.
The crime for which a Sheriff's posse was pursuing the outlaws at the time of the above tragedy, was their attack on William Knox's house in New Madrid county on Monday night, May 9. A gang of four consisting of Jesse Meyers, James O. Hamilton, Robert Rhoades and F. O. Brown went to Knox's house, with the avowed intention of killing him. Being informed of the purpose of their visit, Knox fled by a backdoor and thus saved his life. As the party approached the house they saw George Williams enter the house from the yard, and supposing it was Knox, they immediately opened fire upon him, shooting some twelve or fifteen volleys of buckshot at the house. Williams was wounded in the leg, and a little girl who was living with Knox received two wounds. The women fled from the house to the barn, followed by several volleys of buckshot, but without effect. The villains followed them to the barn, but as the women had climbed up into the loft and hid themselves, they escaped detection, and after a short search the murderers returned to the house, and after shooting a few more shots into it, they entered in search of Knox. In the meantime Williams had left the house and dragged himself to the back of the field, where he passed a sleepless night of agony. Having made diligent search for Knox, they then dressed the wounds of the little girl and left the house, but watched around for Knox until daylight. The girl died from wounds. Being attracted by the cries of Williams, they went to him, and carrying him to a pond near by, they gave him some water, washed and dressed his wounds for him, and assured him they did not wish to hurt him—it was Knox they were after. The origin seems to have been an old grudge.

Knox at once procured a mule from a near neighbor and started to town for help. A warrant was promptly issued, and the sheriff summoned a posse and started in pursuit. Keeping a sharp look out on one of the murderer's houses with a telescope, the sheriff's posse saw one of the women take a basket to the barn, and correctly supposed that it contained dinner for the objects of their search, and that they were in the barn, but in this they were mistaken.

Accordingly they mounted their horses and rode to the spot, but as they approached the place they discovered the four men just emerging from a dense thicket of hazel brush that stood distant but a few hundred yards. The parties discovered each others' presence about the same time, and the fugitives immediately retreated to the thicket, and as the pursuers passed the house they were tauntingly told by one of the women that some of their party would be hauled back from the chase.

The fugitives soon regained the cover of the bushes, and as the place was small, the sheriff's posse immediately surrounded it on all sides, but little did they know of the condition of that fatal thicket, or of the character of the enemy they were confronting. This was their secret hiding place. In the midst of it they had a breastwork of oak logs three feet high, which entirely surrounded them on three sides, and armed with a double-barrelled shotgun and four navy six-shooters to each man, enabling them to fire 101 shots before having to reload. they could fight four times their number with ease. In addition to all this, it now appears that they were shielded both back and front with steel plates made with their own hands from cross cut saws. Unconscious of all these things, and unable to see this pitfall on account of the denseness of the thicket, the sheriff's party formed and started through the thicket, unconsciously dividing and passing on both sides of it. The first note of warning was the crack of a pistol from the murderers, less than ten paces distant from the left wing of the party. The shot struck a pistol in the belt of Mr. John Schafer, shattering the handle and driving the splinters into his body. Scarcely had the sound been heard, when it was followed by a deafening report of firearms from the same spot, and Robert Laforge, a most worthy and exemplary young man, fell dead upon the ground. Next to him stood Albert Hunter, who was shot through the neck with a large ball; the blood streamed forth from the wound in profusion, but his wounds are not considered dangerous. Another man who was near by was wounded in the leg. They next turned their attention to the right wing of the party, and the first move was to order Dr. L. A. Waters to give up his gun, to which the doctor responded by giving them the contents thereof. Mr. J. Ellis also fired two loads of buckshot at them, and then the firing ceased, and as they could not see the parties they were forced to retire.

As soon as the Sheriff could collect his men he sent for a physician and more help. In the meantime, Dr. Bogan went into the thicket and recovered Mr. Laforge's body, by the consent of his murderers, but it was robbed of his gold watch, pistols, and about $19 in currency. His body was horribly mutilated, and made his death the more painful to his relatives and friends. A very short notice was sufficient to fill the country full of armed men, and it does not seem possible that any of the scoundrels can escape.

Robert Rhoads was captured on Wednesday evening, May 11, at the residence of Mr. J. D. Stepp. He received five wounds in the battle of the thicket, and was forced to seek shelter. He died Thursday morning.

A later account gives intelligence of the killing on Thursday, May 19th, of John T. Davis, sheriff, and the wounding of James F. Hatton, collector of Wayne county, by the three desperadoes. pat-rhodes-skidmore-1881-05-12.A26:
A Man Hunt.
Four counties in southeast Missouri have been deeply agitated over a man hunt. The recent slaughter of a deputy sheriff at Sikeston caused the citizens to undertake the extirpation of four desperadoes named Frank Brown, Jesse Myers, James Hamilton and Patrick Rhoades. The latter was found at a farm-house, badly wounded, and sent back under guard, but never reached Sikeston. In a fight with the others near Greenville, Sheriff Davis and J. F. Hatton were badly wounded, and one thousand armed men turned out. Near Piedmont, Hamilton was killed and Myers captured. Brown subsequently surrendered himself. The captured men were afterward hung by a mob.

sam-gaines-springfield-1881-03-01.A1:
An Unoffending Negro Called Out of His Bed to Meet Death at the Hands of Ruffians.
Special to the Appeal.]

NASHVILLE, March 2.—A Springfield special to the American says: Robertson county steps a few paces further to the front in the calendar of crime, and richly deserves the belt for the champion mob county of the State. Last night a party of masked men knocked at the cabin door of Sam Gaines, colored, who bears the reputation of a peaceable man, ten miles north of Springfield, within a short distance of the Kentucky line, and asked, "Gaines, are you asleep?" To which he responded, "No, but I'm in bed." Getting up in his night apparel, without asking them who called him, he opened the door, when two of the mob grabbed him, hastily dragged him a distance of fifty yards from the house, and in the presence of his wife and children shot him down. The guns were so near him as to ignite his shirt, which burned his neck and arms to a crisp. The corpse presented a ghastly sight. Five bullets from as many pistols had been sent through his body. Forty-two duckshot pierced his back, and a hole, from which a part of his liver protruded, was torn in his back. No cause could be given for the killing. Every witness examined before the coroner's jury testified that Gaines had a fair character, and no one knew of any recent difficulty in which he had been engaged. It is thought that the parties came from Kentucky, for the only altercation in which he was said to have been engaged was in Kentucky, resulting in his choking a white man nearly to death, one year ago. Gaines is the ninth man mobbed in Robertson county within the past six months.

NEARLY LYNCHED. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. NASHVILLE. Tenn., March 2.—The mystery surrounding the disappearance of Mrs. White, wife of Annias White (colored), of this city, is yet unsolved. White, who is accused of murdering the missing woman, had a preliminary examination to-day. After the testimony of a number of witnesses, which was rather strong against the prisoner, although purely circumstantial, an officer started to take White back to
Jail. Five hundred negroes, who were very indignant against White, surrounded the magistrate's office and refused to leave. Steps were taken to induce them to disperse. After consultation between the Sheriff and the magistrate, the former, aided by Constables and police, left the office with the prisoner, who was handcuffed. The crowd surged forward at the sight of the prisoner, and for several minutes matters looked serious. White appeared considerably frightened. The crowd kept pressing around the prisoner, and, believing they would take him from the guards, some one ahead of the guards gave a few military commands, which had the effect to stop the maddened throng. Those in the rear who heard the commands believing the Porter Riles were coming to the rescue fell back, but those who were close enough to the prisoner to detect the deception kept on. White was taken to the Court-House, and then to the Jail. The examination will continue to-morrow.

WELSH ESCAPES THE GALLOWS.

Columna, O., March 2.—The Governor to-day commuted the sentence of John Welsh, who was to have been hung for murder at Fremont next Friday, to imprisonment for life.

Columna, O., March 2.—The Governor to-day commuted the sentence of John Welsh, who was to have been hung for murder at Fremont next Friday, to imprisonment for life. Luke Brennan, a well-known Cleveland man, came here yesterday, and, in an interview with Gov. Foster, told a peculiar story. He said that some time ago he was on a train in which Detective John T. Norris, and a woman, who had been a mistress to Welch, and upon whose testimony he was convicted, were riding en route to Fremont for the trial, and that he overheard their conversation. He insists that he heard Norris say that he intended to hang Welch at all hazards as his reward ($1,000 offered by the County Commissioners) depended upon his conviction. Mr. Brennan makes all lavit that he heard this conversation, and declares that he believes Welch was convicted upon testimony collected by the detective to enable him to collect the proposed reward.

PADDY GUERIN.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

GALESHURG, Ill., March 2.—The trial of Paddy Guerin, the bank robber, is set for tomorrow. The defense have tried in vain to get a continuance. The indications are that the trial will be lengthy, and will draw nearly as large an attendance as the celebrated Rand murder case. The people have their case in excellent condition. Davis, one of Guerin's pals, is here, and in all probability will turn State's evidence. Jim Carroll, the leader of the gang, is now in prison in Canada, leaving the entire burden on Guerin. He will be defended by Judge Douglas, Mitchell and several other lawyers from Chicago are here, but it is not known what part they will take. State's Attorney Tunnlellif will be ably assisted.

ANOTHER TENNESSEE MURDER.

Special Dispatch in The Chicago Tribune,
NASHVILLE, Tenn., March 2.—Robertson County, in which the horrible murder of Laprade was committed, and where the lynching of his murderers was done, was last night the scene of another crime. At a late hour unknown persons went to the house of Dennis Galnes (colored), on the farm of W. F. Putterson, and called him to the door. As soon as Galnes made his appearance a volley of shots was fired at him, causing his death. It is understood that Galnes had been suspected of arson and ordered to leave the county. He left, and after resiling for a time in Kentucky came back, thus arousing theire of those who had ordered him to remain away.

KILLED BY AN OFFICER.

KILLED BY AN OFFICER.

SEDALIA, Mo., March 2.—A negro named Burnett was shot and killed by City Marshal Zelhart at Lamonte, ten miles west of here, last night. Burnett went home drunk, beat his mistress, and drove her from the house. She took refuge at a neighbor's named Chaffey. Burnett followed her with a club, and was met by Chaffee, who forbade him to enter his house. At this juncture Marshal Zelhart appeared on the scene and commanded Burnett to surrender. He refused to be arrested and advanced on Zelhart with his club. The Marshal again ordered him to surrender, but the negro still advanced in a menacing manner, when Zelhart shot him. A Coroner's jury justified the act of the Marshal.

GRAIN BROKER ARRESTED.

St. Louis, Mo., March 2.—Charles Wilde, a young man who had been doing a grain brokerage business on 'Change for a year past, was arrested to-day under an indictment charging him with obtaining money under false pretenses. It is alleged that he has been in the habit of purchasing grain for commission merchants for shipment to Baltimore at other places, and hypothecated bills of lading, raising in this way some $12,000 or more, which he has lavished on fast women, and lost speculating in bucket-shops.

KILLED IN A DRUNKEN BRAWL.
Pittsburgh, Pa., March 2.—A special from Millerstown, Butler County, Pa., says Charles Egan was murdered last night by William White in a drunken brawl. The difficulty grew out of a quarrel of two years' standing. Egan struck White, when the latter drew a knife and stabbed him twice in the abdomen and once in the thigh, causing death in seven minutes. White sought safety in flight, and has not yet been apprehended.

"NOT GUILTY."
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
Pour Huron, Mich., March 2.—In the trial of James Mulligan for the murder of Charles Howard, a verdict of "Not guilty" was reached by the jury after they had been out but an hour and a half, at 11:40 to-night.
