WIFE MURDER.
GALVESTON, March 2.—Last night, as the Monus procession was posing the English Kitchen, two shots rang out, and Mrs. Elizabeth Percival, the proprietress, fell mortally wounded by her divorced husband, Richard Stovens.

AFTER THIRTY YEARS.

AFTER THIRTY YEARS.
Columnes, O., March 2.—Gov. Foster to-day granted a pardon to Ferdinand Seltz, of Hamilton County, who was reprieved on a life sentence for murder, thirty years ago, and has spent that length of time in prison.

A DEAD DEFAULT.

A DEAD DEFAULTER. BORDENTOWN, N. J., March 2.—George W. English, City Collector, who killed himself a year ago, is found to have been a defaulter to a considerable amount.

PRIZE-FIGHTER KILLED.

PRIZE-FIGHTER KILLED.
TUCSON, Arl., March 2.—James Jourdan, a saloonkeeper, shot and mortally wounded Ben Hogan, a noted prize-fighter, at Bisbee on the 20th.

A TEXAS REFUGEE.
DENVER, Colo., March 2.—Matt Hangston, wanted at Houston, Tex., for the murder of a street-car driver, was arrested at Como to-day.

IN SELF-DEFENSE.
ALBUQUERQUE, N. M., March 1.—A miner in self-defense shot and killed a dealer of a mute game.

NORTHWESTERN BLIZZARD.

St. Paul, Minn., March 2.—A Pioneer-Press special says: Advices from Fort Dodge and Sioux City show that one of the worst storms of the season is raging thore. All the roads contering thore are blocked. There is no storm here, and the Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul trains have worked their way through, and are now running regularly. Tuesday night the St. Paul & Duluth was visited by a very severe storm of high winds and a fresh snow-fall of from four to five inches. The heaviest proportions were on the northern end of the line, the Northern Pacific Junction, 101 miles distant from St. Paul, being the storm-centre. There was no trouble on the south end of the line. The storm abated at 4 p.m. to-day. Trains were run all day. The passenger-train due at 6 p.m. was four or five hours late.

Henry Clinton, accused of having committed forgery in Trenton, N. J., was arrested in Brooklyn yesterday by Detective Philip Reilly.

Physicians in Brooklyn are to report contagious diseases hereafter to sanitary inspectors appointed to take charge of eleven sanitary districts in the city. Five new cases of diphtheria and 14 of scarlet fever were reported yesterday. Four fatal cases of diphtheria were reported.

Mrs. August Belmont and Mr. August Belmont, Jr., sailed for Europe yesterday in the Gallia.

Gotlieb Foell, 62 years of age, a retired butcher living at 137 Suffolk street, cut himself in the abdomen on Tuesday night and died yesterday morning.

Six men who had been thrown into the North River by the upsetting of a rowboat, about 11½ o'clock yesterday forenoon, were rescued by the hands on the ferryboat Communipaw.

THE Grand Jury of Christian county returned 126 indictments at a single sitting recently.

THE Democrats of Owensboro have determined to meet in convention on the 12th inst., and place a municipal ticket in the field.

It is claimed that John I. Mitchell the new Senator from Pennsylvania is anti-Cameron. The rings in Pennsylvania of late have come out second-best all round.

According to the latest report of John Sherman, Secretary of the Treasury, the decrease of the public debt in the four years since March 1, 1877, amounts to $208,824,730 27.

The Madisonville Times to-day enters on its fourteenth year with prospects bright as the sheet itself. Zeno contemplates issuing a daily soon—that is to say, in fifty years from date.

THANKS to our friend, Wallace Nall, Marion Centre, Kansas, for a copy of his local paper. We see from it that he is in the Real estate and Loan business. Wallace will not be found idle long. Though a new man there he will soon make himself known.

SAM GAINES, a negro, was shot and killed in Robertson county, Tenn., near Allensville, Ky., on the night of the 2d inst., by masked men. He had been driven off last fall for incendiaries he was charged with, and ordered not to return. He disobeyed the order and the above is the result.

GRANT is the only majority President the Republicans have ever had. Lincoln, Hayes and Garfield each failed to get a majority of the popular vote of the country. The fact is, the Democrats are stronger numerically to-day than all other parties combined, and all they lack of success is leadership and organization.

THE Lord deliver the Democrats from any more such contests as the one recently had in Clark county. Thos. G. Stuart, of the Clark County Democrat, was finally nominated for Representative, by a majority of eleven votes by the primary election held Saturday, February 26th. He will, no doubt, be elected and make a safe and efficient Representative.

THE Messenger and Examiner thinks that the municipal offices of Owensboro are in danger of being captured by the Republicans, and that in a short time. This is something that the people of Owensboro cannot afford, and it is time for them to awake to a sense of their duties to themselves and to Democratic principles by nominating a straight, strong Democratic ticket and electing it.

THE final repeal of the code duello is fast being accomplished and rightly, too, for it is nothing more nor less than murder. Col. E. B. C. Cash, of Columbia, S. C., has been indicted for murder for the killing of Wm. Shannon some time last year. True bills have also been found against the seconds and the trials are to soon follow. This is as it should be. The idea of giving respectability to murder by giving it the title of an affair of honor is ridiculous.

WE see that Hon. Clarence U. McElroy has consented to stand for re-election to the Legislature from Warren county. Mr. McElroy was one of the ablest members of the last session and is one of the brightest young men in Kentucky. He will be re-elected without trouble and will quite probably be elected Speaker, as he is well suited for the position. He has a bright future before him and it will not be long before an appreciative constituency places him in the halls of Congress.

WE direct the attention of farmers and tobacco speculators to the advertisement in this issue of the Pike Tobacco Warehouse, Louisville, Ky. Mr. Theodore McGee, late teller of the Louisville Banking Company, is now connected with this house, which is quite an addition to the already popular standing of this firm. We have known Mr. McGee long and favorably, and know him to be an elegant gentleman and a fine business man. Tobacco entrusted to this house will receive proper attention.

THE Cabinet making business since last November has engaged the time and attention of hosts of men. The agony is over and the slate made up; the nominations made and promptly confirmed by the Senate. While other newspapers were telling who would compose the Cabinet, we concluded to wait until we knew and tell our readers who did compose the Cabinet. President Garfield sent to the Senate the following nominations: Jas. G. Blaine, of Maine, Secretary of State; Wm. Windom, of Minnesota, Secretary of the Treasury; Wayne McVeagh, of Pennsylvania, Attorney-General; T. L. James, of New York, Postmaster-General; Samuel J. Kirkwood, of Iowa, Secretary of the Interior; Robert T. Lincoln, of Illinois, Secretary of War; Wm. H. Hunt, of Louisiana, Secretary of the Navy.

It is to be hoped that under the present administration we shall again have a government—not such a one as we lived under during the administration of Grant nor yet like the wishy-washy incumbency of Hayes, but a government that shall be characterized by fairness and honesty in every department, one of which we may not be ashamed, but on the other hand one that every citizen, be he Democrat or Republican, shall be proud of. After the eight years of corruption under Grant followed by the but little less hurtful four years of weakness under

Hayes, Garfield has an opportunity of distinguishing himself which few men, even among Presidents, ever enjoy. If he can bring order out of the chaos which exists in every department, restore harmony between the two great sections of our country and give us an administration free from the bitter blighting partisanship which has heretofore distinguished the Republican party, his name may well occupy a place in the temple of fame second only to that of Washington. Will he do it or will he submit to the demagogues of the party and by them be led into the follies and weaknesses of his predecessor or allow the country to be overrun by the political thieves who lurk at every corner ready to fasten themselves like leaches on the body of the nation and draw the very life-blood from its heart? Time will soon tell and in the meantime let us hope for the best.

ALL honor to the company of Boston militia who attended the recent festivities at New Orleans. After having paraded in the city for a time the marched to Greenwood cemetery—they home of so many thousands of Confederate dead—and formed a line in front of the monument erected in memory of those who fell while fighting for Dixie, and facing the statue of Gen. Lee they presented arms and adorned the bust with a shield of flowers as a tribute of respect to the great chieftain. If such a spirit of magnanimity to a fallen foe were displayed by a few more Northern people, all traces of sectionalism would be obliterated from the page of our history, and we should soon know "no North, no South, no East, no West," but only one great country, which shall be in fact as it is in song, the land of the free and the home of the brave.

MICHIGAN.

John Aulguive a Frenchman shot and killed his mother's paramour, a colored man named Lovels Green with whom she had been living at Grand Haven. Aulguive claims that Green shot his mother who was found dead in the same room and that he killed Green in revenge. It is believed that young Aulguive quarrelled with and killed both.

Otto Lang while prowling around the yard of Bowman Van Kuren at Greenville was shot by VanKuren, 70 shots taking effect in his neck causing a dangerous wound. There's a woman in the case as usual.

Voscamp, the man who murdered Lyman Cady, near Coopersville, some months ago, and who narrowly escaped lynching by an infuriated gang of Cady's neighbors, has been taken to Grand Rapids for safe-keeping.

Base Ball—Cleveland 8, Detroit 5.

Mrs. Cotton, living near the city limits of Detroit, heard a noise in her cellar, and discovering two men there, shot one of them, then looked them in and went for the police. The burglars succeeded in making their escape during her absence, but were traced some distance by a trail of blood.

Chas. Hubbard of Fenton, has lost a barn by fire, the second one within a year.

Thomas Cooper, aged 81, fell dead in the office of a Paw Paw lawyer, while he was transacting some business.

Mahon Barnbart of Union township, aged 60, a prominent citizen of Branch Co., dropped dead at his residence.

R. Kibble, a well-to-do farmer of the township of Browne, has been arrested on complaint of Rhoda Hoyt, a young woman who charges that Kibble is the father of her illegitimate child. Kibble is a married man.

Melissa Yeck, age 15, was killed at Dimondale while riding, by the horse being frightened and hacking the buggy over an embankment.

James Riley and William Burns broke out of jail at Cheboygan. They were charged with larceny. A reward of $100 is offered for their apprehension.

Two former residents of Fenton have recently shipped over 1,000 sheep from Michigan to their farms in Kansas.

The coroner's jury at Grand Haven rendered a verdict that John Alguire killed both his mother and the colored man Green; the latter by shooting him in the head with the shot gun and his mother by a blow on the back of the head with the stock of the gun, which was broken.

Prof. E. W. Wetmore of the Detroit high school resigns to accept the superintendency of the Detroit lined oil work.

Four men entered a flouring mill at Mt. Clemens and while one engaged the attention of the proprietor the others secured $40 from the money drawer. They were discovered and captured. A man fell down a well 80ft. deep at Grand Haven. The doctors are reported still in attendance.

Mrs. Miranda Smith, wife of Moses R. Smith, died at her home in Ada, Kent county, Michigan. Mrs. Smith lived in St. Clair county for many years. The "Matrimonial Aid Society of Michigan has been organized in Detroit.

Base Ball: Detroit 3, Cleveland 0.

Eighty of the Allegan County pioneers have been pioneering at Allegan.

Church, Quartermaster of the State Commissioners, has concluded arrangements with the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad Company, to carry the Governor and staff, Legislature and State troops over the Baltimore & Ohio Railroad to Washington for the Yorktown celebration, leaving Jackson and Detroit October 15, reaching Washington Sunday afternoon, remaining in Washington until Monday evening, then taking a steamer for Yorktown, returning from Yorktown Friday evening for Washington.

THE REFRIGERATING APPARATUS A SUCCESS.

WASHINGTON, July 11.—The success achieved by the refrigerating apparatus insures the uniform temperature of the sick room and adds another feature to the favorable circumstances surrounding the case. By means of a steam fan, air is blown over tons of ice, and the air comes immediately into the room, and it is possible to reduce the temperature to fifty-four degrees. This morning it is at seventy-five degrees, and the doctors have ordered the engine to run slower, as the room is cool enough. None of the other appliances will be used.

VERY LITTLE DANGER FROM SECONDARY HEMORRHAGE.

WASHINGTON, July 11.—The doctors are free to say to-day that the danger from secondary hemorrhage, if not quite past, is now very slight. Indeed, only some unforeseen accident is likely to precipitate that trouble. The doctors have the very best anti-septic dressing at hand and the most improved instruments of all kinds for any emergency. They do not expect pyemia as a direct result of the wound since the channel made by the ball is so isolated by nature as to forefend that complication. The pus corpuscles are too large for absorption into the virus, hence only an accident will produce trouble from that quarter. Thus it will be seen that the immediate danger of the presidents condition is virtually past. The healing process is progressing as far as the preliminary inflammation is concerned and all the patient needs is to have his system kept up to an improving standard, and have close watch kept on every symptom and be made as comfortable as possible. His nourishment is continued in gradually increased quantities. One or more of the physicians is constantly near him and no efforts have been spared to add to his comfort. This thorough system will be continued indefinitely and its effect in the opinion of the doctors will be the patients final recovery.

MORE "CRANKS" IN WASHINGTON.

WASHINGTON, July 11.—The name "cranks" is having a national ventilation lately. They are showing up at the capital promiscuously. The latest arrival is Matilda Bascomb (colored), who was arrested on the square fronting the White House this morning. She had been hanging around the White House grounds for some time, acting strangely and talking wildly. She was taken to the police headquarters, where she declared herself as a warm personal friend of ex-President Hayes. The latter, she maintained, was still president. Her business with him was to collect the interest every week on money loaned Mr. Hayes by her shortly after he entered upon his administration, Gen. Garfield's wound, she claims, was by no means as represented. It was only a flesh wound, but the physicians had exaggerated the case to make political capital. She was sent to the insane asylum.

Another of the same kind, Hannah D. Klunger, came to the police headquarters and inquired for directions as to how she could find the attorney-general. The woman, when questioned, said that she had been swindled by lawyers out of all her property in Bay City, Mich., and that she had name here to see the attorney-general to compel him to have it restored. She said she knew he would do it because President Garfield had refused to do what was right and had been punished and that the same would befall officials who would not listen to the cry of a distressed people. A letter to President Garfield was found amongst her baggage, which contained the clause: "I kindly ask you to send some Christian preachers to look after the wicked town of Bay City, Michigan, and reform its sinful citizens. The rest of the story was composed of attacks on Attorney-General McVeagh and President Garfield, and threats against them, mixed with mourning over the sinful lawyers of Bay City.

A still more peculiar specimen was a late caller on the police to-day. This man was a well-dressed negro and does not wish to assassinate anybody. The tables have been turned in this case, and the poor negro fears that a certain white man named Webb intends to assassinate him for expressing his admiration of the president and his hopes for his recovery. The "crank" remarked from his cell: "I don't want the man to be hung or imprisoned, but I merely want to be allowed to say what I please in regard to the president without being in danger of my life."

DR. BLISS' OPINION ON WHERE THE BULLET IS.

The physicians in the president's case seem to leave most of the talking to Dr. Bliss, but they agree with him in its general aspect and almost every particular. His latest remarks on the special features of the case have been in regard to the location of the ball.

He says there are now certain indications which make it probable that they can remove the ball without danger. "At present," says the doctor, "we deem it prudent to withhold them, but they are such as to make it clear that the track of the ball was rightly stated in the first diagnosis. We know where the ball entered the body. We have felt and developed the course of the ball so far. Where it went we do not definitely know, but from the direction of three inches of the course, which has been ascertained, it is certain that it must have flied the liver and probably passed entirely through the abdominal cavity and it is lodged in the interior wall of the abdomen. That is where I think it now, in the interior wall of the abdomen and not in the abdominal cavity. The ball entering the body where it did, and passing inward three inches, must of necessity pass through a portion of the liver. At that point of the body the liver lies close alongside of the ribs and a ball could not penetrate the body at that point and enter so great a distance and strike the liver. The liver is there and must have been hit. Even if the ball dropped downward afterward it must have grazed the liver in its downward course, but, as I said, the indications of which we have privately advised Drs. Agnew and Hamilton by letter, are that the ball went through the liver to the abdominal cavity and is lodged in the interior wall of the abdomen, as at first supposed, and it will be easy, when the time comes, to remove it from that point without danger.

During the afternoon the president has had considerable fever, but it has been the outgrowth of the inflaming process of heating the preliminaries of which has been noticeable for twenty-four hours, and is consequently not of an alarming nature. It had an increasing effect on the pulsation, respiration and temperature, but it was accompanied by no unfavorable symptoms, and caused no alarm to his physicians. It subsided a little towards night and left no bad traces. This fever was caused partially by the experiment under which the president labored while the cold air apparatus was being brought into his room. About that Confederate Treasure. August 29, 2011
ATLANTA, December 21.—The Constitution of yesterday published the following: "Few publications of late date have provoked a warmer or more general discussion than the publication of the interview with General Johnston, in which he indirectly charges that Mr. Davis in some way or another misapplied two million and a half dollars of the funds of the Confederate government. The strong tendency of the discussion was in favor of Mr. Davis, and deprecating the fact that General Johnston had seen fit to make so serious a charge even indirectly. We met no one who had any idea that Mr. Davis was responsible for these funds. In fact, the whole matter seems to be so easy of access and so plain that it is a wonder that General Johnston ever alluded to it. It is a fact generally believed, if not of actual proof, that all the wagon-train containing this treasure was robbed near Washington, in Wilkes county, Georgia, and the gold seated among the soldiers and citizens.

Mr. Hemphill, business manager of the Constitution, says:

"I was at Washington about a month after this wagon-train passed through there. It was well understood that the wagon-train had been robbed by bribing or killing the guards, or getting them drunk. I do not remember the details, but there is no doubt that the treasure-train of the Confederate government was robbed in that neighborhood. Even when I was there, there were negroes throughout the neighborhood that had large amounts of gold that came to them when the gold was scattered from the wagon-train."

Mr J. M. Maxwell, who formerly lived in Washington, says: "I know that this train was robbed, and that money belonging to the treasury of the Confederate government was taken by soldiers and citizens. There were about sixteen wagons of the bullion, containing a very large amount. They were encountered about one mile and a half from the town of Washington, and in some way or other the crowd got into the wagons, and it was a fight and scramble for the gold."

"You are certain of these facts?"

"I am certain, because I went into one of the wagons and got some of the bullion myself. I filled two large bags full of solid gold bars, but it was taken away from me before I could get away with it to a place of safety. There are hundreds of men who escaped with these bars, and it formed the basis of many a fortune in Georgia. These facts you can get from any citizen of Washington who was there at the time. My testimony is not second-hand, as I told you."

ABOUT AND FOR WOMEN.

Dom Pedro and his wife are expected in Paris in January.

The Princess of Wales has just passed her thirty-seventh birthday. Maud, her youngest child, is twelve.

The wife of Mr. John W. Guiteau is reported to be a sister of Ex-Assistant Postmaster-General Tyner.

The report that Senator David Davis was about to marry his deceased wife's sister is contradicted. Mrs. Davis's two sisters are both married already.

The widow of Emile de Girardin is said to be dying from the abuse of morphine. She cannot sleep, and lies day and night on a sofa praying for death. The woman who was so beautiful eleven ago is now a piteous wreck.

The hereditary Prince of Monaco, the unimportant sovereign from whom Lady Mary Hamilton was divorced a few years ago, is to be married, it is said, to the Duchess of Richelieu, who was in her youth Miss Heine, of New Orleans.

Senator Hampton laughs at the story that his daughter "will soon make her debut on the stage." She has no ambition in that line, and the idea of becoming an actress never occurred to her until she saw a newspaper announcement that she already was one.

Miss Edith Stanley, a daughter of the popular baritone, Mr. Charles Stanley, has made a very successful dbut. Mr. Stanley can now call check to Mr. Sims Reeves, our other representative vocalist, whose son, Mr. Herbert Reeves, has been for some time before the public.

A leading merchant of Louisville refused to buy a sealskin sacque for his daughter. The next day she left the house, and when night came she did not return. For two weeks all efforts to discover her were unavailing, but the detectives employed in the case at length learned that she was employed as a domestic servant, under an assumed name. She refused to return home until her parent promised to get her the sacque.

Miss A. Dyckman, a cabin passenger on board the steamship Nederland, from Autwerp, was so alarmed by the storms encountered during the last voyage that she refused to take any food, and finally died from exhaustion. She came from Brussels and was going to Philadelphia. The Nederland was twenty-two days on the voyage, and most of the time the passengers were confined in the cabin, as the decks were almost constantly under water.

Queen Caroline, of Saxony, is suffering from an illness which is attributed to a cause unusual in royal households. Her Majesty has a mania for cooking, in which she excels, especially in the preparation of fruit preserves. The crop of fruit in Saxony was this year so abundant that the Queen labored night and day in the composition of her jams and jellies, which she was, of course, obliged to taste constantly. The consequent fatigue and indigestion brought on a serious illness.

WEDNESDAY, December 28, : : : 1881.

R. MEANS DAVIS, EDITOR.
GNO. S. REYNOLDS, ASSOCIATE EDITOR.

RIDDLEBERGER has been elected Senator from Virginia. He will act with Mahone, his friends say, going into neither caucus.

The system for local taxation for schools, known as the Winnsboro plan, is gradually working its way in the State. A bill has been introduced to provide for local taxation in the City of Greenville. This shows the awakening influence of last summer's Normal Institute.

SPEAKER KEIFER has put all his brother Stalwarts into fat places on the House committees. Half-breeds and Democrats alike take a back seat—much to the disgust of the former. The programme will be stalwart all the way through. Determined efforts will be made to unseat Democrats in all contested cases. If the Democratic minority permits this, it deserves to suffer.

INFORMATION has been received that the missing Arctic steamer Jeannette was crashed in the ice off the northern coast of Siberia in June last. Two boat-loads of her crew, headed by Captain DeLong and Engineer Melville, arrived safely on land after much suffering. The third boat has not been heard from. The Jeannette was filled up by Bennett, and several other explorers have recently been sent to look after her.

GENERAL Joe Johnston makes the grave charge that when the Confederate Government left Richmond it carried off specie to the amount of two and a half million dollars. General Johnston says that Mr. Davis is responsible for it, and has never explained its disappearance. The trouble is that General Johnston is somewhat billious as regards the ex-President. We do not believe that any such sum existed, and do not for an instant believe that it was taken by Mr. Davis, according to the News Courier, borrowed a hundred dollars from a member of his cabinet in leaving Richmond. The capture of Mr. Davis and his incarceration in Fortress Monroe, effectually acquits him of any participation in the theft if any was committed. The truth is doubtless that the amount was much exaggerated, that what money was brought down was "seized" by different parties at the time of the collapse, and that nobody was made rich.

Mr. Hemphill, business manager of the Atlanta Constitution, says:

"I was at Washington, Georgia, about a month after this wagon passed through there. It was well understood that the wagon train had been robbed by bribing or killing the guards or getting them drunk. I do not remember the details, but there is no doubt that the treasure train of the Confederate Government was robbed in that neighborhood. Even when I was there, there were negroes throughout the neighborhood, that had large amounts of gold that came to them when the gold was scattered from the wagon train."

Mr. J. M. Maxwell, who formerly lived in Washington, says: "I know that this train was robbed, and that money belonging to the treasury of the Confederate Government was taken by soldiers and citizens. There were about sixteen wagons of the bullion, containing a very large amount. They were encountered about one mile and a half from the town of Washington, and in some way or other the crowd got into the wagons, and it was a fight and scramble for the gold."

"You are certain of these facts?"

"I am certain, because I went into one of the wagons and got some of the bullion myself. I filled two large bags full of solid gold bars, but it was taken away from me before I could get away with it to a place of safety. There are hundreds of men who escaped with these bars, and it formed the basis of many a fortune in Georgia. These facts you can get from any citizen of Washington who was there at the time. My testimony is not secondhand, for as I told you, I was then a boy, and went with a crowd that went into the wagons and took out the specie."

There is other testimony corroborative of this, and we have no doubt that this is the explanation of the matter. The idea that Mr. Davis in some way or other secreted any large amount of gold is simply absurd. He was taken to prison from Washington, and since the war he has been living in poverty.

It is believed by many about Washington that there was much gold buried in that neighborhood by some parties who had charge of the Confederate treasury, and a short time ago a negro barber of that village, who stated that he knew where the gold was buried, was taken out and whipped nearly to death by men who insisted on his telling them where it was.

JAMESTOWN, N. Y., Dec. 3.—Mattie M. Blanchard, age twelve, died this morning from, it is supposed, an overdose of morphine, alleged to have been given on a prescription calling for quinine.

SELMA, Ala., Dec. 3.—On tuesday night a difficulty occurred at Rehobeth, Ala., between Captain Daniel Jones, of Mobile, and Max and Morris Michaels, in the course of which Jones was fatally stabbed. He died last night.

MURDERED BY A NEGRO.
FORTRESS MONROE, Va., Dec. 3.—A white man named William Selater, residing on the Bowman Farm, four miles north of Newport News, was murdered last night by a negro named William Allen, who stabbed him through the heart. Allen was arrested.

SHOT IN THE HEAD.
BOSTON, Dec. 3.—On Friday evening two colored men, Alfred Giles and Edward Stewart, living in Squantum Village, Quincy, Mass., had a dispute at their boarding-house, when Stewart, it is alleged, drew a revolver and shot Giles in the head, the ball lodging in the roof of his mouth. His condition is critical.
william-allen-warwick-court-house-1881-1.A5:
A Mule Dispute, Murder, and Lynching.
FORT MONROE, Dec. 6.—William Selater was murdered by William Allen, a negro, on Friday evening. The affair took place at the Bowman farm, four miles north of Newport News. Selater lived in the same house with two brothers named Kelly. All worked on the railroad. The Kellys hired Allen to take them to and from their work daily, they furnishing a wagon, while he furnished a mule. Allen had a grudge against Selater because the latter had accused him of stealing an axe. On Friday evening the Kellys invited Selater to ride home in their wagon. Allen said that his mule should not draw the wagon if Selater was in it. There was an altercation, and Allen became very angry with Selater, who had to walk home. Meanwhile Allen had driven ahead, and, when Selater reached the house, he attacked him, stabbing him three times, one thrust reaching the heart. The murderer was at once seized by the Kellys, and was sent to jail at Warwick Court House. Last night a party of masked men took him out and hanged him.

The much-talked-of Dobler-Rowell walking match in Chicago proved a complete failure. At 12:40 o'clock, when Rowell had completed 23 miles, Dobler claimed to be considerably hurt by an encounter with a drunken fellow and left the track. He did not return, and Rowell was declared winner at 1:47 after making 35 miles.

Counsel for the defendant applied for a new trial, and a stay of thirty days was given.

Another infernal machine has been found in Montreal at the court house. It had gone off, but apparently without doing any injury. The lads who brought it to the police station say it was lying beside the first machine found by them when they removed the latter, but a man who was present told them not to disturb it.

Wm Neal, colored, charged with brute outrage, has been acquitted in Wilmington. The jury stood 11 for conviction and 1 for acquittal. As the judge had convinced the jury that they would be confined until a verdict should be reached, even if it took a year, the eleven gave into the one stubborn man. Neal was convicted of the crime last May and sentenced to be hanged. The verdict was overruled by the United States supreme court on the ground that no colored men were allowed to serve on Delaware juries and a second trial was ordered. FORTRESS MONROE, VIRGINIA, December 6.—Henry Jones, a prominent citizen of Warwick county, arrived in Hampton this evening, and reports that William Allen, the colored man who killed William S. william-allen-warwick-court-house-1881-1.A15:
Lynching of a Negro Murderer.
It will be remembered that on the night of December 2, a white man named William Sclater was stabbed and instantly killed by a negro named William Allen, on Sclater's farm, near Newport News, Va. Allen was promptly arrested and committed to the County Jail, and on the night of the 5th lust. a party of Sclater's friends, having forged a mittimus, which purported to have come from Justice Post, directing the removal of the prisoner to a jail in an adjoining county, presented themselves to the jailer, who, supposing the order genuine, delivered the prisoner to the men. They took him about a mile from the jail and lynched him. None of the parties to the affair are known to the authorities.
william-allen-warwick-court-house-1881-1.A18: A SERIOUS CHARGE.—Yesterday Thomas Valentine, a white barber, whose place of business is at No. 214 west Broad street, was arrested by Constable Harris, of Elizabeth City county, on a warrant charging him with being engaged in the lynching of William Allen (colored), which occurred near Newport News about a week ago. Allen was confined in the Warwick county jail for the murder of William Selater (white), whom he stabbed to death on the 2d instant. At the time of the lynching Allen was being transferred from the Warwick jail to Hampton, the order for his transfer being forged in order that the lynchers might get hold of the prisoner with less trouble. At the time the lynching took place Valentine had a barber-shop at Hampton.

STAUNTON SPECTATOR AND GENERAL ADVERT
PARDON OF LUCIEN BEARD — On last Thursday, Lucien Beard, the noted, horse-thief was pardoned by Gov. Holiday. The State says that "gentlemen who have felt an interest in his case have for a long time been making great efforts to secure his release, as the circumstances connected with his arrest were particularly touching.

While Beard's case was pending before the Supreme Court on an appeal he effected his escape from the city jail. Nothing was heard of him for a year or more when information was conveyed to this city that he was follwying the peaceful pursuit of a farmer in Saline county, Missouri, having with him his wife. He was known out there as a quiet citizen. Gov. Walker issued his requisition for him and appointed Detective Pat Woods to bring him to Virginia. Beard was arrested and brought back. He was sent to the penitentiary for eighteen years for horse-stealing in Prince Edward county, and has served eight or nine years. As a prisoner he always stood well and each Superintendent has expressed the wish to have him pardoned.

'A LIQUOR SELLER ABSCONDS. About a mouth since Jessee Call commenced selling liquor illegally in Greenbrier Co., W. Va., across the river from Alderson, Monroe county. On Friday week, he was summoned to appear for trial before Justice Robert McVay of Greenbrier, whereupon he absconded. The Alderson Enterprise says that "the court proceeded, however, to hear the testimony which elicited twelve cases of selling. Warrants were issued at once for the arrest of Mr. Call and if he be found in the State, he will be arrested and brought before the Greenbrier justice and be required to give bond for his appearance to answer the action of the Grand Jury."

COLLIDED WITH A TRAIN.—The Winchester Times says that on last Tuesday "morning about daylight, Mr. J. Vance Bell's team, driven by Mr. Lewis, collided with the Harrisonburg train on the Millwood road crossing. Mr. Lewis was thrown over a fence, one of his ears nearly cut off, and he was severely bruised. The wagon was demolished, and one of the horses very severely injured. The train stopped as soon as possible and backed to the scene of the accident, where the train hands rendered all the assistance to their power to Mr. Lewis. Dr. Miller attended to his injuries."

RIDDLEBERGER TO BE SENATOR — At the caucus of the Coalition party on last Tuesd y night, Riddleberger was nominated without opposition, in obeience to the will of the Boss, Mahone, and to day he will be accordingly elect ed as Mahone's colleague in the United States Senate, so that Mahone will prac tically have two votes which he can cast at his will in favor of the Republi can party, and the Democratic Readjusters who voted with the Coalition party may bite their thumbs in vain rage.

ARRESTED AS A LYNCHER.—Thos Valentine, white, a barber, was arrested in Richmond Wednesday, on a warrant charging him with having been one of a party of men who week before last took Wm. Allen, colored, from the Warwick county jail and lynched him. Allen was awaiting trial for the murder of Wm. Selater, whom he stabbed to death in an affray at Newport News. Valentine kept a barbershop in Hampton at the time of the killing of Selater. He will be taken to Elizabeth City county jail.

LYNCHING IN NEVADA.—About half-past one o'clock Wednesday morning a party of masked men forcibly entered the jailer's room in the court-house building at Austin, Nevada, overpowered the jailer and forced him to give up the keys to the jail and the cell door where Richard Jennings was confined, who, without provocation and in cold blood, shot and killed John A. Barrett, an old and respected citizen, Monday night of last week. Jennings was then taken out and hanged from a balcony over the front door.

SAD DEATH.—We learn from the Alleghany Tribune that Geo. A. Kyle, aged 28 years, the only child and son of Edwin and Emma Kyle, died on Saturday, December 11th, 1881, at 11 o'clock, at the residence of his parents near Saltpetre Cave, in Botetourt county, Va. He was attacked with pneumonia and survived only eight days.

His remains were taken to Alleghany county, and were buried in the old family burrying ground of his grandfather, John Mallow, on Tuesday, the 13th inst.

FALL FROM A ROOF.—We learn from the Shenandoah Valley that, on Friday week, while Mr. Jacob Gochenour was putting on a roof on Mrs. J. D. Zirkle's house in New Market, "when at the comb of the roof, he slipped, sliding down the roof, and lit on his feet, or toes rather on the pavement—the perpendicular hight through which he passed was about 25 feet. Strange to say, he was not seriously hurt. He is yet confined to the house by soreness about the balls of his feet."

Skaggs and Burdett, was broken into and $30 in money, several overcoats, hats and other goods stolen therefrom. The thief or thieves gained access to the store by boring an auger hole in one of the shutters, directly opposite the inside fastening, and by that means succeeded in opening the shutters and gaining entrance.

McMullan, died unexpectedly, from a relapse from typhoid fever, from which she seemed to be recovering. THE ASSASSINATION OF THE CZAR.
It has already been stated in the cable dispatches that three policemen were tried at St. Petersburg and convicted of negligence in having failed to discover the plot to assassinate the Czar Alexander in time to prevent it from being carried out. They were each sentenced to three years exile in New Archangel. This would be a very severe punishment for an ordinary case of inefficiency or negligence, but it seems that these men were absent from their appointed post of duty on the morning of the 13th of March, and they may possibly have been privy to the conspiracy. One of the conspirators, Emilianoff by name, has given a detailed account of the incidents of the assassination. He and his three companions came to the quay of the canal and took their places without seeing a single policeman. When the Czar appeared the first one, and then the second, threw his bomb. When Emilianoff saw the Czar reel and fall he ran and seized him in his arms and supported him until other help came, and then he assisted in lifting the dying man into a sleigh. None of the police dared to come near the explosion. While Emilianoff was performing these offices of kindness he had the bomb concealed under his arm which he intended to throw if the others had not proved effective.

wilson-calder-edisto-island-1881-07-01.A1:
MULISH JURORS.
Complications Growing Out of the Edisto Trouble.
the correspondent of the Savannah News, who has just returned from the scene of the reported troubles on Edisto Island, reports that quiet has been restored, although the body of the dead man has not yet been interred, and a perfect understanding and peace will not take place until an inquest is held. The negroes believe that the dead man died from the effects of injuries received by him in a scuffle with a white boy, which is not probable, and asked that an autopsy be made. The physician was ready to make the autopsy, but could not do it without the order of the Deputy Coroner, who refused to order it. The negroes on the jury thereupon refused to agree to a verdict or to bury the body, which still lies in the open air.

A great many of the whites attribute the blame of the excitement to the Deputy Coroner, who does not seem to know his business. The whole matter could be settled by the sending down of a Deputy Coroner to hold an inquest after an autopsy, and it is hoped that this will be done. When the correspondent left the island this noon the negroes were at work as usual, and there were no signs of a disturbance, although an uneasy feeling prevails.

The cause of the trouble, as told by the constable, is that on the 1st instant Mr. Marlon Seabrook and his brother, Mr. Harry Seabrook, sons of Mr. Edward W. Seabrook, got into a difficulty with the negro Wilson Calder, who used such language towards them that Mr. Marlon Seabrook struck him with his fist. A regular fisticuff ensued in which it appears that Mr. Harry Seabrook picked up a brick, but did not use it. The next day Calder went about his work as usual and ploughed in the field all day with out complaining of any ill effects from the fight. On the night of the 2d instant, when he went home, he is said to have eaten a potful of parboiled hominy, and the next morning he died.

Mr. Seabrook Whaley organized a Coroner's jury, consisting of seven white men and five negroes and started to hold the inquest. The negroes, became very much excited and claimed that the man had been killed by Mr. Seabrook during the fight on the 1st instant. Ten witnesses were examined, including Dr. Murray, who held an external examination of the body, and who testified that there were no marks of violence on the body, except a bad burn between the shoulders, which it was proved the deceased had recently received by falling into the fire during an epileptic fit, to which disease he was subject.

The negroes, however, were not satisfied with the doctor's testimony, and insisted that the jury should bring in a verdict of willful murder. This, of course, the jury refused to do, and the negroes then refused to allow the body to be buried until it was opened and an examination made to discover if there were any internal injuries. Dr. Murray, it appears, was not well and insisted that the opening of the body was entirely useless. The negroes then became more violent, and the jury dispersed without arriving at a result.

The crops on the island are better than they have ever been known to be before at this time of the year.

NOTES FROM CHARLESTON.
The Edisto Trouble-An Autopsy Held and an Inquest in Progress- A Colored Lathario's Shortcomings.
CHARLESTON, S. C., July 11.—Information has been received from Edisto that the Coroner has empannelled a new jury of inquest on the body of the negro Wilson Calder, and that after an autopsy had been held, the body, which had been allowed by the negroes to remain above ground for a week, was buried. The jury met today to hear the evidence and the result of the post mortem. No further trouble is apprehended. If the negrges interfere with the inquest they will be arrested.

The Rev. G. S. Wellons, a Baptist preacher among the colored people, who is supposed to have left his wife and three children in Dallas, Texas, several years ago and eloped with a woman named Rowland, with whom he came to Charleston, has disappeared. He is supposed to be the Rev. G. T. Wilburn, who went from Americus, Ga., in 1873 to Dallas. He came here in 1878. Wellons left some weeks ago, and the woman followed him. Their destination is not known.

The total Irish population has decreased as follows, 1881, 5,160,000; 1871, 5,411,000; 1861, 5,798,000; 1851, 6,552,000; 1841, 8,-175,000.

Ex- Congressman R. B. Elliott, of South Carolina, is now a special Treasury agent, with an office in the New Orleans custom-house.

—A woman's Christian Temperance Union was organized in the colored Methodist church at Walhalla, S. C., recently, with eighty-five members.

—The exports of cotton from Savannah, Ga., to continental ports since September 1st, has been 266,878 bales, against 220,990 for same time last year.

—Silas M. Waite, President of the Brattleboro' National Bank, is serving a term in the Vermont penitentiary for misappropriation of fiduciary funds.

—There is one case of yellow fever on board of a vessel at the quarantine station at Pensacola. The quarantine regulations are being vigorously enforced.

—The arrivals of immigrants in New York during 1880 exceeded those of any previous year, but the first six months of 1881 this year, is 64,513 ahead of last year.

—The Governor has appointed twenty-six of the most prominent citizens of the State to represent South Carolina at the Atlanta Cotton Exposition, as Vice-Presidents.

—Chauncey DePew has withdrawn from the senatorial contest at Albany. The Republican nominees are Warren Miller and Elbridge D. Lapham. Conkling still remains firm.

—The Marquas & Son's carriage factory, and the adjoining buildings, in Cincinnati, were destroyed by fire on July 8th. Twenty-four lives were lost. Pecuniary loss over $1,000,000.

—The Chamber of Commerce, of New York, has presented $250,000 to Mrs. Garfield, to relieve the mind of the President entirely from anxiety of the future support of his family.

—The Coroner of Charleston County was prevented from holding an inquest over the dead body of a negro, on Edisto Island, who had been burned to death in his cabin, on account of the wild excitement of the negro inhabitants.
